Title: Russian APT29 Targets Mobile Users with Watering Hole Attacks
Context: “It remains unclear whether the attackers intended to target visitors to specific websites or sought to compromise as many unpatched mobile devices as possible, indiscriminately...
Full Text:
Russia-linked group APT29 targeted iOS and Android users through hijacked websites and a compromised analytics service.

Sekoia says a large-scale watering hole campaign is going after iOS and Android users, and it links the campaign to APT29 (aka SVR group, Cozy Bear, Nobelium, BlueBravo, Midnight Blizzard, and The Dukes), the Russian group tied to the SVR foreign intelligence service. A watering hole is a site that attackers poison so visitors infect themselves.

Sekoia found the campaign in mid-October 2026. It involved hacked or cloned high-profile websites in the US, Ukraine, the Czech Republic and Bulgaria. There’s also a supply-chain attack on a Ukrainian web analytics service, Plerdy, loaded by thousands of websites, most of them Ukrainian.

The attackers used three different methods to reach victims, but all led to the same malicious payload. They injected JavaScript into hacked websites, created fake websites that copied legitimate ones and secretly added malicious code, and compromised the Plerdy analytics service to infect websites using its script.

Sekoia first spotted the campaign on the website of a Ukrainian gas production company. Other compromised sites included a major US chemical industry association, a European far-right political party and a Bulgarian website linked to the military. In the Bulgarian case, attackers modified an existing JavaScript library without changing the website’s visible pages. Researchers found no clear pattern in the targeted organizations, although they believe some websites may have been selected to reach specific individuals.

Sekoia also identified two fake websites designed to impersonate legitimate services. One copied America250, the US initiative marking the country’s 250th anniversary, while another reproduced the website of Raffles London at The OWO, a luxury hotel close to the UK Ministry of Defence and Downing Street.

“The second website, theowo[.]club, now offline, acted as a reverse proxy for the website of Raffles London at The OWO, a prestigious luxury hotel housed in the historic Old War Office building.” reads the report published by Sekoia. “The hotel’s location is particularly noteworthy because of its proximity to some of the United Kingdom’s most sensitive government institutions, including the Ministry of Defence and 10 Downing Street, the official residence and office of the British Prime Minister.”

The hotel connection is particularly interesting because Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky reportedly stayed there during a visit to London on October 14. Sekoia believes the fake website may have been used to target diplomatic delegations through spear-phishing, but stresses that this remains an unconfirmed possibility.

Between August 27 and September 3, 2026, the attackers compromised the Plerdy tracker at a.plerdy[.]com. For a week, visitors loaded both Plerdy’s script and the attackers’ profiling script. Several affected sites relate to the military and military recruitment, including army, special forces and military equipment websites.

“Between 27 August and 3 September 2026, the intrusion set compromised the Ukrainian Plerdy analytics tracker hosted under the domain a.plerdy[.]com, which is loaded by thousands of websites, the large majority of them Ukrainian.” reads the report. “It remains unclear whether the attackers intended to target visitors to specific websites or sought to compromise as many unpatched mobile devices as possible, indiscriminately exfiltrating data before selectively identifying and exploiting information of interest.”

Sekoia can’t say whether the aim was specific visitors or as many unpatched phones as possible, with the sorting done later. It also considers that the attackers may have used Plerdy after failing to inject code directly into Ukrainian high-value sites that relied on it. The Plerdy payload pointed to a load-balancing domain that sent traffic across several delivery servers.

The profiling script, which the attackers call UltimateFingerprinter, is attached to a minified AngularJS library that makes up 98 percent of a 2.3 MB file. Sekoia thinks that bulk might stop analysis by large language models, or make the script look legitimate. The script runs 61 collectors that build 394 fields, then sends them to a server that decides whether to answer with exploit code.

Strangely, almost none of that data matters. Only implausible screen sizes, like 99999, or a device reporting zero touch points block delivery. Sekoia doesn’t know why the attackers collect so much and sees no sign the data was used later.

Sekoia pulled three exploit chains from the delivery server. Class A hits iOS 16.7 and steals cookies. Class B hits iOS 18.5 and takes full device data. Class C hits Android Chrome versions 139 to 145, minus 143 for reasons Sekoia can’t explain, and steals Chrome cookies and Wi-Fi passwords.

“During the investigation, we tested different browser profiles against the fingerprinting endpoint at static[.]flux-telemetry[.]com in order to retrieve the exploits served to visitors.” states the report. “This allowed us to retrieve three complete exploit chains (afternamed A, B and C), along with their final payloads, targeting both Android and iOS. Here is a summary of what we found:”

Class B is DarkSword, which Sekoia describes as a suspected iOS exploit kit from a commercial surveillance vendor, uploaded to VirusTotal in September 2026. It takes text messages and iMessages, Mail indexes, voicemail, WhatsApp and Telegram databases, Keychain passwords and tokens, account credentials and Wi-Fi keys. It also takes contacts, call history, calendar, notes, Safari history and cookies, location caches, Health data, photos and iCloud Drive.

The Android payload, which Sekoia calls AndroSnitch, collects Chrome cookies, saved logins and history, plus Wi-Fi settings. It stops on one phone model, the Samsung Galaxy S25 Ultra. It resembles a 2024 payload that Google TAG documented, called AndroSnatch, but the sample is too small to prove lineage. The iOS cookie chains set a marker cookie meant to block reinfection for a day, but a coding mistake makes it expire in a minute.

All stolen data goes to ad.starx-net[.]com:8881/telemetry/v12. None of the chains persist on the device. All of them rely on known flaws, and none uses a zero-day.

For attribution, Sekoia has several threads. A CERT said a compromised site’s backend files held traces matching a private report on a 2025 APT29 watering hole campaign, and Google TAG said the framework resembles an APT29 campaign against Mongolian government websites in 2024. Victims also skew to Europe and the US with a focus on Ukraine, infrastructure sits across multiple hosters, and a hacked Czech far-right site fits APT29’s record of targeting European political parties. It rates the link moderate to high confidence, and it’s coordinating with the CERTs of affected countries.

The campaign shows how exploit kits move down the market. Sekoia says state-backed groups keep reusing frameworks from commercial surveillance vendors such as DarkSword, and that packaged exploit chains lower the cost and skill needed for advanced mobile attacks. It expects such reuse to become more frequent.

The good news is that Sekoia’s attackers don’t have fresh tricks. Every flaw was fixed by its vendor before the campaign began, and none works against fully updated devices.

“None of them contain zero-days or work against fully updated devices. Each flaw was resolved by the respective vendor before this campaign began. This operation targets unpatched devices using n-days; a user running an up-to-date operating system is safe from these attacks.” concludes the report.

“This watering hole campaign, which we assess with moderate to high confidence to be linked to APT29, combines multiple web delivery vectors with n-day mobile exploit chains targeting Android and iOS devices. Across the directly compromised websites, no single sectoral targeting pattern emerges from our analysis. While the victimology shows a focus on Ukraine and the United States, the inclusion of unrelated entities such as an Australian medical clinic complicates a broad strategic interpretation. However, we assess that these websites may have been selected to profile and infect specific individuals of interest based on targeting intelligence to which we do not have visibility. The operators adapted by deploying Adversary-in-the-Middle-ish to intercept visitors associated with diplomatic or high-profile events.”

Follow me on Twitter: @securityaffairs and Facebook and Mastodon

Title: The SOC Files 5: Ghost in the pipeline, or a fileless SharePoint breach by Storm-2603
Context: Executive summary In 2025, several threat actors exploited CVE-2025-53770 and CVE-2025-53771 (ToolShell vulnerabilities) in on-premises Microsoft SharePoint to achieve remote...
Full Text:
Executive summary

In 2025, several threat actors exploited CVE-2025-53770 and CVE-2025-53771 (ToolShell vulnerabilities) in on-premises Microsoft SharePoint to achieve remote code execution through crafted HTTP requests. One of the threat actors deployed ransomware on the target’s systems after successful exploitation. Microsoft attributed this ransomware-related ToolShell activity to Storm-2603, distinguishing it from other actors whose observed activity was primarily focused on credential theft, espionage, and data exfiltration.

In December, our retrospective analysis identified activity consistent with Storm-2603’s TTPs. This activity involved the attacker using the IIS worker process as an in-memory bridge to the customer’s infrastructure, keeping the access and control layer entirely within w3wp.exe without writing anything to disk. Although subsequent post-exploitation activity generated disk artifacts, the bridge used to maintain access remained memory-resident.

Let’s look in more detail at this attack.

The attack chain, from reconnaissance to infrastructure compromise

Intrusion timeline: Strategic latency and exploitation

The intrusion analyzed in this report occurred in two stages, with a temporal gap between initial access and subsequent exploitation activity. The attack timeline was as follows:

Dec 20 – Vulnerability fingerprinting: A single HTTP request targeted a SharePoint administrative endpoint associated with the ToolPane component to determine whether the host was vulnerable to CVE-2025-53770.

Dec 21-23 – Tactical latency: A three-day period of silence followed the initial probe, separating the vulnerability fingerprinting from subsequent malicious activity and potentially reducing the likelihood of immediate detection.

Dec 24 – High-intensity re-engagement: On Christmas Eve, when security staffing at many companies is reduced, the full RCE chain was executed through the IIS worker process (w3wp.exe) on the same endpoint as the initial probe.

Dec 26 – Incident discovery: The three-day gap initially prevented the December 20 probe from being correlated with subsequent malicious activity, marking the event as low priority. Retrospective analysis established that the probe was the initial phase of the subsequent intrusion.

Intrusion timeline

Initial access validation phase

Vulnerability fingerprinting

A vulnerability fingerprinting request on December 20 marked the first observed interaction with the target. The request originated from infrastructure associated with ONYPHE, an internet-scale attack surface discovery and management platform for identifying exposed assets, vulnerabilities, and cyberthreats. Unlike widely used tools such as Shodan and Censys, which merely provide a list of internet-facing assets correlated with the open-source data about known vulnerabilities, ONYPHE actually checks if the target system is vulnerable.

Fingerprinting with ONYPHE

The request characteristics were consistent with ONYPHE’s vulnerability checks, which use active, non-intrusive probes to identify internet-exposed systems vulnerable to specific CVEs. For ToolShell, ONYPHE adopted the approach used by Niels Hofmans (hazcod). Namely, it attempts to inject a harmless marker into the target server to find out if it is vulnerable.

OFFICIAL ONYPHE CVE CHECKER (TOOLSHELL)

This phase served as a validation step against the SharePoint execution surface exposed over HTTP:

The target processed structured requests through the ASP.NET pipeline without rejection.

The request path reached application logic capable of handling serialized input.

No defensive controls interrupted or altered the execution flow at the application boundary.

Approximately 12 minutes later, a second inbound connection originated from infrastructure associated with Pfcloud UG, a provider operating under a bulletproof hosting (BPH) model. Given the timing and the IP’s documented history of scanning and abusive activity, the connection may represent follow-on reconnaissance against the newly identified target. No exploitation was attempted at this stage.

A connection from an IP address belonging to Pfcloud UG BPH

Active exploitation: Santa took your data and left a backdoor

The main malicious activity occurred on December 24. The actor targeted the same SharePoint host with a crafted request from 45.91.94.204 (45.91.92.0/22, ASN 63473, HostHatch, LLC). This resulted in a webshell execution within the IIS worker process (w3wp.exe). The payload was not written to disk; rather, it was loaded directly into the ASP.NET runtime and used during subsequent request processing. The implant remained resident for the lifetime of the affected application domain. This runtime state was lost when the application pool was recycled or IIS was restarted.

Attack originated from an SPN node

The IP address 45.91.94.204 is a Safing Privacy Network (SPN) node. SPN routes each connection through a multilayer VPN path with multiple relay nodes that can obscure the originating IP.

SPN promotes itself as a network that offers strong privacy protection for internet traffic. Its infrastructure resembles Tor’s in many ways, but with some differences. It features the following capabilities:

Speed: Near-VPN performance for high-speed data transfer.

Layer 3 support: Supports multiple protocols like TCP, UDP, ICMP (unlike Tor, which only supports TCP).

App-routing: Direct tunneling without a browser.

Multi-identity: Simultaneous exit nodes to bypass IP rate limits.

Fixed-size packets and padding make it harder to analyze its traffic.

It is less common than Tor, and frequently bypasses standard Tor blocklists.

Webshell architecture

The webshell the attackers injected into the w3wp.exe runtime is a multi-module in-memory framework, where execution is orchestrated through the main component (G.cs) and extended via multiple functional units across namespaces.

The implementation follows a modular C# project structure in which each capability is isolated into its own compilation unit and invoked dynamically at runtime.

Webshell components

“G.cs” pipeline control and C2

Pipeline control

The main webshell component is G.cs. It orchestrates the implant’s execution context, lifecycle, C2 and session management.

To ensure persistence within the runtime, G.cs performs the following actions:

Registers a custom VirtualPathProvider using the non-public RegisterVirtualPassProviderInternal method from the ASP.NET HostingEnvironment class so that ASP.NET uses it for virtual-path processing. The provider is automatically added to the chain of registered virtual path providers.

Delegates the provider’s .NET Remoting lifetime policy to the previous provider in the chain, preserving the existing lifetime behavior.

Additionally, to evade defenses and enable the VirtualPathProvider to be registered even if the application in whose AppDomain the webshell is running is precompiled, the module implements the trust control subversion (T1553) technique:

Uses reflection to check if the application is precompiled.

Extracts pointers for internal state fields for the BuildManager class, which manages application compilation, and modifies them at runtime.

Uses reflection once again to force runtime injection.

G.cs uses the GetCacheKey() function as the interception point for the virtual path processing flow. It processes incoming requests to the SharePoint server and checks their headers to filter out requests from the attacker.

The specific User-Agent in the request headers triggers the webshell execution. If the request doesn’t match this condition, the implant remains dormant, making its traffic harder to recognize.

Command and control layer (in-memory transport)

The same core module (G.cs) implements the communication layer.

Instead of relying on external frameworks or standard beacons, it uses a custom binary protocol with XOR-based obfuscation to exchange data with the C2. These communications blend into normal application traffic. The module uses the GetCacheKey() hook to intercept standard HTTP requests. When a specific User-Agent is detected in the request headers, the module parses it, extracts the payload, and establishes a TCP connection to a target host inside the target’s network if needed.

Bidirectional TCP tunnel initialization

G.cs establishes a full-duplex proxy tunnel to support interactive control. It stores active target sockets in memory to pair concurrent HTTP read and write channels.

TCP connections from the C2 server to arbitrary hosts inside the target network are supported for pivoting and lateral movement. The traffic is proxied through the SharePoint host.

Target-to-attacker data channel

Attacker-to-target data channel

As can be seen in the screenshots, the attackers used the suo5 tool to implement traffic proxying. Its authors promote it as a stable forward-proxying tool for scenarios where outbound internet connections are prohibited.

To increase its performance, G.cs manipulates ThreadPool by raising its limits for concurrent operations and maximum timeout.

ThreadPool manipulation

“Prog.cs”: Execution entry point and task dispatcher

Prog.cs is the entry point that receives command-line arguments and passes them to uk/London.cs. The latter acts as the orchestrator, handling command parsing and privilege escalation (via named pipe impersonation). We’ll review it in more detail later. If the “suo5” command is provided, London.cs triggers G.cs to hook into the ASP.NET runtime as a memory shell. Once active, G.cs independently processes incoming web traffic inside the web server memory.

Host interaction modules

The following modules provide direct system interaction capabilities, each implemented as a separate unit. London.cs triggers these modules when it receives a corresponding command from Prog.cs.

“FileDownloader.cs”

The FileDownloader.cs module downloads arbitrary files from external URLs provided by the C2. It stores the downloaded files in the Program Data directory without any user interaction.

“LoggedOnUsers.cs”

This module enumerates logged-on users and identifies their session types (interactive, service, remote). The results are stored in memory. The attackers can retrieve them using the proxy and tunneling capabilities provided by G.cs.

“ProcessList.cs”

This module lists running processes with full paths to the corresponding executables on the disk. The results are stored in memory and the attackers can retrieve them via G.cs.

“NetworkInfo.cs”

This module extracts information about existing network connections, including protocols, local and remote IPs and ports, and connection state. It also enumerates network interfaces and headers. The results are stored in memory and can be retrieved by the attackers via G.cs.

“MSI.cs”

This module silently installs and executes MSI packages previously downloaded by FileDownloader.cs.

“User.cs”

This module creates administrative accounts using the native SAM RPC subsystem (SAMRPCNative namespace) rather than standard command-line tooling. This may indicate an attempt to evade detection and provide the attackers with privileged stealthy access to target systems that persists after the webshell has finished its work.

SAMRPCNative

The SAMRPCNative namespace implements a low-level C# P/Invoke wrapper for the native Windows samlib.dll library, comprising three types: SAMStructs.cs, SAMMethods.cs, and SAMEnums.cs.

“SAMEnums.cs”

Implements structured bitwise lists and constant flags mapping numeric codes to their security meaning in SAM, and translates system status return codes.

“SAMStructs.cs”

Defines native data structures required for P/Invoke memory alignment and for marshalling. It securely formats and aligns data structures.

“SAMMethods.cs”

Contains external API declarations (P/Invoke) imported from samlib.dll to perform actions such as connecting to the SAM server, creating users and opening domains.

This layer is crucial for the attackers because it enables account operations.

Privilege escalation

The uk namespace contains offensive primitives for privilege escalation. To elevate privileges to SYSTEM, it uses a local token impersonation technique via the Encrypting File System Remote Protocol (EFSRPC) interface adopted from the EfsPotato tool.

This functionality is implemented in the uk/London class. It creates a malicious named pipe while the EfsrTiny class (a tiny version of the EfsPotato tool) connects to the LSASS.exe RPC server. Then it’s London.RpcThread function calls the EfsRpcEncryptFileSrv function from EfsrTiny with a crafted \\localhost path. This tricks LSASS.exe into connecting back to the attacker’s named pipe. Finally, the London.Exp function uses ImpersonateNamedPipeClient to coerce and impersonate the LSASS.exe token and spawn a new process via CreateProcessAsUser with SYSTEM privileges. As the webshell resides in the IIS worker process, it has the necessary SeImpersonatePrivilege to perform this technique.

The uk namespace also implements a minimal MSRPC client layer by explicitly defining structures such as RPC_CLIENT_INTERFACE and MIDL_STUB_DESC, thereby spoofing an interface stub. This enables direct interaction with the Windows RPC runtime (Rpcrt4.dll) without relying on MIDL-generated stubs or higher-level RPC abstractions. This provides direct control over binding and marshaling that goes beyond the constraints of standard client APIs.

Post-exploitation activity

Shortly after the webshell injection, the infected worker process spawned msiexec.exe to install a remote MSI payload hosted in Supabase cloud storage. The payload was Velociraptor, an open-source digital forensics and incident response tool – namely version 0.73.4.0 vulnerable to CVE-2025-6264 – that the attackers abused for command execution on the target network.

In October 2025, Cisco Talos reported Velociraptor being leveraged by threat actors as a post-compromise execution framework and attributed this activity to Storm-2603. This tool enables arbitrary command execution, and can be used for various purposes. In our case, it was used for persistence, discovery, data collection and payload execution.

The threat actor used Velociraptor to deploy multiple independent tunneling mechanisms, including Zoho Assist-Unattended Support for unauthorized remote access, VS Code CLI tunneling, Cloudflare Tunnel, and a lightweight reverse proxy utility. By doing so, they attempted to maintain access even if some of their tools were detected and deleted. At this stage, they also no longer depended on the IIS worker process lifecycle and ToolShell vulnerability.

EDR-killing attempts

Once the threat actor had access to the target system, they were able to upload a vulnerable driver that is used by many attackers to terminate EDR solutions. We were able to detect the main driver at C:\programdata\rsndispot.sys (054a32d6033b1744dca7f49b2e466ea2). In addition, the adversary used a malicious DLL (2d9ebf9c042f596f435865b40edad928) in a sideloading attack. This DLL was identified as Warlock ransomware’s AV killer. It was possibly intended to kill security solutions using the vulnerable rsndispot.sys driver.

Ransomware deployment attempt

The attackers made attempts to launch ransomware on the compromised system. However, the Proactive Defense Module in Kaspersky Endpoint Security blocked the ransomware process, effectively preventing this activity. The malware DLL we obtained was identified as Warlock ransomware.

What defenders really need to look for

ToolPane deserialization and CLR artifacts

When the attackers tried to access ToolPane, both the dynamically compiled App_Web_toolpane.aspx assembly and the Microsoft.GeneratedCode helper assembly were present within the same application domain.

Both assemblies are used in legitimate scenarios. App_Web_* assemblies are generated during normal ASP.NET page compilation, while Microsoft.GeneratedCode is typically produced by the XmlSerializer during legitimate serialization workflows. However, a request to the ToolPane endpoint that results in immediate loading of Microsoft.GeneratedCode within the same execution window indicates that the runtime is processing serialized data supplied through the request.

Detecting deserialization exploitation

First, it is highly recommended to read this article (in Russian) on how deserialization exploit attempts in the CLR should be detected, with examples of YARA rules and monitoring recommendations. A summary of the main idea of the detection logic is provided below.

Deserialization vulnerabilities should be treated as a distinct class of exploitation events. In the CLR, deserialization is not merely the conversion of bytes into values – it is the reconstruction of an object graph from an incoming stream. Serialization and deserialization are performed by formatters. One of the most widely used formatters is BinaryFormatter. It uses the NRBF format, which defines the stream as a sequence of records describing classes, arrays, primitives, and references between objects. The shape of the resulting graph is determined by the data supplied to the deserializer. This means that the input stream defines not only the values but also the specific types, relationships, and lifecycle points that the runtime must materialize.

Microsoft states explicitly that BinaryFormatter is unsafe and cannot be made safe; beginning with .NET 9, the in-box implementation is effectively removed from ordinary use. However, Microsoft continues to use it in its products, including SharePoint, because it is powerful and easy to use. To fix BinaryFormatter-related issues, architectural changes are needed. Similar warnings also apply to related unsafe mechanisms, including LosFormatter (used in the vulnerable page).

The primary risk of unsafe deserialization is that the CLR may resolve unexpected types, instantiate objects outside normal constructor invariants, and invoke special lifecycle mechanisms such as ISerializable, IObjectReference, IDeserializationCallback, and methods marked [OnDeserialized]. In other words, the attacker-controlled data can force the runtime to construct a graph containing types with executable side effects.

A practical detection strategy should therefore focus on graph-construction artifacts. CLR loader events identify the relevant assemblies and application domains. Memory and metadata inspection then reveal the type names and generated serializer structures associated with the suspected gadget chain. In ToolShell-like scenarios, unsafe deserialization usually produces helper assemblies (evidence in loader events) with metadata containing fully qualified type names, gadget class names, and string representations of the constructed generic types (just scan via YARA for it). In our case, the artifacts to look for include Microsoft.GeneratedCode, App_Web_toolpane.aspx* (evidence of deserialization in loader events) as well as strings identifying ObjectDataProvider, ExpandedWrapper, and LosFormatter (evidence that the input stream was deserialized into dangerous objects). Note that these indicators are not significant in isolation; their value lies in the fact that they show the runtime has already received data requiring helper code generation to reconstruct a dangerous object graph.

Gadget objects that exploit vulnerabilities like those associated with ToolShell are conveniently represented in corpus-style tooling such as ysoserial.net/YSoNet, which aggregate known gadget chains for unsafe .NET deserialization. For defensive purposes, the value of these projects lies not in their offensive capability but in the catalog of types and structures that can be searched for in streams, memory, and helper assemblies. The presence of any of them in memory or in a helper assembly should be treated as a strong indicator of exploitation.

To simplify deserialization exploit detection, we created a tool named CLRDeserializationExploitFinder. It can detect ToolShell exploitation attempts, as well as other gadget chains covered by ysoserial.net.

Detecting a VPP-based webshell/runtime implant

A mechanism based on VirtualPathProvider should be treated as a separate class of runtime implant (no files involved). In ASP.NET, HostingEnvironment.RegisterVirtualPathProvider registers a new virtual-path provider (VPP) in the application’s compilation system. Once registered, the application can serve virtual paths during dynamic compilation as though they were ordinary on-disk pages. Dynamic compilation does not require the payload to exist as a file in the filesystem. It operates entirely within the trust boundary of the application itself. During the compilation process, temporary files may be generated, but they cannot be treated as reliable forensic artifacts. Because VPPs can also be used for legitimate purposes, the defensive model should begin with an inventory of the legitimate VirtualPathProvider implementations. In all other cases, the registration or use of a new VPP should be considered anomalous.

To see how the dynamic generation of virtual pages using ASP.NET, IIS, and the CLR works, and to learn how to detect such activity, use our project VirtualPathProvider Lab.

The most useful telemetry source for this technique is the Microsoft-Windows-IIS-Configuration ETW provider. To detect virtual paths, events 25 and 47 are of primary value. Event 25 records the mapping of ConfigPath to PhysicalPath, and event 47 records the mapping of the configuration path to a directory. In the case of a VPP-backed path, these events create an inconsistency: IIS and ASP.NET behave as if the path has a physical representation, while the corresponding file does not exist on disk. In the example provided by VirtualPathProvider Lab, this appears as a mapping of the virtual resource googlecheck.aspx to a physical path where no real file is present. This discrepancy between configuration resolution and filesystem reality is the primary indicator of virtual content.

The second indicator is more negative than positive. For disk-backed files, IIS normally creates a FileChangeNotificationMonitor chain, as reflected in events 17, 18, 19, and 21. For virtual paths served by a custom VirtualPathProvider, this chain is absent or does not match the normal profile of an ordinary file because there is no physical object or corresponding on-disk change lifecycle. Consequently, the presence of positive events 25 and 47 combined with the absence of the expected events 17, 18, 19, and 21 for the same path forms a reliable detection pattern: the path exists for IIS as a configuration-resolved resource, yet it is not backed by the filesystem and is not accompanied by normal file-change monitoring.

To sum up, the hunting target here is the discrepancy between how IIS/ASP.NET resolves a resource and what is actually present on the disk and in the change-monitoring chain. For known applications, such cases can be filtered through an allowlist of legitimate VirtualPathProvider implementations. Anything else should be treated as a potential runtime implant and examined using ETW, filesystem verification, and memory inspection of the w3wp.exe process.

Attribution

Microsoft tracks Storm-2603 as a standalone threat actor with no known links to other groups. While they are careful about assessing the actor’s motivation, they mention that it has previously deployed Warlock and LockBit ransomware following active exploitation of on-premises SharePoint vulnerabilities. In the analyzed incident, we observed similar SharePoint exploitation activities, as well as an EDR killer associated with Warlock ransomware and unsuccessful Warlock launch attempts.

Other documented intrusions have identified Storm-2603 as leveraging known flaws within perimeter mail gateways to achieve initial access, subsequently staging the Velociraptor framework with elevated privileges and establishing persistent encrypted tunnels via commercial remote management software to orchestrate secondary lateral movement. This aligns with the post-exploitation behavior we observed in our case. Together with the ToolShell exploitation scenario, this allows us to attribute this case to Storm-2603 with moderate confidence.

Conclusion

From the incident analyzed in this article, the main defensive lesson is that exploiting an internet-facing SharePoint server can enable fileless code execution directly inside the application trust boundary. Storm-2603 did not require a conventional dropper, persistent service, or exposed C2 endpoint; instead, it deployed a webshell inside w3wp.exe, from which tunneling, privilege escalation, credential access, and lateral movement could be orchestrated. Detection therefore needs to move beyond file-based webshell hunting toward runtime behavior, such as anomalous w3wp.exe activity, unexpected outbound connections, RPC coercion, token impersonation, and the introduction of remote-management or DFIR tooling after application compromise.

To correctly attribute malicious activity and develop appropriate response measures, defenders should reconstruct execution chains and temporal relationships across application, host, and identity layers. They should also preserve memory and IIS telemetry, and correlate low-signal reconnaissance with subsequent privileged activity rather than evaluating events in isolation. A confirmed SharePoint exploit with code execution should trigger host-level containment, persistence hunting, credential and exposed MachineKey rotation, and TTP-driven investigation rather than remediation limited to the initial exploit or known IOCs.

Title: Building incident playbooks for machine identity breaches
Context: An attacker with a valid token makes authenticated calls to the same endpoints the integration hits every day, and a patient one will even keep to its usual hours
Full Text:
Pull up your SOC’s compromised account playbook and read through the first 15 minutes. Most SOCs begin their response by calling or messaging the user via Teams to ask whether the 2:00 am sign-in from an unfamiliar country was indeed them. Their subsequent actions depend upon what the user responds with.

Try that with a service account, and you’ll be waiting a long time. The same goes for an API key buried in a build pipeline, or an OAuth token somebody granted to a SaaS integration back in 2022 and hasn’t thought about since. Once one of those is stolen, your analysts are running a script that was written with people in mind, and the cracks tend to show well before the first shift handover.

There are also far more of them than most boards realise. CyberArk’s research puts machine identities at roughly 82 for every human identity. Very few sit behind MFA, and a fair number hold far more access than the job they were built for. I’d add a problem that gets less airtime, which is that their traffic lives in the background noise your monitoring was tuned to filter out.

Where the human playbook stalls

Ownership is usually the first thing to slow you down. When a person’s account is compromised, HR can tell you who they are and who their manager is before you’ve finished your coffee. A service account pulling data it shouldn’t comes with no such shortcut, so the analyst burns the first hour working out which team built it. More often than anyone likes to admit, that trail ends at a contractor who left the business a year earlier.

Say you do find an owner; containment still isn’t the clean step it is for a person. Lock a user out and one employee loses an afternoon. Pull a credential that a payments integration depends on, though, and you might take a customer-facing service down, which no analyst wants on their name at 11 p.m. without sign-off. So, they go hunting for somebody senior enough to approve the outage while the attacker carries on.

Detection is the part people underestimate. An attacker with a valid token makes authenticated calls to the same endpoints the integration hits every day, and a patient one will even keep to its usual hours. Your impossible-travel rules were built around people moving between cities, so they have nothing to compare against here.

Figure 1: One alert split into two paths.

Ashish Mishra

What recent breaches show

Cloudflare’s write-up of its Thanksgiving 2023 security incident is worth a quarter of an hour of any CISO’s time. The attackers came in with one access token and three service account credentials lifted during the earlier Okta support breach. Cloudflare had rotated thousands of credentials after Okta, yet missed those four because the team believed, wrongly, that nothing was using them. The alert that finally fired came more than a week after the attackers first logged in, when they added one of those service accounts to an administrator group.

Microsoft’s case turned on a test application nobody had cleaned up. Its guidance for responders on the Midnight Blizzard attack describes a password spray against a legacy test tenant account with no MFA. Inside that tenant sat an old test OAuth app that still held elevated access to the corporate environment, and the attackers used it to get into corporate email accounts.

Drift is the case I’d put in front of a board. In August 2025, attackers got hold of the OAuth tokens that Salesloft’s Drift chatbot used to talk to Salesforce, and for roughly ten days they pulled records out of one customer’s Salesforce instance after another. Google’s threat intelligence team, which tracked the campaign closely, concluded the attackers were mostly after credentials. Once the data was out, they went digging through it for AWS access keys and passwords, anything that might get them into the next company along.

I don’t think any of the three needed a clever attacker at the front door. In each case, a credential was issued for a piece of work and then left alone long after the work had finished.

Getting the groundwork in first

It is a relatively simple task to create a playbook. However, a playbook relies upon an inventory. In many organizations, this inventory consists of a service account list generated from Active Directory where half of the description fields have been left blank. Each time you identify a high-privilege non-human identity, document the team responsible for that identity, and provide a brief explanation (one or two sentences) describing what will fail should you remove that identity. Many people do not include the explanation as to why something would fail if removed, since obtaining this information requires contacting the application team for clarification; this contact would otherwise be initiated by your analyst at 3:00 AM while the attacker remains active within your network.

Next, sort those identities by blast radius. I wouldn’t put a read-only reporting token on the same response path as a cloud admin service principal, and I doubt your auditors would either. For the top tier, settle in advance who’s allowed to authorise an immediate revoke even if it knocks something over, and put that role in the playbook by name. Executives must own that call. If you leave it with whoever’s on shift, you’ll get a polite wait for permission while the token stays live. For SOCI-regulated entities, there’s an extra edge to this, because the 12-hour window for reporting a significant cyber incident to ASD can be running while that conversation drags on.

Triage that fits a machine

No one can provide a response to “was this you?”, thus, replace it with questions that can be answered by the log files. A rapid means of verification is location: where do the credentials usually sign in from, and where are they signing in from at present? Logging is readily available via Cloud Audit Logs and Workload Identity Platforms, if someone turned the logging on.

Permissions take longer but tell you more. Line up what the identity holds against what it has used over the last few months, because attackers tend to go straight for high-risk scopes that have been sitting idle. I’d give persistence the same attention. With a privileged service principal in hand, an attacker will often mint new secrets or register an app of their own, and none of that goes away when you revoke the original credential.

Containment without breaking the business

The “trigger” for rotation and revocation should be written separately in the playbook. Rotation would be appropriate when you are reasonably confident that the attacker has not escalated and the organization cannot afford to lose the integration. Revocation is the obvious choice if you find evidence of an ongoing attack; this will be clear enough so there will be no debate at midnight.

Pre-staging your replacement credentials will make revocations tolerable. When the team that owns the application has previously tested how to generate a new credential and then store it in their secret management system, revoking old credentials can cost you about ten minutes of downtime instead of being a full-day disruption. Ask the team to practice generating and storing new credentials during a low-traffic week. Do not find out mid-incident that the runbook references a vault location that was renamed last year.

Scoping and recovery

To understand the full scope of an incident, look at the entire lifespan of the machine credential, not just the period after the alert was generated. Because machines may be able to go undetected as being compromised for many months prior to discovery, the first unusual activity reported will most likely not be the first unusual activity performed. Also, keep in mind that “drift” is a great way to remember to see what information the identity has access to, and if anyone has placed credentials into that identity. If so, each addition of a secret will require you to add a new rotation to your list.

Recovery is when you fix what caused the problem in the first place. For example, if a static secret was compromised, determine if that workload can use short-lived tokens using Workload Identity Federation; or perhaps a short-lived token can be generated on demand (Just-In-Time) and will expire automatically. Recovery is a tedious, non-sexy task, and most of the time it requires financial support from an entity outside of the Security Operations Center (SOC).

Before finalizing the playbook, conduct a tabletop simulation with the application owners in attendance along with the Security Operations Center (SOC). Select your highest-privilege integration and simulate a stolen-token event (from first alert through recovery). During the simulation, when a decision needs to be made regarding who approves revoking the token, and revoking the token will disrupt production, observe how much time it takes for the team to identify who should make this approval.

Title: CERT-In Flags AI-Driven Attacks as Backdoored ARTEX Exposes 62 Consoles to Root Access
Context: Describing the threat as active and ongoing, the activity involves the use of publicly-available AI-driven offensive security tools like ARTEX, PentAGI, Cairn, and CyberStrikeAI
Full Text:
The Indian Computer Emergency Response Team (CERT-In) has disclosed that an artificial intelligence (AI)-assisted threat actor it tracks as Crafty Falcon is targeting organizations in the Banking, Financial Services, and Insurance (BFSI) sectors in the country.

Describing the threat as active and ongoing, the activity involves the use of publicly-available AI-driven offensive security tools like ARTEX, PentAGI, Cairn, and CyberStrikeAI.

"These tools execute complete attack chains autonomously at machine speed, generate and refine large numbers of tailored attack scripts in rapid succession, and adapt their payloads based on target responses," CERT-In said. "The supporting attack infrastructure rotates IP addresses within hours to days."

The agency said the attacks have also targeted cryptocurrency exchanges and digital asset service providers, resulting in the theft of keys and funds.

The update follows an October 2026 alert issued by CERT-In, which warned of multiple cyber attack campaigns targeting non-banking financial companies (NBFCs), digital lending platforms, fintech entities, payment service providers, and cryptocurrency wallet operators.

Threat actors have been observed exploiting internet-facing applications and exposed APIs and privileged endpoints to steal payment aggregator/gateway and partner-bank API credentials, and then invoke fund-transfer APIs directly from within the entities' own allow-listed infrastructure.

Some of the other notable initial access vectors are listed below -

Use of stolen long-lived static, hard-coded API tokens

Supply chain compromise of source code repositories via forged commits

Exploitation of plaintext credentials in configuration files, source code, or databases

Access to applications and remote services lacking multi-factor authentication (MFA)

This approach, CERT-In added, defeats application-level controls such as loan creation, KYC, sanction, beneficiary verification, balance sufficiency, and per-transaction limits.

The rapidly executed fraudulent transactions are designed to move funds to attacker-controlled mule accounts across multiple banks. In addition, the attacks involve the operators taking steps to delete logs and tamper with endpoint security tools in an attempt to complicate detection and incident response efforts.

CERT-In also warned that attackers are targeting cloud infrastructure to execute commands and deploy malicious payloads, as well as publicly-accessible non-production environments to obtain shared credentials, tokens, or network paths, and then use them to pivot to production systems.

Other notable post-exploitation actions undertaken by the adversary are as follows -

Reverse-engineering application codebases to develop tailored exploits

Initiating unauthorized API calls using modified application packages, undermining controls that "assumed only the legitimate client application would call the APIs"

Executing micro-value test transactions (such as Rs. 1) to validate unauthorized fund flows before executing large-value transfers

Abusing merchant settlement APIs of payment aggregators to move funds

Exploiting newly disclosed vulnerabilities, including file-upload and deserialization exploit chains leading to web shells in PHP and Node.js applications

Creating a large number of custom scripts on the fly and iteratively improving them in quick succession, a pattern consistent with AI-assisted development

The development comes as CERT-In has published the Artificial Intelligence Security Auditing Guidelines, laying out specific requirements to ensure the "governance, security, privacy, fairness, transparency, resilience and auditability of AI systems."

The framework calls for testing an AI agent's documented identities, authorized objectives, approved tool use, permission boundaries, and its adherence to the principle of least privilege (PoLP). It also requires AI agents to require human approval for consequential actions, while ensuring high-risk AI systems incorporate emergency interruption, credential revocation, and controls for preventing automatic restarts.

"Effective assurance requires organisational accountability, technical testing, data and model governance, continuous monitoring, human oversight, incident response and third-party assurance," the agency said. "Accordingly, the framework provides auditable requirements proportionate to the nature, scale, autonomy and potential impact of each AI system."

Copycat ARTEX Version Hands Out Root Shell

The abuse of open-source penetration testing tools like ARTEX in real-world intrusions prompted its developer to take down the repository from GitHub. But multiple copies have sprung up on the Microsoft-owned code-hosting platform to fill the void -

github[.]com/trhhubsd/ARTEXX

github[.]com/mhtsec/ARTEX ("mianhuatang11/artex" on Docker Hub)

github[.]com/RuoJi6/ARTEX

The first two GitHub repositories are no longer available for download. According to an independent cybersecurity researcher who goes by the online alias Badbyte, the "trhhubsd/ARTEX" repository was starred 2,449 times and forked over 600 times.

What's notable about the GitHub copy is that it changed a single line in "docker-compose.yml" to pull the "tomicdd/artex" image from Docker Hub. The modified version conceals a new routine that grants a root shell during an unauthenticated request to the login endpoint. Per statistics shared by Docker Hub, the image has been downloaded 9,000 times.

"It adds a hidden verifyCaptcha() function to the login handler: if the CAPTCHA field starts with a secret marker, the rest runs through sh -c as root and the output is returned, before any credential check," the researcher said in a statement shared with The Hacker News via email. "That's an unauthenticated root shell on every install, and it never shows up in a code review."

"A compromised ARTEX instance holds its targets' unpatched findings, live credentials, captured sessions and network position. Whoever holds the backdoor can also quietly change what the agents do on the next run."

As many as 62 ARTEX consoles on the internet have been found to serve the backdoored build between November 2 and 4, 2026, with the first instance going up by October 20, 2026, twelve days after the Docker image was pushed. Of these, 26 consoles are located in the U.S., followed by 17 in Hong Kong and seven in China.

In all, a total of 1,645 hosts have been found serving the ARTEX console as of November 4, 2026. Besides "tomicdd/artex," a number of Docker Hub namespaces have been identified as publishing images named "artex." Some of them are listed below -

congdonglinux/artex (also backdoored and identical to "tomicdd/artex")

mianhuatang11/artex

autumn26/artex

andy1099zz/artex

dgddw/artex

trhhubsd/ARTEX

ylh440104/artex

"The backdoor's author needed nothing more. The people they were after had already chosen to run an unvetted attack tool as root on an open port," Badbyte said. "We know ARTEX has been used maliciously in the wild, and it will keep being used that way. We also know that plenty of legitimate, curious people installed it to see what the fuss was about. They did not sign up for a root shell on their own server."

Title: AI-Powered Ransomware Is Coming for UK Critical Infrastructure, and Europe Is Already the Testing Ground
Context: In its 2026 Annual Review, The State of the Cyber Nation, the agency assesses it is highly likely that AI-powered malware will be used in a ransomware attack on UK Critical...
Full Text:
Overview

The UK's National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC) has put a date on a threat that security teams across Europe have been bracing for. In its 2026 Annual Review, The State of the Cyber Nation, the agency assesses it is highly likely that AI-powered malware will be used in a ransomware attack on UK Critical National Infrastructure by 2028.

That is not a distant, speculative scenario. It is a two-year window, and it lands alongside a second judgement. By 2028, China, Russia and other nation-states will highly likely be using AI-enabled cyber capabilities routinely to pursue geopolitical goals, with the UK facing sophisticated attacks at greater scale and speed.

The review also recorded that UK and EU member states jointly attributed a December 2025 attack on Poland's energy grid to Russia's FSB Centre 16. Had it succeeded, roughly 500,000 citizens could have lost power. Europe is not watching this threat from the sidelines; it is where the playbook is being tested.

Key Takeaways

2028 is the marker. The NCSC judges AI malware will highly likely be used in ransomware against UK CNI before the end of 2028.

Europe's grid is already a target. Russia's FSB Centre 16 was attributed to the December 2025 attack on Poland's energy grid, and a July 2026 advisory from 18 partners in 12 countries flagged the same group exploiting vulnerable routers to reach CNI networks worldwide.

China is best positioned to use AI against CNI. The NCSC rates China's activity as the most sophisticated and sustained cyber challenge facing the UK.

AI speeds up old tricks rather than inventing new ones. For large organizations, 88% of incidents the NCSC handled began through just four initial access vectors.

A "patch wave" is coming. AI-assisted vulnerability discovery will shrink the time defenders have between disclosure and exploitation.

The gap is widening. Organizations with legacy technology and slow remediation will become the preferred targets of both states and criminals.

The 2028 Warning

The NCSC's assessment is precise about where AI makes the difference. It calls AI an almost certain "force multiplier" that improves reconnaissance, social engineering, vulnerability discovery and exploit development. The biggest effect, it says, will be faster and larger versions of existing tactics rather than brand-new attack vectors.

Ransomware is where that acceleration hits CNI hardest. The review expects criminal adoption of AI to raise the scale and efficiency of ransomware, social engineering and exploitation. It also warns that open-source AI tools built for security researchers are likely to be repurposed to automate criminal workflows, cutting costs and raising attack volumes against less resilient targets.

The agency is careful not to overstate today's reality. Its Incident Management team has begun to see attackers using AI tools, but none of the observed uses enabled a new class of attack. Human operators remain essential, and the NCSC notes that losing control of an agentic AI is likely to hinder threat actors from reaching their goals.

The review's pessimistic 2028 scenario shows why that caveat may not last. In it, frontier AI is available to everyone from state actors to novice hackers, jailbroken models are sold in criminal marketplaces, and attribution becomes harder as capability spreads. It even describes a realistic possibility of an automated cyber actor operating beyond its operator's control. Cloud-controlled CNI and AI-driven robotics raise the chance that a digital compromise causes physical harm.

The NCSC stresses this is an illustration of the cost of inaction, not a forecast. But it is a scenario written by the agency responsible for defending UK infrastructure, and it is set just two years out.

Europe: The Proving Ground for CNI Attacks

If the UK is looking at 2028, continental Europe is already living with the threat. The NCSC names Russia as the most audacious cyber threat to the UK today. GCHQ Director Anne Keast-Butler goes further in the review's foreword, warning that tactics Russia developed against Ukraine are now being turned more widely on states and their institutions.

Three data points from the review frame the European picture:

Poland's energy grid (December 2025). The UK and EU member states formally attributed the attack to FSB Centre 16. If successful, it could have cut electricity to around 500,000 people.

Router exploitation on a global scale (July 2026). The NCSC and 18 international partners from 12 countries issued a joint advisory on FSB Centre 16 actors exploiting vulnerable routers to target CNI networks worldwide. On the same day, the UK sanctioned 24 individuals and entities tied to destructive cyber and hybrid operations, including criminals running proxy networks linked to Russian intelligence.

Operational technology in crosshairs. The review points to recent attacks on programmable logic controllers (PLCs) as evidence that organizations failing to modernize are falling behind.

The pattern matters for anyone running energy, water, transport or telecoms in Europe. Grids, interconnectors and supply chains cross borders, and a disruptive attack in one country can cascade into its neighbors. The review also describes how cyber threats to the UK can escalate rapidly and without warning during periods of geopolitical tension.

Add AI to this mix and the timeline compresses. A state actor that today relies on patience and known router flaws could, with AI-assisted discovery and exploitation, find and weaponize new weaknesses across thousands of European edge devices far faster than defenders can patch them.

China is Best Positioned to Turn AI on Critical Infrastructure

While Russia is the loudest threat, the NCSC sees China as the most capable. It judges that China highly likely has both the intent and the best position to use AI against CNI and other strategic targets. Its frontier AI programmes are expected to sharpen vulnerability identification, targeting efficiency and access operations.

Data sits at the center of that strategy. The review describes China collecting large volumes of information from the UK and elsewhere, then using it to train models and improve capability. In the AI era, stolen data is no longer just espionage material; it is fuel.

The UK has already acted on this. In December 2025, it sanctioned two China-based firms: i-Soon, which targeted more than 80 government and private IT systems globally, and Integrity Technology Group, which the FBI has linked to the Flax Typhoon intrusions. In April 2026, the NCSC and 15 partners across nine other countries published guidance on the covert networks most China-linked actors use to hide their activity.

The 2028 scenario adds a further concern: China, as a leading developer, may help spread advanced AI-cyber capability to other actors, letting them hide in the noise and making attribution harder for European defenders.

AI Runs the Old Playbook, Only Faster

The most useful finding in the review is also the least dramatic: attackers are still getting in through the basics. Over the past year, the NCSC received 1,831 reports of cyber attacks. Of these, 337 needed its direct support, and 80 were classed as nationally significant.

For large organizations, 88% of incidents started through four initial access vectors:

Exploiting public-facing applications

Phishing

Misuse of valid accounts

Exploiting external remote services

Even state-linked intrusions often used flaws for which patches already existed but had not been applied quickly enough. As the review puts it, sophisticated actors do not need to be sophisticated to gain initial access; their skill shows in what they do once inside.

This is exactly where AI changes the economics. The NCSC expects AI-assisted vulnerability discovery to give attackers more chances to hit systems before owners patch them. It is urging every organization to prepare for a "patch wave": a surge of security updates across the technology stack, many of them critical, as AI exposes years of technical debt.

Two further risks deserve attention:

Shadow AI. Staff moving sensitive data to personal devices to use unsanctioned AI tools leaves organizations blind to where that data goes, and open to both APT groups and criminals.

The widening gap. Mature, well-resourced organizations will use AI to detect and fix faster. Those running legacy systems will fall further behind and become more attractive targets.

The financial stakes are already clear. UK government research cited in the review puts the annual cost of malicious cyber activity to UK organizations at about £14.7 billion. The 2025 attack on Jaguar Land Rover alone cost the company around £196 million in direct costs and contributed to UK GDP growing just 0.1% in Q3 2025.

How the UK Is Fighting Back With AI

The NCSC's answer is to meet machine-speed attacks with machine-speed defense. Several initiatives in the review stand out:

Cyber Shield. A joint NCSC and DCMS programme to build a national agentic cyber defense ecosystem over five years. The NCSC supplies the platform and intelligence, while defensive agents are built by the security market and open-source community. Early phases focus on detection and blocking, where automation is already practical.

Project DROMOS. Launched in 2026 by the Government Cyber Coordination Centre and the AI Security Institute, it used frontier AI models to review government codebases. Expanded into live environments, it surfaced hundreds of potential security issues, including critical vulnerabilities.

National Detect Strategy. A pilot aiming, by 2030, to ensure defenders across critical systems can detect and respond to known vulnerabilities and attacker techniques at organizational, community and national scale.

Regulation and benchmarks. The Cyber Security and Resilience Bill brings new sectors into scope and adds national security powers. The new CAF Core Profile sets a minimum resilience baseline for essential services.

There are early results. Under the Government Cyber Action Plan, the median time to fix domain-related vulnerabilities fell from 50 days to 8. The Early Warning service now covers 19,922 organizations, up 52% on last year.

For Europe, the lesson is that partnership is now part of the defense. The review highlights the world's first AI security standard developed through ETSI, the European standards body, as proof that allies can shape AI security while the technology is still evolving.

National defense at machine speed also depends on seeing adversaries before they reach the network. Groups like FSB Centre 16 and China-linked operators plan, recruit, and trade access in places most defenders never look. As AI makes attribution harder, government agencies, national CERTs, and defense bodies need intelligence that tracks threat actors across the open, deep, and dark web and connects that activity to the infrastructure being targeted. Cyble Hawk is built for exactly this. It gives national security teams sovereign threat intelligence, adversary profiling, and investigative support. That means early warning of campaigns against critical infrastructure and stronger attribution when an attack does land. Book a demo to see how your agency can move from reacting to incidents to anticipating them.

Recommendations for CNI Operators in the UK and Europe

The NCSC's core message is that AI did not create these weaknesses; it is exposing them faster. Operators of critical infrastructure should act on the following now:

Harden the edge first. Inventory and patch internet-facing applications, VPNs, routers, and remote access services. These are the routes FSB Centre 16 and others are actively exploiting.

Prepare for the patch wave. Build processes to test and deploy security updates more often, faster and across suppliers. Track time-to-remediate as a board-level metric.

Kill password-based access where you can. Move privileged and remote users to phishing-resistant authentication such as passkeys, and audit valid accounts for misuse.

Segment IT from OT. Limit the paths from corporate networks to PLCs and industrial control systems, and monitor those boundaries continuously.

Govern AI use internally. Map what data AI tools and agents can access, what actions they can take, and how they are monitored. Close off shadow AI with approved alternatives.

Rehearse recovery, not just prevention. Test ransomware response playbooks against scenarios where operational systems must run during disruption. Use the NCSC's guidance on recovering from highly disruptive attacks.

Lock down the supply chain. Require baseline controls such as Cyber Essentials, or equivalent standards in EU frameworks, from suppliers with access to critical systems.

Use threat intelligence that moves at AI speed. Monitor for exploitation of newly disclosed flaws, stolen credentials, and chatter about your sector, so you can act before an incident escalates.

Start post-quantum planning. The NCSC wants discovery and migration planning finished by 2028, priority migrations by 2031 and full migration by 2035.

Conclusion

The NCSC has given Europe a deadline. By 2028, AI-powered ransomware against UK critical infrastructure moves from possibility to expectation, and state actors will be using AI as a routine part of their operations. The Poland grid attack and the global router campaign show the targeting is already in place; AI simply adds speed and scale.

The agency's own framing is a "moment of choice." Organizations that modernize, patch fast, and build resilience now will be able to absorb what comes next. Those that defer will find AI exposing their technical debt faster than they can repay it.

For CNI operators across the UK and Europe, the next two years are the window to close the gap. Continuous visibility into emerging vulnerabilities, active exploitation and threat actor activity will be central to staying ahead of attacks that move at machine speed.

Title: Attackers turned OpsShield’s trusted update channel into a supply-chain attack
Context: ” What’s particularly concerning here is that the attackers didn’t have to go after thousands of customers one by one; they only had to compromise a single distribution...
Full Text:
The kinks in the software supply chain are once again being exposed, with attackers now targeting OpsShield’s update process.

This week, threat actors used compromised credentials to push malicious updates out to cPGuard customers. They then accessed data stored on the vendor’s servers and in its billing portal accounts, and made copies of at least three of OpsShield’s cloud servers.

The company said in an advisory that it has “shut the attacker out of every system we know they reached, and … are rebuilding the ones we cannot fully trust.” It has also released updates and urges customers to update to the latest version of cPGuard, change passwords, and generate new SSH keys.

Ultimately, the breadth of this unsanctioned access underscores the continued fragility of the software supply chain, as well as the vulnerability of security tools themselves.

“The real danger here is that attackers were able to turn a trusted security update mechanism into a vector to break into servers,” said Erik Avakian, a technical counselor at Infotech. “The software that’s supposed to protect those servers became the source that compromised them.”

The anatomy of the attack

OpsShield specializes in server protection and web security software. Its cPGuard product is a security suite, malware scanner, and firewall designed for Linux web hosting servers.

The company disclosed that, between November 1 and 2, attackers were able to gain unauthorized access to the OpsShield update distribution infrastructure, and, for about 70 minutes, pushed out a malicious update.

The threat actors began by probing OpsShield’s billing portal, registering a customer account under a false identity, and ordering a free cPGuard trial. They then sent crafted requests that allowed them to gain the ability to run commands on the server to collect data. They used stolen access keys to publish fake updates that ran as root (the highest level of admin privilege), and to copy sensitive files and make copies of three OpsShield cloud servers.

About 2,950 customer servers ran the fake update, exposing password hashes, root SSH keys, MySQL root passwords, and shell history, OpsShield reported. Attackers also accessed about 7,900 billing portal accounts containing customer names, addresses, emails, and hashed passwords.

OpsShield says it is still reviewing the exact request that provided access, and has patched two possible entry points and verified related vendor components “line by line.” It closed the attacker’s account, revoked the stolen update-storage key as well as “every cloud API token and access key on our account.”

The company also removed the attacker’s secure shell (SSH); deleted the clones of its servers created by the attacker plus any snapshots; turned on stronger login protection and replaced every SSH key and password; reset all billing portal login sessions and rotated all keys; and began rebuilding its billing, licensing, and internal management servers with tighter PHP and firewall settings.

The company has also published clean updates: v5.88.26, which removes the hidden root shell; plus a follow-up which removes the scheduled task left by the attacker. Further, it began re-issuing all cPGuard license private and public keys so that the copies the attacker gained access to stopped working.

The company advised admins to:

Update cPGuard to the latest version, then confirm that /etc/cron.d/i93677, /var/tmp/.i93677/ and /var/tmp/.cpg91511_sh are gone; delete them if not;

Change root passwords and every local user password on the server;

Generate new root SSH keys and remove old ones from every server that trusted them; until the keys are changed, treat the servers as compromised;

Change MySQL root passwords and any database passwords and rotate any password, API key, or token existing in root shell histories;

Reset the OpsShield billing portal passwords and turn on two-factor authentication.

Finally, it said, “if we told you the attacker logged in to your server by hand, rebuild it from a clean backup taken before 1 November.”

OpsShield being transparent, but the impacts are still real

“Frankly, few vendors write a breach disclosure this candid,” said Frank Dickson of Dickson Research. “OpsShield deserves a lot of credit for that.”

However, he pointed out, the worst kind of breach is the one a security tool delivers. Update channels are left unlocked on purpose, and security tools run as root because they have to see everything, “so the fake update ran as root too.”

For a hosting provider, one server can hold hundreds of customer websites and databases. A MySQL root password opens all of them, and a root SSH key grants access to every other server that trusts it. Shell history also often contains typed passwords and tokens.

The downstream customer may be hit hardest while knowing the least, Dickson pointed out, as most website owners have no idea which security agent their hosting provider runs. Every server that updates itself trusts the vendor’s pipeline.

OpsShield describes itself as a small team selling to smaller hosts at a low price, which is the uncomfortable truth of the supply chain, Dickson said. “Your exposure is set by the smallest vendor holding root on your servers, not the largest.”

Avakian agreed that this serves as a reminder that an enterprise’s software supply chain is only as secure as the systems, identities, and processes behind it. “You can do everything you can to secure your own infrastructure and still get compromised through a third-party supplier you trust.”

What’s particularly concerning here is that the attackers didn’t have to go after thousands of customers one by one; they only had to compromise a single distribution mechanism to turn the vendor’s own trusted infrastructure against its customers, he noted.

Third parties extend risk, which is a fact that organizations still underestimate, he said. “Enterprises need to pay much more attention to third-party and supply chain risk management.”

Zero-trust a must-have

Avakian also pointed out that the impact on downstream customers could go well beyond initial compromise, as stolen credentials can be used to carry out further attacks. Enterprises should take a zero-trust approach that includes their software suppliers and the updates they rely on.

“Just because an update comes from a trusted source doesn’t mean you can assume it’s safe,” he said. Enterprises should take a closer look at vendor risk, protect privileged credentials, and examine software integrity. Also, continuously monitor for unexpected behavior after an update and be ready to isolate systems quickly if and when something goes wrong.

“You have to plan for the possibility that even a trusted supplier can be compromised,” he emphasized. “And you need to practice those types of scenarios as part of a regular table-top exercise program.”

Dickson advised starting with an inventory, and knowing every vendor agent running with root or administrator privilege, as each one is an update channel. Customers should ask vendors where update publishing keys live and what separates them from customer-facing systems, watch outbound traffic from servers, keep secrets out of shell history, and treat SSH keys as credentials with an expiration date. Downstream customers should ask their host directly whether it runs cPGuard, then change their own passwords.

“The most dangerous software on your server may be the software you trust to update itself,” he said. “Choose those vendors as if they hold root, because they do.”

Title: Vercel rolls out new protection against stolen session cookie attacks
Context: The new feature, announced by Vercel's CTO Malte Ubl on X, binds a login session to the user's device with a private key stored in a TPM, so even if the session cookie is...
Full Text:
Vercel is gradually rolling out Device Bound Session Credentials (DBSC) on its platform as a key defense against information stealer malware.

The new feature, announced by Vercel's CTO Malte Ubl on X, binds a login session to the user's device with a private key stored in a TPM, so even if the session cookie is stolen, it can't be reused on another device.

Vercel is a cloud platform developers use to deploy and host websites, web applications, and AI agents. The company also develops the popular Next.js web framework.

Its latest announcement concerns logins to Vercel's platform at vercel.com, where developers manage their projects and deployments.

"DBSC works by storing a private key in your device's TPM (the same device that the fingerprint sensor or similar biometric devices on your laptop or phone uses) and using that key to sign your cookie," explained Ubl.

"The private key can never be retrieved ever again. Not by us, not by you, not by the malware."

Vercel's DBSC rollout also complements Chrome's App-Bound Encryption, which makes it harder for infostealer malware to extract browser cookies. DBSC adds another layer of protection by preventing stolen session cookies from being reused on other devices.

DBSC currently works in Chrome on macOS and Windows, but the rollout is gradual to ensure edge cases involving OAuth apps are handled appropriately.

Separately, Vercel is rolling out a similar protective technology called DPoP for the Vercel CLI.

Security Review also lands

Earlier this week, Vercel launched Security Review in public beta for Pro and Enterprise teams, adding a feature to Vercel Agent that scans code changes on every push to connected GitHub repositories once enabled.

The new system uses code and team-defined policies to flag issues such as missing authorization checks and exposed secrets.

If permissions allow, the Vercel Agent can validate and commit fixes.

Vercel says Security Review scans will be free until November 10, 2026, while agent-generated fixes will be billed separately.

Ubl said that Vercel's security team shipped this new feature internally a couple of months back, and it has already proven its worth, so the platform decided to make it broadly available.

In April, Vercel suffered a security breach impacting a subset of customers, in which attackers gained access to its systems by compromising an employee's Google Workspace account at Context.ai.

Vercel said the attacker used that access to reach internal systems and view environment variables that hadn't been marked as sensitive.

A threat actor impersonating ShinyHunters attempted to sell the allegedly stolen source code, access keys, and database data.

Title: PolinRider Loader Reappears in Hijacked npm Packages
Context: Hidden Loaders Found in 12 npm Releases On November 4, 2026, Sonatype Research Labs investigated malicious runtime loaders in npm packages and confirmed 12 affected releases...
Full Text:
TL;DR

Sonatype Research Labs identified concealed runtime loaders in 12 npm releases across 10 hijacked packages.

All 12 releases contain loaders designed to decode payload-server IP addresses from Ethereum transactions sent by the same hard-coded wallet previously reported in PolinRider activity, then retrieve, XOR-decode, and execute JavaScript. Six conceal the loader in eval(atob(...)); six use a character-permutation bootstrap and the JavaScript Function constructor.

The manifests show no consumer install or postinstall hooks. The code can run when an affected entrypoint is loaded or, for server-hemera-mongo, when the bundled application starts.

Check direct and transitive dependencies, lockfiles, internal npm mirrors, and build records. If affected code ran, treat the host as compromised and investigate its processes, network activity, and accessible credentials.

Hidden Loaders Found in 12 npm Releases

On November 4, 2026, Sonatype Research Labs investigated malicious runtime loaders in npm packages and confirmed 12 affected releases across 10 hijacked packages. The examined releases contain two loader variants that use the same Ethereum sender wallet and payload-retrieval infrastructure. Sonatype tracks the finding as sonatype-2026-010515.The affected packages support unrelated developer functions, from Redux integration and health APIs to browser activity tracking, utilities, and server examples. Their shared issue is concealed behavior embedded in code that otherwise serves those ordinary purposes.These releases don't rely on a consumer-side installation script to activate that behavior. An application can reach the code when it loads an affected package; the server-hemera-mongo releases run it as the service starts.
