Title: 2nd November – Threat Intelligence Report
Context: Cisco confirmed that the vulnerability had been exploited in attacks before the security updates became available
Full Text:
For the latest discoveries in cyber research for the week of 2nd November, please download our Threat Intelligence Bulletin.

TOP ATTACKS AND BREACHES

Binance, a global cryptocurrency exchange, has suffered a cyberattack resulting in the theft of approximately $6.3 billion in digital assets. Attackers reportedly compromised a DevOps engineer’s laptop and abused internal wallet infrastructure to authorize unauthorized withdrawals. The incident ranks among the largest cryptocurrency thefts ever recorded and is linked to North Korean group.

Polymarket, a US-based prediction market platform, has disclosed a cyberattack involving a compromised third-party service that distributed malicious JavaScript to its website. The script hijacked authenticated trading sessions and attempted unauthorized transactions. Approximately $2.7 million in cryptocurrency was traced to a suspected attacker-controlled wallet.

Japan Airlines, a major Japanese international airline, has disclosed a third-party data breach affecting approximately 92,000 passengers through the Amadeus reservation system. Exposed records included passenger names and flight information. Approximately 2,000 individuals also had contact information, passport details, and additional travel records potentially accessed.

The Florida Department of Education has disclosed a data breach involving unauthorized access to its student financial aid website, potentially affecting 4.9 million individuals. Compromised information reportedly includes names, Social Security numbers, dates of birth, addresses, and contact details. The incident was identified on October 19.

AI THREATS

Researchers have identified extensive use of AI agents by the GOLD OGRE ransomware group during Aur0ra attacks. Operators supplied compromised credentials and objectives, allowing AI tools to perform network reconnaissance, identify privileged accounts, and support lateral movement. The group also used AI-assisted development to test endpoint security evasion techniques.

Researchers have documented expanding AI adoption among North Korean cyber threat actors. The activity includes using language models to support reconnaissance, develop malicious tools, refine social engineering, and accelerate intrusion workflows. The findings describe how established espionage and financially motivated operations are incorporating AI into existing attack techniques.

Researchers have uncovered a global espionage campaign in which the China-linked VAPOR PANDA group used the AI-enabled ARTEX framework against more than 200 organizations. Targets included government agencies, telecommunications providers, and defense companies across at least 14 countries. Confirmed intrusions involved credential theft and deployment of the BLOODALCHEMY backdoor.

VULNERABILITIES AND PATCHES

Check Point Research have analyzed HTTP2Shell (CVE-2026-111497), an actively exploited remote code execution vulnerability affecting Brotli decompression implementations. Initially associated with Node.js, the flaw may also affect other components, including Python packages, .NET, and proxies. Automated scanning and suspicious exploitation attempts have been observed.

Check Point IPS provides protection against this threat (Node.js Brotli Remote Code Execution (CVE-2026-111497)))

A critical Linux kernel vulnerability, CVE-2026-98432, has been disclosed with a CVSS score of 9.8. The memory management flaw affects TCP networking and can enable unauthenticated remote code execution with root privileges on systems exposing Multipath TCP listeners.

Drupal has addressed CVE-2026-118539, a highly critical access control vulnerability in the Commerce Core module used by online stores. Insufficient protection of application routes and data fields allows unauthenticated attackers to bypass authorization restrictions. The flaw has been exploited in attacks and may affect commercial transactions.

Cisco has patched CVE-2026-76418, a high-severity vulnerability affecting Adaptive Security Appliance and Firepower Threat Defense software. The flaw allows unauthenticated attackers to remotely crash devices configured with SSL VPN functionality. Cisco confirmed that the vulnerability had been exploited in attacks before the security updates became available.

THREAT INTELLIGENCE REPORTS

Check Point Research has uncovered the Yoba malware campaign, which distributes malicious installers disguised as ChatGPT and Claude desktop applications through fraudulent GitHub projects. Attackers exploit legitimate signed executables to load malicious components and establish persistence. The campaign uses trusted online services for payload delivery and communication.

Check Point researchers have analyzed unexpected network activity generated by Alibaba’s Qwen model during a security-related task. Repeated testing produced numerous different destination addresses rather than one consistent endpoint. The findings suggest unstable model behavior is a more plausible explanation than a deliberately embedded data-exfiltration mechanism.

Researchers have identified UAT-11473, an advanced threat actor exploiting a Cisco Catalyst SD-WAN authentication bypass to deploy the KeyDrift malware framework. The campaign targeted organizations in aerospace, defense, satellites and policy research. KeyDrift enables persistent access and extraction of sensitive encryption material from compromised network controllers.

Researchers have documented more than 400 incidents involving abuse of Microsoft Teams external chat functionality for initial access. Attackers impersonated internal IT support personnel to persuade employees to initiate remote sessions and install access tools. Some campaigns progressed to credential theft, lateral movement, and ransomware-related activity.

Title: DarkBlinders Compromises Israeli Target and Iraqi Kurdish Government Cloud Environment
Context: The activity has been attributed to a threat actor known as DarkBlinders, an Iran-nexus group assessed to be active since at least September 2024 and linked to attacks aimed at...
Full Text:
Cybersecurity researchers have disclosed details of a cyber espionage campaign targeting Israel and the Kurdistan Region of Iraq by an Iran state-aligned threat actor between August and October 2026.

According to a report published by Dream Research Labs, the campaign has led to the compromise of a high-profile individual in Israel, along with additional compromises affecting a government cloud environment in the Kurdistan Region.

The activity has been attributed to a threat actor known as DarkBlinders, an Iran-nexus group assessed to be active since at least September 2024 and linked to attacks aimed at aviation infrastructure and telecommunications in the U.A.E. and Iraq. It exhibits no technical overlap with other known hacking groups.

Attacks mounted by the group are known to rely on spear-phishing as an initial access pathway to lure recipients into opening trojanized utilities or clicking on attacker-controlled websites that host similar tools as direct downloads.

Previous attack chains documented by Elastic Security Labs and Group-IB have led to the deployment of SHELBYLOADER (aka HOTAIR), which is launched via DLL sideloading to ultimately execute a backdoor called SHELBYC2 (aka AEROSTAT) that uses GitHub for command-and-control (C2), data exfiltration, and remote control. Elastic is tracking the threat cluster under the moniker REF8685.

Then early last month, Palo Alto Networks shed light on a campaign dubbed Blinder Tunnel in which the threat actor, which it calls CL-STA-1178, was observed masquerading as the Dubai Airports IT department to distribute malware-laced coding challenges to high-value targets.

The bogus recruitment scheme was first detected in late March 2026, although evidence indicates that the attackers were staging and testing attack infrastructure as far back as November 2025.

The social engineering campaign is assessed to have approached specific targets with lucrative job offers to trick them into executing a self-contained application that mimicked a career portal and instructed them to complete a questionnaire.

Submitting the questionnaire does not cause any data to be exfiltrated or initiate any response from an external domain. Instead, it's meant to serve as a harmless decoy and build credibility before delivering the next stage payload containing the malware in the form of a Microsoft Visual Studio project archive that's dressed up as a coding assessment.

The attack chain makes use of three techniques to establish persistent access: A malicious C# project ".csproj" file is used to trigger AppDomainManager injection, followed by DLL sideloading to deliver an updated version of SHELBYLOADER (aka ShelbyLoader V2), which then launches SHELBYC2. Also deployed via SHELBYC2 is a tunneling utility called Blackwood.

"The attackers behind the activity used tailored social engineering techniques to masquerade as Dubai Airports recruiters, using a trojanized Visual Studio coding challenge to target a high-value job seeker based in Iraq," Unit 42 said.

"The campaign is characterized by misuse of built-in developer tools and DLL sideloading. Attackers also used AppDomainManager hijacking to bypass security monitors like ETW [Event Tracing for Windows]."

The latest findings from Dream show that the threat actor continues to rely on social engineering, while combining both credential phishing and malware delivery. This involves the use of government, webmail, and cloud-service lookalike domains to collect credentials or present attacker-controlled file downloads. Some of the highlighted domains include -

gcc-sg[.]cloud/owa/auth/logon.aspx

mfakuwait[.]online/owa/auth/logon.aspx

moelcloud[.]online/drive/file/d/1JpH3ySmJpvX6TyGnF7C-S8qYiaoxyC5O

The threat actor has also been observed setting decoy brand domains for a fake videoconferencing application called StarkMeet (stark-meet[.]com, stark-meet[.]online, and stark-meet[.]website). Installing and launching the app leads to the execution of ShelbyLoader V2 and SHELBYC2.

The development is also a sign that the threat actor is trying out different methods for malware delivery, ranging from coding assessments to counterfeit software.

Dream said the DarkBlinders activity belongs to the same operational cluster as UNC5795 and Dust Specter, citing infrastructure and malware overlaps. Dust Specter, documented by Zscaler in March 2026, refers to a suspected Iran-nexus operation targeting government officials in Iraq by impersonating the country's Ministry of Foreign Affairs.

"Historical server fingerprints, overlapping victimology, and supporting attribution research lead us to assess with medium confidence that UNC5795 and UNC5187 may represent related sub-clusters within the broader APT34 group," it added.

"Their overlapping focus on Iraqi government entities adds context to this technical connection and suggests a shared intelligence collection interest. Combined with their respective APT34 associations, these findings support a medium-confidence assessment that the two clusters are operationally related and may belong to the same broader group."

Prince of Persia Hosts C2 in the U.S. for the First Time in a Decade

The disclosure comes as Prince of Persia (aka Infy), a lesser-known threat group sponsored by the Iranian government, has been observed running one of its C2 servers ("68.65.122[.]203") from the U.S. this year. The server was likely built in July 2026.

The infrastructure is a second-stage C2 server associated with Tornado, a Tonnerre variant that's dropped via one-day software vulnerabilities and uses both HTTPS and the Telegram API for C2. The emergence of new C2 servers in late May 2026 follows three months of inactivity, which has been described as the "longest downtime in nearly two decades of activity by the threat actor."

"We have been monitoring Prince of Persia's exfiltration activity for the past six months," Tomer Bar, associate vice president of security research at Semperis, said. "The number of victims remains low, which could indicate either targeted attacks or difficulties infecting new victims."

"The Iranian threat actor decided to host its new C2 server on U.S. soil — at the same time as the beginning of the recent hostilities between Iran and the United States. This is the last place we expected to find the threat actor hiding."

Title: Nuclear threats and street brawls: Russia, Ukraine report attacks on their emergency alert apps
Context: According to the messages sent to devices after the compromise of Ukraine's alert app, the fake warnings pertained to various threats, such as street fights in Kyiv, chemical...
Full Text: Cyberattacks on both Russia’s and Ukraine’s emergency alert apps resulted in fake messages about missile and nuclear strikes broadcast to the public. Officials from both countries confirmed the attacks, which occurred at similar times, on Sunday evening. According to public statements and messages sent via social media, Ukraine’s alert app was hit first, with the country’s Air Force quick to dispel nuclear fears. "The Air Alert app has likely been compromised," it said via Telegram at around 2100 UTC. "There is no radiation threat! Stay calm, follow our messages on our channel!" At around 0030 UTC on Monday, Russia's Ministry of Emergency Situations confirmed the country’s app had also been abused, with fake messages sent to citizens' devices. "Attention! The Russian Ministry of Emergency Situations' mobile app has been subjected to a massive cyberattack, allowing attackers to send fake information to the public," it said, also via Telegram. "Work is currently underway to patch the vulnerability and restore normal operation." The ministry issued an update around 90 minutes later, saying the app was once again functioning normally, and pointing out that an attack on the app was not the same as a compromise of the state’s national alert system. "Citizens are alerted through primary channels: regional and municipal alert systems (sirens, loudspeakers), communication networks (SMS messaging), and television and radio broadcasts. The mobile app is merely an additional, supporting information service," it stated. Ukraine's Ministry of Digital Affairs also issued a public announcement reminding citizens about how to receive emergency warnings while its “Alarm!” app was down. These include enabling iOS and Android emergency alerts, state-controlled sirens, and other official sources, such as the official social media accounts of Ukraine's government. According to the messages sent to devices after the compromise of Ukraine's alert app, the fake warnings pertained to various threats, such as street fights in Kyiv, chemical attacks, and radiation hazards. Alerts about the threat of nuclear fallout from official government warning systems would normally lead to panic, however, one of the earliest messages sent to citizens was written in Russian and referenced the "Oreshnik" missile, which was an immediate signal that the message may not be genuine. Equivalent alerts sent to Russian citizens also warned of impending nuclear strikes "at all regions of Russia," referencing "P1-Sun," the name of a Ukrainian attack drone. Oleksander Merezhko, who chairs the Ukrainian parliament's foreign affairs committee and noted the suspicious Russian-language alert, told the BBC the attack was almost certainly part of Russia's cyber war. "It's a very unpleasant fact but it is part of cyber war and people in Ukraine understand that," he said. "It is possible and we are quite prepared for such possibilities." Russia has not explicitly blamed Ukraine for the attack on its app, and official sources say the app is running as normal. Ukraine's announcement of the alert app cyberattack came almost simultaneously with the official conclusion of a six-day ceasefire in Kherson. Russia agreed to the rare temporary suspension of conflict to allow hundreds of Ukrainians to evacuate the Russian-occupied city of Olehsky. Russia did not agree to a proposed extension of the ceasefire, which officially ended at around 2100 UTC – around the same time Ukrainians began receiving fake warning messages. ®

Recently, our team exposed sophisticated scam kits designed to steal sensitive data and trick consumers. But underground marketplaces are not just for malware and stolen passwords. They also offer services designed to manipulate your opinion of the products and services you buy every day.

In our latest research, we examined cybercrime forums where sellers advertise illicit “reputation management” services. For the right price, these underground operators offer to flood a product with glowing, five-star ratings or remove negative reviews. This shadowy industry works both ways—artificially boosting reputations and deliberately hiding legitimate complaints.

A major shift we are seeing in this space is the adoption of new technology. We also found that cybercriminals are using AI to automate these fake review campaigns. This could allow them to quickly generate realistic, human-sounding feedback in large volumes without much manual effort.

5 stars as a service

In the first example, discovered on a major English-language underground forum, a seller operating under the handle “aqenova” advertises both five-star review generation and negative review removal services.

The seller’s operations span widely used platforms, including Google, Trustpilot, Yelp, and various mobile app stores. By simply asking prospective buyers, “Just tell me which platform reviews you need?” the seller presents reputation manipulation as something buyers can just order on demand.

Five-star reviews and removal services

Decoding the seller’s FAQ

Analyzing another seller’s (TrustForge) “Frequently Asked Questions” section revealed some surprising details about how these operations reportedly run behind the scenes.

First, the seller emphasizes that real people manually post these reviews, offering a guarantee for both successful delivery and “non-drop”—meaning the platform won’t flag and remove the feedback later.

Remember, a real person posting a review doesn’t mean they’re a real customer. The important question is whether they actually used the product or service and are describing an honest experience.

Second, it appears this is a well-coordinated team effort rather than a solo operation, as the seller charges an extra fee if a buyer wants the main operator to write the review text personally.

However, what caught our attention most was their confidence in beating platform checks. The seller guarantees their fake reviews will stay active, claiming they rely on a closely guarded “private method.” According to TrustForge’s own statements, this method has allowed them to post more than 10,000 fake reviews.

Reputation management FAQ

The clean-up crew: Making bad reviews disappear

A single negative review is often all it takes to create a bad first impression of a product or service. When those negative comments start to pile up, they can completely ruin a business’s reputation and bottom line.

Recognizing how desperate businesses can be to protect their image, our research team discovered underground services specifically offering to remove “fake” or “unfair” reviews from major platforms like Google and Trustpilot.

Of course, the boundary between what is genuinely fake and what a business simply considers “unfair” can be blurry. Businesses can legitimately challenge fabricated reviews, but these services raise concerns about whether genuine customer complaints could also be targeted.

If legitimate customer complaints disappear, consumers lose information that could help them decide where to spend their money.

An offer to remove “fake” or “unfair” Google reviewsAn offer to remove ”fake” or “unfair” review Google reviews

On average, having a single review removed through these underground services costs between $100 and $200. However, the pricing jumps dramatically depending on the platform.

For instance, one seller advertised Airbnb review removal for around $1,100 per review.

When you check a business’s reviews, you’re looking for patterns in other customers’ experiences. If genuine complaints disappear, you could miss repeated problems with refunds, product quality, or customer service.

$1,100 to remove a “fake” or “unfair” Airbnb review

Artificial intelligence, artificial reviews

During the last few months, our research team spotted an interesting thread on an underground forum where two users discussed using AI to mimic human E-E-A-T.

E-E-A-T stands for Experience, Expertise, Authoritativeness, and Trustworthiness. It is a quality evaluation framework outlined in Google’s Search Quality Rater Guidelines, which human evaluators use to assess content quality. E-E-A-T itself is not a direct ranking factor.

In the discussion we observed, one user asked the community if it was possible to use AI to effectively fake these qualities when writing product reviews and artificially boost website rankings. The answer was a resounding yes.

Another user claimed they had never experienced problems getting Google to index their completely AI-generated reviews.

AI vs. E-E-A-T

Behind the scenes: The IP addresses for fake reviews

To keep fake reviews from being flagged and deleted, scammers need to look like everyday consumers. To help do this, they can use something called “residential and mobile proxies,” which route their traffic through other internet connections to disguise where it comes from.

Think of an IP address as your computer’s caller ID. When scammers use bulk IP addresses from giant data centers, platforms may spot and block that traffic as coming from commercially hosted infrastructure. Residential proxies, on the other hand, route traffic through real, physical home internet connections—just like the Wi-Fi you use in your living room. Mobile proxies work the same way, but use real cellular networks.

Our team recently discovered a seller on an underground forum acting as a direct supplier of these residential and mobile connections. The seller explicitly advertises them as perfect for running fake review campaigns.

Residential and mobile proxies advertised for fake review campaigns

How to avoid being misled by fake reviews

The main goal of this research isn’t to make you panic or stop trusting every online review you read. We want to raise awareness about what happens behind the scenes, so you can make more informed buying decisions.

If a product or offer seems too good to be true, but is backed by a mountain of perfect five-star reviews, take a moment to pause. Scammers often use these artificially boosted ratings to make a bad deal look reassuring.

Read recent reviews and some of the middle-rated ones, rather than relying on the overall score. Look for recurring details about the things that matter to you, such as durability, delivery, or getting your money back.

Look for repeated wording or sudden bursts of glowing feedback. These signs don’t prove a review is fake, but they’re reasons to take a closer look. Check the seller’s contact details and return policy, too.

Title: Applebee’s customer data exposed by password left in app
Context: Applebee’s has fixed a security flaw that exposed customers’ personal information after a researcher discovered a database password embedded in the restaurant chain’s Android app
Full Text:
Applebee’s has fixed a security flaw that exposed customers’ personal information after a researcher discovered a database password embedded in the restaurant chain’s Android app.

The researcher, Robert Wiggins, found the password with help from AI. It gave him access to an internal Applebee’s customer database. A password written directly into an app’s code or configuration is known as a hardcoded credential. Anyone who extracts it may be able to use it to access the system.

The exposed database contained:

Names, email addresses, and email-verification status

Dates of birth, phone numbers, and ZIP codes

Veteran status

Account-creation dates and login counts

IP addresses from customers’ most recent logins, which can indicate their approximate location

TechCrunch independently checked Wiggins’ findings. It created an Applebee’s account with dummy information, which Wiggins successfully retrieved from the database.

According to TechCrunch, Wiggins could not find a suitable way to report the issue to Applebee’s or its parent company, Dine Brands, so he asked the publication to help contact them. TechCrunch held its story until the fix was confirmed. Applebee’s confirmed on October 29 that it had addressed the issue.

It’s unclear how many customers’ records were in the database. Dine Brands says it has not found evidence of unauthorized access, but its investigation is ongoing.

How to stay safe

The database fields described by TechCrunch did not include payment card details or account passwords. That does not tell us whether anyone accessed the database before the fix, so customers should watch for targeted scams.

Names, email addresses, phone numbers, and other personal details could help scammers make messages look relevant and convincing.

Be wary of unexpected Applebee’s-themed emails, texts, or calls. Be especially skeptical of messages offering refunds or compensation, warning that your account will be closed, or asking you to “verify” payment details.

Check security notices through a route you trust. Open the app directly or visit Applebee’s website yourself rather than following a link in an unexpected message. If necessary, contact the company using details you find independently.

Unsure whether a message is a scam? Check it with Malwarebytes’ Scam Guard for an assessment and advice on what to do next.

When sharing personal information, consider why the company needs it and whether you trust it to keep the information safe.

Title: Report: Most Fraud Attacks Target Existing Customer Relationships
Context: A new report from TransUnion has found that 81% of digital fraud attacks target existing customer relationships, with more than half of U
Full Text:
A new report from TransUnion has found that 81% of digital fraud attacks target existing customer relationships, with more than half of U.S. businesses reporting increased scam and fraud activity over the past year.

“Identity-based fraud attacks often arise before organizations have sufficient information to establish trust in new customers,” the report says. “While account creation is a critical trust-establishing event, most fraud exposure occurs after the customer relationship has already been established. Different risk patterns appear across account creation, login, and financial transaction activities, especially for AI-enabled fraud. For instance, AI can help fraudsters rapidly generate or modify identities, credentials and interactions to target the weakest controls across the customer lifecycle.”

Most respondents cited synthetic identity fraud, which uses exposed consumer information and AI to craft phony personas, as their top concern over the next two years.

“Forty-three percent of U.S. business leaders said the growing scale and sophistication of fraud is placing significant or severe pressure on their organizations,” TransUnion says. “Synthetic identity fraud is a key concern, with 67% expecting it to increase over the next two years and 53% citing it as the threat they are least prepared to address. In the U.S., 51% of business leaders reported increased scam and authorized fraud activity over the past year. U.S. lenders face an estimated $2.4 billion in exposure tied to synthetic identities as of June 30, 2026.”

The increase is partly due to adversarial use of AI tools, which allow attackers to drastically improve the scale and sophistication of social engineering attacks.

“AI has fundamentally changed the economics of fraud by automating activities that once required significant human effort, including creating identities, generating content, and targeting victims,” TransUnion says. “This allows fraudsters to accelerate and scale their attacks faster than organizations can adapt their detection capabilities and mitigation strategies.

TransUnion has the story: https://newsroom.transunion.com/81-of-suspected-digital-fraud-attacks-target-existing-customer-relationships-transunion-finds/

Title: Bitter Deploys PapRAT in Asian Cyber-Espionage Campaign
Context: " He warned that deleting the first implant found might not remove the attacker
Full Text:
A suspected South Asian cyber-espionage group has been observed pairing native Windows tools with a custom remote access trojan (RAT) dubbed PapRAT to maintain access to targeted organizations.

Cara Lin of Fortinet's FortiGuard Labs detailed the campaign in research published on November 2, attributing it with high confidence to Bitter, also tracked as TA397, based on lure filenames, command-and-control (C2) patterns, file metadata and malware analysis.

FortiGuard Labs tracked the campaign over several months and it described the targets as South Asian organizations, though its telemetry maps also show activity in Southeast Asia and South Korea. Lure files referred to a bilateral meeting request, an ambassador's letter about the 11th Belt and Road Summit and a 2026 gala dinner invitation.

Read more on Bitter: Middle East Hack-for-Hire Operation Traced to South Asian Cyber Espionage Group

Three Infection Chains, One Without a Malware Binary

The first chain took a living-off-the-land approach: a malicious Windows shortcut (LNK) file abused the built-in ftp.exe utility to run scripts and create scheduled tasks.

Those tasks used curl to fetch fresh commands from attacker servers, and the chain deployed no traditional malware executable. FortiGuard Labs said operators could change their instructions on the server without pushing a new binary.

"When an intrusion leverages trusted system processes, signature-based controls simply have nothing to alert on," said Shane Barney, CISO at Keeper Security. He argued for least-privilege access, tighter limits on native scripting engines and the removal of standing administrative rights.

The other two chains delivered PapRAT through Windows Installer (MSI) packages, one hidden with a decoy spreadsheet in a virtual hard disk (VHDX) image and the other fetched via an internet shortcut in a RAR archive.

PapRAT Shifts to Rust and Pulls In WmRAT

The C++ build of PapRAT posed as a Microsoft component, beaconed over plaintext HTTP and supported eight commands, including remote shell access, file transfers and screenshots. A Rust variant obtained more recently switched to HTTPS and added three more, for PowerShell execution, pausing and exiting.

In the third chain, PapRAT downloaded WmRAT, a C++ RAT previously documented by other researchers, which FortiGuard Labs cited as a further indicator linking the campaign to Bitter.

Jason Soroko, senior fellow at certificate lifecycle management firm Sectigo, said the Windows-tools route meant "a search for PapRAT alone could miss part of the campaign." He warned that deleting the first implant found might not remove the attacker.

FortiGuard's recommendations included handling unexpected LNK files, internet shortcuts, disk images and MSI installers with care.

In the first chain, though, FortiGuard found no PapRAT at all, only a shortcut file, Windows tools, scripts and scheduled tasks.

Title: Shutting the Door on the XCPE Botnet
Context: We found this malicious software built directly into many different device models and brands over multiple years, supported by dedicated infrastructure and constantly evolving...
Full Text:
Introduction

Last week, Google and industry partners dismantled the XCPE backdoor which enrolled more than 1.3 million set-top boxes into a botnet. We assess with high confidence that the backdoor and botnet were intentionally developed, deployed, and operated for financial gain by Videostrong Technology Co., an Android Original Equipment Manufacturer (OEM) and Original Design Manufacturer (ODM).

Videostrong monetized the backdoor by selling access to criminal affiliates and loading those affiliates’ malware modules onto infected devices. These secondary modules were conducting ad-fraud; silently enrolling infected devices into residential proxy networks; and loading additional malware onto XCPE-compromised devices. We also took action to disrupt the command and control (C2) domains that operate these affiliate modules. Because these affiliates each have diversified distribution channels for their modules beyond XCPE, we assess that taking down their C2 domains will sever access to at least 10 million additional compromised devices.

We found this malicious software built directly into many different device models and brands over multiple years, supported by dedicated infrastructure and constantly evolving configurations to evade detection and manage their affiliates. We believe this campaign wasn’t an isolated rogue insider or a development oversight. As a result, Google has cut ties with Videostrong and banned them from making devices with preloaded Google apps.

Google requires OEMs go through a comprehensive suite of compatibility and security tests to ensure a consistent and safe user experience across the Android ecosystem. However, Videostrong employed obfuscation techniques to exploit a gap in our tests and load malicious code after the device's first boot. As a result, Google has implemented changes to its existing review process to better safeguard against similar activity in the future. A device manufacturer intentionally infecting their users with malware is an unacceptable breach of trust, and represents a serious risk to those users. Without users’ knowledge or consent, infected devices were offered as a distribution mechanism for a wide array of criminal actors. This led to a variety of malicious activities being conducted on and through the devices, including ad-fraud, data exfiltration, and routing malicious network traffic through the devices.

We worked closely with Japan’s National Police Agency, Lumen, HUMAN Security, Plume, Synthient, and TrendAI to analyze this malware ecosystem and disrupt its operations.

While we expect this disruption to have a significant effect on these criminal operations, this is not the end of our work combatting malicious activity. Backdoor operators, ad-fraud rings, and residential proxy providers operate as an interconnected supply chain. Point-in-time disruptions are a critical tool to protect our users, but lasting disruption in this fluid ecosystem will require continued targeting of this infrastructure.

Google undertook the following actions to support disruption of the XCPE botnet:

Legal action to take down the domains and servers Videostrong used to control the botnet and install malware modules

Legal action to take down C2 domains used by over a dozen malware families loaded as modules via this backdoor

Banned Videostrong and any future subsidiaries or affiliates from building and selling certified Android devices in the future, or supplying software to other certified vendors

Implementing improvements to how we ensure the integrity of firmware on certified Android TV devices

Overview

The x.cpe network was built for ongoing profit. By giving malware affiliates backdoor access, the operators conspired to monetize these devices long after purchase.

Figure 1: XCPE malware overview

Malware

Since at least late 2024, Videostrong has evolved its pre-installed malware from simple single-stage droppers into a modular, three-stage architecture designed for resilience and multi-tenant monetization:

Primary Backdoor: Operating at the android.uid.system privilege level, x.cpe (running as com.oemservice in some builds) is preloaded in the firmware partition. If uninstalled by a user, it automatically reinstalls from the /oem/ partition upon reboot, maintaining persistent system-level access. Its main function is to establish and facilitate communications between the C2 server and the loader and execution engine.

Loader and Execution Engine: To evade security scans, x.cpe acts primarily as the C2 communicator and offloads module execution to an external loader, com.abc.nexus. This file employs native anti-analysis utilities to thwart sandbox detection, and configures and initializes the monetization modules. Most recently, com.abc.nexus has itself been phased out in favor of using more tailored dropper malware that loads and executes single modules.

Monetization Modules: Videostrong monetizes its backdoored devices by loading monetization modules which are developed by entities other than Videostrong that act as affiliates. These modules are deployed as native ELF daemons, embedded SDKs compiled directly into the com.abc.nexus DEX bytecode, or are fetched as secondary APKs from the malware staging infrastructure. The loaded modules transform infected devices into residential proxy exit nodes (e.g., Linkfog, AppSalt, NetNut), ad-fraud engines (e.g., CBOXTV, HiddenView), or execute additional backdoors that load even more monetization modules (e.g. Moyu, Spirit).

Infrastructure

Command and Control: The botnet uses a two-stage C2 process. It first initiates HTTP POST requests to fetch dynamic configuration settings, geolocation data, and STUN server parameters. It then establishes a persistent, real-time Message Queuing Telemetry Transport (MQTT) connection to receive instructions for silent app installations, arbitrary shell commands, screen captures, and network reconnaissance. MQTT is a lightweight, publish-and-subscribe network protocol designed for low-bandwidth, high-latency, or unreliable remote networks.

Malware staging infrastructure: Additional monetization modules as well as various shell scripts and legitimate applications are hosted remotely and downloaded by infected devices upon command from the operator via the MQTT broker. A significant majority of these files are hosted as Github releases on operator-owned Github pages. Other files are hosted on operator-controlled servers and file hosting sites.

Malware Deep Dive

Backdoor Initialization

The infection chain begins with a stub package (called x.cpe in some builds and com.oemservice in others) preloaded in the system partition of the firmware and running at the android.uid.system privilege level. This stub has limited functionality. Upon boot, it checks the device's oem/ directory for the corresponding x.cpe package and initiates installation into the /data/app/ directory as outlined below.

To maintain inter-process state across the firmware ecosystem, x.cpe exports two ContentProviders, which expose structured configuration tables storing runtime parameters, device identifiers, proxy configuration blobs, and execution flags accessible by co-installed system applications. This enables other apps in Videostrong’s ecosystem, such as their YokaTV Player streaming software, to fetch configuration parameters provided by the C2 server mentioned below.

C2 Configuration

The malware utilizes a two-stage communications protocol. It first fetches initial bootstrap configurations via an HTTP request, followed by a persistent MQTT subscription to receive commands and module download instructions.

To dynamically derive the HTTP C2 bootstrap server, it follows the following routine:

Queries content://com.release.debug.provider/configs for private_url via x.cpe.util.ExtraReadUtils.

Queries the Android system property to determine if ro.mecool.device is true.

If true, it defaults to http://mcstb.anyevonline.com:8000

If false, it dynamically generates the following: http://stb[AndroidVersion][Type].anyevonline.com:8000.

Using the selected hostname, the client makes an HTTP POST request with an AES-encrypted JSON object containing hardware telemetry (SN, MAC, model, firmware version) to the following endpoints:

/router/config/mqtt: This endpoint provides MQTT broker details (including Broker Hostname, TCP Port, Authentication Tokens/Passwords, and the specific Topic structure: /device/{model}/{chipId}/{action}. After receiving this data, the device initiates a persistent, real-time socket connection to the MQTT broker.

/router/config/acs: This endpoint response returns URLs for ip-api[.]com and a Google STUN server to enable the malware to identify geolocation and public IP and port mapping to traverse network address translation (NAT) boundaries. It also returns a URL (http://ott.szbboys[.]com:8000/cpe/file/upload for uploading files, logs, or diagnostic dumps from the device, and returns flags to configure ad modules (adBwmActive, adDevourUse, adDevourCode), and to enable or disable core malware modules.

/router/config/app: This endpoint provides module-level configs, including server mappings and parameters, which x.cpe decrypts and passes to a SQLite ContentProvider named ShareProvider (com.oem.share.provider). By exposing this inter-process data interface, x.cpe enables modules to retrieve up-to-date upstream infrastructure parameters (such as URLs for additional configs, user manuals, etc).

MQTT Capabilities

Following initial configuration, persistent real-time C2 communication is managed by the MQTT library (x.cpe.mqtt.MqttUtils). All identified samples analyzed to date utilize a single broker hostname, mqtt.szbboys[.]com.

Specific MQTT topics are mapped to specific actions, including:

Silent Application Installation: Fetches remote APKs to a temporary directory.

Disable Google Play Protect: To bypass security, AppUtils.disablePackageVerify() targets the global setting "package_verifier_user_consent" via Settings.Global.putInt and sets it to -1, disabling Google Play Protect app verification.

Arbitrary Shell Execution: Executes remote commands via sh under system UID privilege level. Results are published to the MQTT broker.

Shell Script Execution: Downloads and executes shell scripts via x.cpe.util.RunCmds.

Remote Desktop Monitor & Screen Capture: Utilizes android.app.Instrumentation.sendKeyDownUpSync() to inject keycodes and Java reflection on hidden APIs (android.view.SurfaceControl.screenshot / SurfaceControl$ScreenshotHardwareBuffer) to continuously capture the screen, compress to JPEG, and publish over MQTT.

Network Reconnaissance: Invokes embedded binaries (libtraceroute.so) to fingerprint the victim network, and perform standard ping tests. The binaries also perform robust AS-lookup WHOIS routing queries.

Our analysis of the C2 data indicates the preponderance of interactions with victim devices were related to module install, uninstall, and configuration actions. We also observed Videostrong operators executing sensitive actions on the device, including capturing live screenshots; injecting keystrokes; exfiltrating sensitive data including account information, device information, package inventories, and system logs; and executing shell scripts and commands, including to establish reverse shells on devices.

Loader and Execution Engine Details

Earlier versions of x.cpe directly embedded malicious monetization modules. In late 2024 – possibly as a response to earlier Google enforcement related to BadBox – Videostrong removed malicious modules from x.cpe and introduced a separate malicious package they developed, com.abc.nexus, which x.cpe routes instructions and data to via Inter-Process Communication (IPC). Modern variants of x.cpe facilitate C2 communications but pass configuration parameters, module updates, and other payloads to com.abc.nexus as the execution engine. We believe the actor may have evolved the malware in this way in an attempt to ensure x.cpe could remain undetected.

Upon boot, com.abc.nexus.broadcast.BootReceiver broadcasts the com.abc.nexus.data intent, bootstrapping com.abc.nexus.service.CoreService. Within CoreService.onCreate, the application performs maintenance and persistence tasks. The main logic sets up a listener through RemoteMessageHandler for IPC communications from x.cpe,and parses JSON payloads received from it.

After these steps, CoreService initializes the monetization modules. com.abc.nexus services extract and orchestrate a series of nested native libraries and dynamically downloaded secondary payloads which vary significantly based on sample. Many versions of com.abc.nexus come preloaded with four or more embedded modules, while other versions contain as few as one. The most common malware modules include TitanService, BwmService, AdtimeService, lb102Service, and LinkfogService (sometimes called AgentService). Discussion of these and other modules can be found in the monetization modules section.

Persistence and Evasion

The malware operators implement a number of mechanisms to establish persistence and thwart detection and analysis.

As a system preload, x.cpe cannot be removed by the user. If x.cpe is uninstalled from /data/app/, upon reboot the x.cpe service BootReceiver follows the same routine outlined above and reinstalls the package.

The backdoor is able to silently download additional files to the device and execute them without user consent because it first wipes user consent configuration on the device and then disables Google Play Protect:

public static void disablePackageVerify() { PreferenceUtils.setPackageVerifyFromUser(CPEApp.instance, true); AppUtils.setPackageVerify(-1); // Actioning a bypass against GPP evaluation }

Figure 2: Disabling Google Play Protect

In many variants of com.abc.nexus, we observed the extraction of a sophisticated anti-analysis and process hardening utility libseccomp_guard.so, which runs prior to the initialization of malware modules, to ensure they remain protected from automated sandboxes and security instrumentation. It filters system calls to prevent the pausing or termination of individual threads, denies cross-process interference to ensure isolation, and prevents the spawning of child processes.

Evolution

Since August 2026, new dropper packages have been installed via the MQTT channel, which appear to be synchronized with the mass-uninstallation of com.abc.nexus across the botnet. We assess this may represent a new evolution of the malware to further evade detection. These new packages are disguised as Android system applications, with names such as com.android.system.ntp and com.android.sso.auth.handler. Where com.abc.nexus could act as a general purpose loader and execution engine (executing instructions passed to it from x.cpe), these packages instead install single monetization modules (such as AppSalt). Multiple variants of these packages extract a native ELF file, libexploit.so, which in turn executes functions nativeAdbRoot() and nativeAdbShell(). These functions restart the local adbd service as root, and initiate an ADB shell connection. Following this, the app uses the connection to install itself in the system partition. The system partition is remounted as read-write and the payload replicates itself to a newly minted directory in /system/priv-app/ and creates an XML file at /system/etc/permissions/privapp-permissions-<app name>.xml. This file grants the malware android.permission.INSTALL_PACKAGES and android.permission.REBOOT.

The app configures the malware modules through hardcoded configuration parameters, and does not listen for x.cpe IPC messages. The app itself is controlled by the operators via shell scripts pushed via the broker and executed by x.cpe. These include setting the property persist.networkstack.uninstall (which, when read by the app, triggers uninstallation and cleanup), persist.networkstack.skip_system_install (which skips system installation, forcing it to remain running in /data/app/), and persist.networkstack.install_time (which implements timestomping, overriding the default timestamp of the app to align with the other packages installed in the system directory).

Botnet composition

The botnet is globally dispersed, with certain concentrations possibly implying market penetration for the brand distributor.

Figure 3: Global distribution of x.cpe

While the overwhelming majority of the infected devices in the XCPE botnet are Android TV set-top boxes, we observed a number of other infected Android-based IoT devices, including telehealth devices, karaoke machines, and digital signage devices.

Monetization

x.cpe loads a variety of malicious modules for monetization. Most often the modules are associated with residential proxy services and bandwidth sharing, but we've also observed ad fraud modules. Given that a single device may be running multiple modules providing the same or similar functionality (e.g., as many as three residential proxy SDKs installed on a single device) it is clear that Videostrong seeks to monetize every infected device to the greatest extent possible.

Services are loaded by com.abc.nexus via three methods:

Native Daemons: Native ELF binaries prepackaged with com.abc.nexus, which are unpacked to data directories and spawned as background processes with system/root privileges.

Embedded SDKs / Services: Java/Kotlin SDKs compiled directly into Nexus and invoked via Android Service lifecycles or IPC broadcast triggers.

Dynamic Droppers & Secondary APK Installers: Downloader function that pulls remote native ELFs or secondary standalone APKs and invokes system package managers. Nexus receives messages from x.cpe directing it to download specific modules.

Malware modules loaded via the backdoor include the following:

Residential Proxy / Bandwidth Sharing Modules

LINKFOG

Com.abc.nexus’s LinkfogService unpacks a Go binary named lw_android_agent from assets/ to local app storage and supplies it with vendor parameters. This service silently turns infected devices into residential edge computing and PCDN proxy exit nodes. It connects to FRP reverse tunnels, and uploads bandwidth accounting metrics to Linkfog API backends. Linkfog (operated by Beijing Linkfog Technology via 点心云 / Dianxinyun) brands itself as a “Peer-to-Peer Content Delivery Network”.

Jaguar

The com.abc.nexus AdtimeService extracts libjaguar.so from assets/. The file is an unobfuscated 32-bit ELF binary written in C, compiled as a native Android binary. It utilizes JNI (Java Native Interface) to initialize its core routines, dynamically derives a ChaCha20 decryption key via ARM NEON SIMD instructions to decode heavily obfuscated configurations , and establishes an encrypted C2 channel. Upon successful registration, the C2 responds with JSON configuration specifying proxy endpoints. The proxy command loop x_ctrl_do_ctrl_msg delegates proxy operations based on incoming JSON variable commands, and is capable of both TCP and UDP relay.

AppSalt / Honeygain

AppSalt SDK is the residential proxy SDK owned by Honeygain, which is in turn owned by Oxylabs. com.abc.nexus.service.CoreService initializes Appsalt SDK. First, the application obtains an Appsalt SDK API key from a native library libnative_keys.so by calling its getAppsaltKey() function. Appsalt SDK is initialized without displaying a consent screen - instead it explicitly calls the optIn() method which sets a consent flag without displaying any user interface. During Appsalt SDK startup it checks the application's installation source and stops execution if the application was installed from the official Google Play Store.

Once Appsalt is successfully initialized it establishes a WebSocket connection with the primary command and control domain. Appsalt uses JSON-formatted messages for initial check-in (registration) and heartbeat requests. Appsalt command and control servers use MessagePack formatted messages to issue commands pertaining to proxy operations. Appsalt SDK is configured with an initial set of domains that act as proxy gateways. The list of proxy gateways can be updated by the command and control server. The device establishes UDP / QUIC connections with these gateways.

BWM / IPWeb

This residential proxy and bandwidth-sharing node is implemented through the com.abc.nexus.service.BwmService component (sometimes named com.abc.nexus.service.SN4Service) and its associated SDK. Upon initialization, it secures itself within an isolated sandbox environment, captures device telemetry, and registers with a remote server over UDP. From this C2, it receives instructions to initiate a Java NIO TCP multiplexed proxy tunnel. The service functions to route arbitrary traffic through the infected device on behalf of a remote threat actor.

GaGaNode

GaGaNode is the first-party SDK owned by residential proxy operator IPCola. It connects over TCP to a primary C2 server and sends heartbeat beacon data over HTTP POST to a separate server. The SDK both contains its own proxy relay functionality, and it initializes additional proxy SDKs from affiliates. Upon device registration to the C2, com.gaganode.sdk.node.endpoint.a receives incoming packets from relay servers and places them in queue for the client to read and proxy through its exit node socket. The service manages multiple proxy sessions at once (referred to as clients), and each client has its own tcp/udp queue for messages.

We observe GaGaNode initializing PopaNet/NetNut and EarnFM Fleet residential proxy SDKs. GaGaNode/IPCola is thus likely able to further monetize its SDK and offer these affiliates access to the infected exit nodes.

NetNut / Popanet

Popanet is a residential proxy SDK developed by NetNut, a residential proxy operator. The GaGaNode module initiates the Popanet SDK (io.popanet.Popa). This malware is identical to the malware described in our previous disruption of NetNut. All C2 infrastructure used by Popanet samples connected to x.cpe was taken down as part of the earlier Netnut disruption.

Traffmonetizer

The Traffmonetizer SDK is initialized inside the primary background service com.abc.nexus.service.CoreService. CoreService operation depends on the availability of policy JSON provided by the XCPE backdoor via IPC. Before calling Traffmonetizer SDK initialization methods, the application obtains a Traffmonetizer SDK API key from the native library libnative_keys.so by calling its getTraffmonetizerKey() function.

Traffmonetizer functionality is split between two components where the Android SDK acts as a state machine which handles native library callbacks through asynchronous event dispatchers. ServiceBloc monitors connection status updates from the native callbacks and ConnectivityBloc monitors Wi-Fi and mobile data network changes.

Traffmonetizer native library initialization and configuration is followed by a call to baseClientStart() which establishes a WebSocket connection to a C2 server. Traffmonetizer uses a single WebSocket (TLS) connection to the command and control server to multiplex control messages and tunneled connections (supports both TCP and UDP). Traffmonetizer also supports “Content Delivery” tunneling which allows nodes to tunnel bandwidth-intensive traffic.

EarnFM

EarnFM is a residential proxy provider, and Fleet SDK is the provider’s SDK that enrolls devices as exit nodes into the proxy network. In com.abc.nexus, FleetSDK is initialized by com.gaganode.sdk as mentioned above. FleetSdk then loads native binary libfleetshare.so.

FleetSDK establishes a persistent WebSocket connection with its primary C2 server for routing arbitrary network traffic. Incoming tasking frames are received over the WebSocket channel and processed in a continuous loop. Messages contain structured JSON commands instructing the daemon to connect to specific remote hosts, with support for both TCP and UDP.

Backdoor Modules

Spirit

Spirit is a dynamic code loading backdoor. Spirit employs multiple stages. The first stage payload fetches device information (hardware, operating system, and manufacturer/brand information and geolocation), posting it over HTTP to a hardcoded C2 server, and fetches a list of additional modules to download from the server. The second stage communicates with a separate server, and is used for tasking, config sync, module retrieval, heartbeats, and reporting. We have observed Spirit loading a significant amount of additional malware monetization modules, including some of the families already directly loaded by com.abc.nexus.

Moyu

Moyu is a 3-stage backdoor previously observed as part of the BadBox enterprise. On x.cpe-backdoored devices, we observed it initialized by com.abc.nexus.service.DevourService. The first stage is an offline dropper that reconstructs and loads an embedded second stage. Stage two polls an update C2 to download, decrypt, and load the third stage. Stage three implements a backdoor with hidden Double-WebView click/conversion fraud, persistent clipboard hijacking, and secondary dynamically loaded JAR execution and a separate residential proxy trojan.

Bird

Bird is a 2-stage backdoor previously tied to the BadBox enterprise. Stage 1 beacons a device and analysis-environment profile to its C2 server and, when the server approves, downloads, decrypts, and loads the Stage 2 JAR. Stage 2 implements a dynamic code loading backdoor (two plugin loaders plus a C2-driven reflective method invoker), a separate downloader (silent APK installation and Accessibility-driven Google Play installs), and ad abuse (lockscreen ads, overlays, browser launches).

Fission

Fission is a dynamic code loading (DCL) backdoor embedded within standard video applications (e.g., com.newtv.cboxtv). Upon initialization, the first stage plugin contacts its C2 server to download additional modules. The decrypted second stage payload fetches execution targets and tracking URLs from the C2. The request sends an unencrypted POST request with tracking metrics from the internal DeviceManager.

The payload we observed was configured to commit ad fraud. Rather than rendering visible advertisements in a WebView or UI component, the Stage 2 plugin executes headlessly in the background. The module queries ad server endpoints in the background to retrieve ad placement responses, parses out both primary impression beacons (pvm) and third-party tracking monitor URLs (pvtpm), and immediately fires HTTP GET requests to each tracking endpoint to register a fake ad view without displaying creative content. When executing inside specific smart-TV application stores (com.changhong.appstore or com.tcl.appmarket2), the plugin initializes and triggers the ad SDK directly to report synthetic ad exposures.

Ad-Fraud

HiddenView

We observed HiddenView loaded remotely from the attacker’s Github channel as com.ota.service. It is a standalone ad fraud application capable of running in the background using a transparent window overlay, using hidden WebViews to load targeted web pages and simulate user interaction (scrolling, clicking, typing, media playback), playing media unattended, and capturing the user’s screen.

How the pieces come together

Configuration messages pushed via MQTT (action ext/lib/config) demonstrate how x.cpe, com.abc.nexus and various monetization modules function together.

Upon registration, subscribed devices receive a ext/lib/config message, which contains configuration parameters for malicious plugins. This includes:

Limits on system resources:

"constraints": [ { "cpu": 70, "ioRead": 5000, "ioWrite": 5000, "libCode": "linkfog", "memory": 50, "reportAlarm": true, "trigger": 3 }

Figure 4: System resource limits configuration payload

Module name, download location per architecture, hashes, and weight (relative priority for system resources):

"infos": [ { "libChannel": "SZKJ", "libCode": "linkfog", "libResource": [ { "address": "https://github.com/Aviciiii/ott/releases/download/cpe_ext_lib/lw_android_agent_special_ndk_64", "architecture": "arm64-v8a", "md5": "abd0b6de6fdf78234f5dab098d5dd229" }, { "address": "https://github.com/Aviciiii/ott/releases/download/cpe_ext_lib/lw_android_agent_special_ndk_32_20250717", "architecture": "armeabi-v7a", "md5": "d8971688d1929b6ed915b80eca7e7e3f" } ], "libWeight": 5 },

Figure 5: Module configuration payload

Devices are assigned to one of six timezone-separated pools on the ott.szbboys[.]com domain:

"region": "Iraq", "serverPool": { "defaultPool": "Pool5", "lastUpdated": "2025-08-06 17:00:00",

Figure 6: Server Pool configuration payload

The “policys” section instructs com.abc.nexus which modules to download and run:

"status": [ { "enable": true, "libCode": "linkfog" }, { "enable": false, "libCode": "bwm" }, { "enable": false, "libCode": "adtime" }, { "enable": false, "libCode": "admoyu" }, { "enable": false, "libCode": "titan" }, { "enable": false, "libCode": "lb102" } ],

Figure 7: Module activation payload

x.cpe passes on these configuration parameters to com.abc.nexus for the given module on the device. Devices report bandwidth usage and alarms back to serverPool to stay within the configured constraints.

When com.abc.nexus acknowledges receiving the bundle, x.cpe immediately publishes ext/lib/config/reply back to the MQTT broker:

"code": 0, "msg": "success", "data": "received data success and applying", "async": true, "immediately": false

Figure 8: x.cpe response payload

Infrastructure

As previously mentioned, devices first connect to various endpoints on *.anyevonline[.]com for initial bootstrap, registration, and configuration. Earlier malware versions used various hostnames of {*tms | *ott | *ota}.szbboys[.]com for the same purpose.

While earlier versions of the malware used HTTP for C2, and then a blended C2 approach with both HTTP and MQTT, static analysis of current versions indicate they exclusively send/receive C2 communications via MQTT. A single MQTT broker orchestrates all MQTT C2 communications for samples we’ve identified. Hostname mqtt.szbboys[.]com is resolved by hosts 219.134.163[.]210 and 219.134.163[.]211. It listens on non-standard MQTT ports 3885-3887.

The malware constructs OkHttp requests for file downloads after tasking via the MQTT broker. Files are hosted on several services:

Several Github release pages

The filemail[.]com file sharing service

Two operator-controlled servers hosted on IPs 38.145.197[.]135 and 23.94.49[.]57

Netflow telemetry on the broker nodes (219.134.163[.]210/.211) indicates that while infected devices communicate over ports 3885–3887, operators likely manage the broker and dispatch tasking via interactive HTTP REST API (port 8082), WebSocket (port 8083), and EMQX web administration console (port 18083) sessions originating from non-bot IP space.

Call to Action

While we believe our actions have seriously impacted over a dozen malicious actors, the underlying illicit market is resilient. Backdoor operators, ad-fraud rings, and residential proxy providers operate as an interconnected supply chain, and when one component is disrupted, operators quickly pivot to new loaders or rival monetization SDKs. Creating lasting change requires accountability across the hardware supply chain, the residential proxy industry, and the broader technology ecosystem.

Accountability and Reform

A device manufacturer intentionally infecting their users with malware is an unacceptable breach of trust. By turning everyday hardware into persistent beachheads for criminal affiliates, Videostrong prioritized illicit post-sale recurring revenue over the safety and privacy of its users. Downstream hardware brands, white-label resellers, telecommunications providers, and online e-commerce marketplaces also share responsibility for closing this vector.
