Title: Unwrapping Retail Peak Season Cyber Threats
Context: This includes the SolarWinds software supply chain compromise in December 2020 and the exploitation of a Log4j zero-day vulnerability in December 2021
Full Text:
Introduction

During the 2025 peak holiday shopping season, the National Retail Federation predicted that retail sales would surpass $1 trillion USD for the first time, with Salesforce later reporting that online sales equated to $1.3 trillion globally. This included $294 billion in the United States and $262 billion influenced by AI and agents. Cybercriminals are highly aware that the holiday season is generally the most profitable for retailers, and look to capitalize on it for their own financial gain.

This blog explores the main cyber threats that retail organizations need to be aware of and prepared to defend against as we approach peak shopping season in 2026. We highlight notable security events that occurred in prior years during this time period. We also examine relevant threats from both an enterprise and guest point of view and provide examples of the evolving trend of autonomous attacks that could impact retailers.

Background

Since 2020, there have been several notable security events disclosed toward the end of peak shopping season. This includes the SolarWinds software supply chain compromise in December 2020 and the exploitation of a Log4j zero-day vulnerability in December 2021. Both events posed complexities for retail security teams as they occurred during a period where code freezes were likely in place. This limited the ability for organizations to make changes to critical technology systems to prevent any operational disruption to core technology infrastructure.

In addition to these broader threat landscape events, retailers typically face an increase in many types of financially-motivated attacks during this time period. This includes tactics and techniques designed to target both enterprises and guests alike.

Based on years of previous activity against Fortune 100 retailers from cyber threats during peak shopping season, these are the types of attacks that retailers should be primarily focused on detecting and responding to this time of year.

Enterprise-Focused Threats

Ransomware

Ransomware continues to pose a major risk for retail organizations heading into peak shopping season due to potential for operational disruption that could negatively impact the guest experience (in-store and online) and supply chain requirements (inventory).

As of Sept. 30, 2026, ransomware operators have claimed 565 retail organizations as victims this year, with the median company revenue hovering around $22 million. The top three ransomware operators that claimed retail victims are TGR-CRI-1173 (aka The Gentlemen), Spikey Scorpius (aka Qilin) and Howling Scorpius (aka Akira).

One example of a ransomware incident that impacted a retailer during peak shopping season occurred in December 2023, when Ambitious Scorpius (aka ALPHV) stole millions of customer records from a victim and caused significant operational disruption in terms of delayed order fulfillment, canceled e-commerce orders and slowed inventory replenishment.

To mitigate ransomware risks that jeopardize uptime, retailers need to deploy automated containment mechanisms alongside robust network segmentation strategies. Security teams should:

Leverage advanced endpoint protection featuring real-time behavioral analysis to rapidly isolate compromised assets

Enforce zero trust access across the enterprise to limit lateral movement

Utilize inline sandboxing capabilities to inspect suspicious binaries and stop zero-day exploits before execution

Data Theft and Extortion

Data theft and extortion attacks continue to rise in volume as cybercriminals like Bling Libra (aka ShinyHunters) and Hazy Scorpius (aka CL0P) forgo ransomware to accelerate their attack lifecycles without compromising their actions on objectives.

The 2026 Unit 42 Global Incident Response Report found that extortion incidents without the use of encryption (78%) in 2025 dropped below the 90% range for the first time in several years. Consumers put a lot of trust in retailers safeguarding their personal data, and such extortion incidents this time of year severely damage it.

One notable example occurred in December 2021, when Bling Libra stole hundreds of gigabytes of data from a victim. This included customer email addresses, hashed passwords, customer payment invoices and internal employee files containing salaries and tax IDs.

To mitigate data theft and extortion risks threatening customer personal information and transactional records, organizations must deploy comprehensive enterprise data loss prevention (DLP) controls across their enterprise environments to identify and restrict illicit data exfiltration. Security teams should combine DLP capabilities with continuous attack surface management (ASM) to identify and remediate publicly accessible systems, while implementing zero trust access to strictly limit access privileges based on the principle of least privilege.

Distributed Denial of Service (DDoS)

DDoS also poses a major risk for retailers during peak shopping season because these attacks severely impact the operational uptime for e-commerce platforms if successful.

During the December 2025 holiday rush, the pro-Russian hacktivist group Noname057(16) used the DDoSia botnet to launch coordinated TCP SYN and HTTP GET request floods targeting the victim's web-facing portals and API endpoints. This DDoS attack knocked its central systems offline, paralyzed package tracking tools, disrupted e-commerce merchant payment services and delayed parcel processing across their retail distribution networks.

To mitigate DDoS risks threatening e-commerce and payment processing platforms, organizations must combine inline application-layer protections. Security teams should:

Deploy dynamic rate-limiting controls to protect against web site request floods

Implement automated mitigation to filter malicious connections

Utilize distributed edge networks to absorb large-scale traffic spikes before impacting critical systems

Digital Skimming

Although carding shops are not as prevalent as they were in prior years, digital skimming continues to be a popular technique used by cybercriminals to steal and monetize payment card information.

One example of a digital skimming incident that impacted retailers during peak shopping season occurred in October 2024, when unspecified threat actors exploited the CosmicSting vulnerability (CVE-2024-34102) to execute remote code on unpatched servers. This led to the installation of persistent backdoors and the injection of payment skimming scripts into checkout flows, affecting roughly 5% of all online stores running on prominent e-commerce platforms worldwide leading into Black Friday and Cyber Monday.

To mitigate digital skimming risks threatening payment processing workflows, organizations must implement web application and API protection (WAAP) solutions to monitor web traffic, intercept remote code execution attempts and prevent unauthorized client-side script manipulation. Security teams should:

Leverage cloud security posture management (CSPM) alongside application security posture management (ASPM) to continuously identify server vulnerabilities

Remediate unpatched flaws

Correct security configuration drift prior to holiday code freezes

Guest-Focused Threats

Account Takeover

Credential stuffing attacks are a major concern for retailers during peak shopping season as they directly impact the trust of their customers if an account is compromised. This is even more damaging if the customer has payment card information saved in their account.

One key example occurred in December 2022, when unspecified threat actors used automated scripts targeting the victim’s mobile app and web login APIs. They used large databases of stolen credentials to conduct the attack, which ultimately led to the compromise of thousands of loyalty accounts. The actors were able to drain stored gift card balances, steal mobile payment funds and collect rewards points before advertising access to the compromised accounts on dark web forums.

To mitigate account takeover risks threatening mobile applications and authentication APIs, organizations must implement WAAP solutions with advanced bot mitigation capabilities to effectively distinguish credential stuffing campaigns from legitimate customer access without friction. Security teams should complement this by deploying advanced security to identify and block traffic attempting to communicate with malicious command-and-control (C2) infrastructure used to orchestrate automated login attempts.

Gift Card Fraud

Retail customers typically increase their purchase of gift cards during holiday periods. Cybercriminals are aware of this trend and typically ramp up their targeting of this form of digital currency during peak shopping season.

Unit 42 reported on the credit card fraud-based Jingle Thief campaign in October 2025. We continue to track this activity as CL‑CRI‑1032 (aka Storm-0539).

These threat actors send phishing and smishing messages to socially engineer employees at targeted retailers to obtain credentials for initial access. From there, they typically exploit cloud-based infrastructure, gain unauthorized access to sensitive data and issue unauthorized gift cards to monetize them at scale for financial gain.

AI-Powered Attacks

Back in May 2026, we predicted that threat actors would weaponize frontier AI models within 3–5 months. That prediction has already come true. Unit 42 recently disclosed an incident where a human attacker used frontier AI models to autonomously conduct various aspects of their intrusion to condense the timespan of their attack to under 10 hours. This typically would’ve taken multiple human operators at least two weeks to accomplish.

Since our report, several other security vendors have disclosed similar findings that directly relate to the types of threat that retailers are likely to face this peak shopping season. This includes Anthropic's reporting on Bling Libra using Claude to accelerate reconnaissance and exfiltration activities. Gambit Security has reported on an attacker using multiple open source harnesses to steal more than 600,000 payment card records from retailers using JavaScript-based web skimmers. NorForge also published their own findings related to Gambit Security's report on the usage of the Cairn autonomous penetration testing agent by a threat actor to infiltrate retail e-commerce sites, POS infrastructure, and web applications across the globe.

To defend against autonomous AI threats capable of compressing intrusion timelines to less than 10 hours, retailers must unify endpoint, network, cloud and identity data into an automated security operations infrastructure. Integrating centralized visibility with machine-learning triage and real-time automation orchestration enables security teams to:

Conclusion

Peak shopping season is the most critical time of the year for retailers to ensure consistent operational uptime and maintenance of customer trust. The types of enterprise and guest-facing threats listed in this blog pose a clear and present risk to disrupting the core tenants of the retail shopping experience.

The ability for cyber defenders at retailers to reduce their MTTD and MTTR from hours to minutes is even more critical given the adoption of frontier AI models by financially-motivated actors.

Title: Weaponize your identity debt: Identity Security, decoys, and tripwires in the age of AI attacks
Context: Without this differential between appearance and security, and supported by traditional detection and response alone, adding designed ‘honey tokens’ in the age of machine-speed...
Full Text:
Every enterprise has identity debt: over-privileged accounts, insecure credential storage, and poor control of account lifecycle are just a few weaknesses we see all the time. But what if that debt could be turned into a strategic advantage against attackers?

CISA recently described decoys, tripwires, breadcrumbs, and honeytokens as practical mechanisms for detecting post-compromise activity. It got me thinking about how we can apply this defensive concept at the identity layer, where an attempted authentication can become both a detection signal and an inline containment decision. In other words, is there a world where we can weaponize Identity Security controls as a set of simple but effective tripwires across enterprise environments?

I think there is—and, even better, I think it has potential to turn any environment into the kind of classic laser hallway you see in heist movies, with red beams criss-crossing the route to the goal, ready to alert and ready to stop the latest threats.

So, in this blog, we’re going to look at how organizations can turn the same weaknesses attackers target into opportunities to generate rapid, high-fidelity signals with minimal operational risk.

But first: What are cyber decoys?

Cyber decoys are legitimate-looking systems, accounts, and data designed to distract and detect adversaries or facilitate collection of threat intelligence.

When operationalized with monitoring and alerting, they can become tripwires to provide high-fidelity signals to defenders. CISA also recommends mapping decoy coverage to MITRE ATT&CK and MITRE Engage, continuously testing the controls, and refining them based on observed adversary behaviour.

Why does this matter now?

The Hugging Face attack alone generated 17,000 unique events to analyse and correlate in a matter of a few days. As we prepare for a reality where attacks like these are commonplace, generating signal from noise to drive effective detection, response and containment has never been more important.

The focus is primarily on enhancing correlation. Hugging Face recommended that organizations focus on this in their post-incident call, having used an open-source model successfully—evidently a good investment. However, even the world’s most effective correlation engine will remain subject to data pipeline and ingestion constraints, some of which are owned by platform providers and cannot be optimized directly.

Generating high-fidelity signals as events unfold complements runtime controls that contain the threat, providing deeper visibility into attacker activity while enabling more informed defensive actions in real time.

Safe deception in the age of machine-speed threats

The aim of a deception strategy is to expose attackers and increase the cost and difficulty of attacks by creating a misleading picture of the environment and its resources (i.e., identities).

In agentic terms, the goal is to increase the compute/token cost of attack, use up context window, and buy time. In the future, it’ll be to funnel agentic attackers towards pre-designed traps to cause the agent to loop without escape.

Deception relies on something—for example, an identity with high privileges and easily-acquired credentials—appearing significantly less monitored, controlled, and secure than it actually is.

Without this differential between appearance and security, and supported by traditional detection and response alone, adding designed ‘honey tokens’ in the age of machine-speed threats may not generate a response fast enough to prevent exploitation of the token itself. Decoys and tripwires must therefore be safe. In other words, they must not have possible negative security implications in and of themselves.

Importantly, a safe tripwire turns the traditional detect > contain methodology, and reliance on response-time, on its head: the containment action that took place is the detection that arms your SOC with a signal, with full context of what happened.

Finally, given the rise of machine-speed threats, tripwires must not provide additional information as to the defensive posture of the organization when triggered. Transparency of the tripwire—which must not be able to be enumerated or discovered directly will become key to identifying and defeating machine-speed threats.

Identity is where the attack becomes the control point

AI attacks do not move through an environment in neat, human-sized steps. They enumerate identities, test permissions, reuse valid credentials and tokens, and pivot across trust boundaries until they find a path that works.

As we’ve already seen, the Hugging Face investigation reconstructed more than 17,000 attacker actions, grouped into approximately 6,280 clusters. The important lesson is not only the volume of activity, but the repeated identity pivots hidden inside it: credential theft, workload impersonation, token reuse, privilege escalation, and lateral movement.

That makes identity a powerful place to deploy tripwires. The tripwire should not only sit on a file, share, or endpoint. It should sit on the attempted identity path itself:

An identity requests access to an unexpected resource, in an unexpected protocol, or in a way that deviates from its baseline.

The request is evaluated using identity, source, destination, protocol, behaviour, and context.

The access is denied or fenced inline.

The same event generates a high-fidelity signal for the SOC.

Related identities and adjacent attack paths can be investigated or contained.

The attacker sees a normal access denial. The SOC sees the identity, attempted destination, protocol, source, sequence of activity, and potential attack path.

Silverfort sits inside the authentication path, where it can enforce identity-based deny and segmentation before an attacker completes lateral movement or privilege escalation.

For a machine-speed attack, detection alone often arrives too late. An identity tripwire functions as a control-flow interrupt: it breaks the sequence between authentication and the next step in the attack chain.

Instead of allowing the attacker to authenticate, discover, pivot, and escalate while defenders correlate events after the fact, the control can deny the risky authentication attempt at the point where the path is exercised. This changes the operating model from detect → correlate → respond to deny → detect → contain, resulting in a synchronous control that limits blast radius while preserving the evidence needed for investigation.

How can we leverage identity debt for this?

Identity is ripe for deception. Traditional identity debt such as over-privileged accounts, shadow admins, insecure credential storage, use of legacy protocols, and loose account lifecycle management is common—maybe even ubiquitous. These do not need to be designed and created because they already exist!

I want to be clear here: hygiene is still really important. Just because it’s possible to weaponize these existing issues, doesn’t mean good hygiene practices can be neglected.

The real question is how do we create safe tripwires?

There are three key premises to creating effective, safe tripwires:

A differential exists between the outward appearance of the account (utility to attackers), and the security state (monitored, controlled).

Usage of the tripwire does not have security implications (i.e., it does not make our security position worse).

Tripping the tripwire must not provide additional defensive context to the attacker to learn from; it must be to the attacker.

Inline identity controls allow for us to meet these three conditions. For example, deny policies create the tripwire alert to the SOC team, while denying the attacker information about why the containment activity occurred. Likewise, service accounts can be ‘fenced’ down to their standard, accepted, recorded usage behaviour and deny anomalies so, should anomalous usage be detected, we can both directly deny the usage of the account, and notify the SOC with a high-fidelity, rapid alert with full context for further action and wider correlation. All of this can happen without the agent seeing anything except ‘access denied’.

Some other cases where we can weaponize identity as tripwires (you can read more in the appendix below):

If connections to Tier 0/1 must be via bastions or PAW and are not

If dormant accounts become active

If admin accounts are used in a highly unusual way

If a legacy protocol is being used to access a sensitive server

If a low-privilege identity is attempting to reach a Tier 0 system

When one of these edges is exercised, the response should combine three actions: deny or restrict the attempted access, generate a high-confidence alert, and expose the surrounding identity relationships for investigation. This is specifically a control against AI attacks and their speed, persistence, and ability to test many paths in parallel.

What this means for security in the age of machine-speed threats

As we move into the next phase of threats—autonomously driven by AI models with the capacity to enumerate and hold your full environment and its vulnerabilities in their context window—two challenges emerge:

How do we generate signal amongst the massive volume of noise?

How do we do this in a way that does not require a loop of detect > correlate > respond, dependent on replication and processing times and humans in the loop?

CISA defines tripwires as decoys where interaction generates an alert. Silverfort extends that idea into the authentication path, where identity-based deny and segmentation can block access before lateral movement or privilege escalation completes. While a conventional tripwire detects interaction, an identity tripwire can detect, deny, and contain the attempted path in the same control loop.

Rethinking how we weaponize identity against attackers—by leveraging the identity debt that already exists—allows us to generate high-quality signal to cut through the noise, while having containment built-in. The containment activity generates the signal, rather than the signal requiring containment activity.

Doing this allows for more rapid threat detection, safely, while denying any information to the model that may help it progress its attack—and gives us a pathway to active defense in the future by funnelling agents to useless traps in an endless loop.

If you want to see how Silverfort can stop AI attacks inline and at runtime, book a demo here.

Identity tripwire appendix

Tripwire

Suspicious interaction

Recommended response

Decoy service account

Authentication from any source or destination outside its tightly defined baseline

Generate an alert and apply a virtual fence

Dormant privileged account

Login attempt against a disabled, unused, or never-used account

Deny the request and investigate the originating identity and host

Decoy SPN/Kerberos path

TGS request for a decoy service identity from an unexpected system

Alert on possible service-account discovery or credential theft and virtually fence it

Tier-0 access edge

Non-admin identity attempts authentication to domain controllers or identity infrastructure

Block inline and surface the full attempted path

Legacy protocol path

NTLM or other weak protocol used against a sensitive resource from an unusual source

Deny or segment the protocol-level access and generate an alert

Executive/admin breadcrumb

A decoy link, file, or share is accessed by an identity that should never touch it

Treat as a likely compromise signal and initiate identity containment

Title: Managed for Malice: How Attackers Turn MDM into Remote Access
Context: Background Huntress has observed several incidents recently where threat actors have leveraged mobile device management (MDM) applications to carry out attacks
Full Text:
Acknowledgements: Special thanks to Lindsey Welch, Anton Ovrutsky, and Harlan Carvey for their contributions to this investigation and writeup.

Background

Huntress has observed several incidents recently where threat actors have leveraged mobile device management (MDM) applications to carry out attacks. In these cases, legitimate management tools are being weaponized for malicious purposes, as opposed to threat actors taking advantage of inherent weaknesses in the applications themselves, such as vulnerabilities.

MDM platforms are legitimate tools that organizations use to manage employee laptops, phones, and other devices. These tools help IT teams to enroll and configure company devices remotely, enforce security policies, and deploy approved applications. However, these applications' centralized control and trusted level of access can create an entry point for threat actors if the tools are misused.

These incidents often begin with social engineering—users falling subject to business-themed lures that arrive through messaging applications and email. While not a definitive list of MDMs that could be used in such attacks, we have seen threat actors recently using well-known applications from Hexnode and Rippling.

Once registered with the MDM application, the attacker gains a trusted and privileged management path on the system. In both cases described here, Huntress observed the threat actors installing unauthorized RMM (remote monitoring and management) tools in order to further their attacks.

Mystery of the reappearing ScreenConnect

Imagine receiving an alert for an unauthorized ScreenConnect installation. Naturally, given the severity of such an alert, you prioritize it and remove the ScreenConnect agent immediately. However, several hours later, you receive another alert—same unauthorized installation. Something's clearly going on behind the scenes.

A recurring ScreenConnect installation is the first clue that this is more than an isolated, rogue RMM deployment. If both installations connected to the same destination relay, this would suggest the same threat actor was involved both times.

So how are they managing to get back in after being removed once?

We observed this activity in a recent incident, where two Huntress alerts for unauthorized ScreenConnect activity on the same device, separated by several hours, connected to the same relay.

As it happened, a threat actor had previously managed to install an MDM client from Hexnode on the system that ScreenConnect kept appearing on. Removing the RMM did little to deter them. They simply staged and installed the RMM software again.

The attack began with a phishing email. The target received several emails with proposal-related subjects like "ATTN: Official Invitation to Submit Proposal" and "Review Required" that mentioned an organization that the target likely had a business relationship with.

Clicking a link contained within the email downloaded a file from https://webdocusign.viewportal[.]es/Windows/download/index.php

which was saved to the Microsoft Edge temporary downloads folder as eD0cuSign_Installer.msi.

While the file had been named to mimic a DocuSign installer, it actually contained an installation package for a Hexnode MDM, a legitimate device management application. The package included Hexnode Gateway, the Hexnode agent, and supporting PostgreSQL components, all of which were installed on the system.

Figure 1: Execution of the Hexnode MSI, designed to resemble a (fake) DocuSign installer.

The threat actor followed up by installing ScreenConnect shortly thereafter and connecting to the attacker-controlled relay, relay.bobdthjau[.]com:8041. This resulted in a Huntress alert for an unauthorized ScreenConnect installation, and the MSP removed the RMM from the compromised computer shortly thereafter.

However, several hours later another instance of ScreenConnect was installed and reconnected to the relay. This triggered another alert, which led Huntress to isolate the endpoint, and a thorough remediation began.

Enrollment from a link

Not all incidents involve phishing techniques that trick a user into running an MSI installer. In another instance, a receptionist opened an email titled "Re: Tax Planning and Preparation Inquiry." The email included a link to what appeared to be a Microsoft Teams meeting invitation.

Clicking the link brought the target to a page titled "Calendar." While the site was taken down shortly after the attempt, it likely impersonated a Teams scheduling calendar. This page redirected to a .php file that appears to have helped facilitate enrollment into an attacker-controlled Rippling MDM tenant. All three links resided on the following domain (see the IoCs section for full URLs):

https://teams-microsoftcom5d41402abc4b2a76b9719d911017c592.kiratham[.]com

About a minute after clicking the link, a Rippling enrollment registry key appeared on the compromised system, which is consistent with registration in the MDM platform. An installation MSI for the Rippling agent was subsequently downloaded to C:\Windows\System32\config\systemprofile\AppData\Local\mdm\{GUID}.msi. The agent was then installed with SYSTEM-level permissions as C:\Rippling\daemon.exe.

Further investigation by Huntress determined that this activity originated from the online Rippling management agent, suggesting that the threat actor had previously created an account to carry out the attack.

Approximately 35 minutes after installation, the attackers used the MDM to stage and run a ScreenConnect installer as SYSTEM, connecting back to an attacker-controlled domain relay.pronconetydesire[.]online:8041, triggering a Huntress alert for a malicious ScreenConnect instance.

Tradecraft patterns & motivations

These instances, and the abuse of MDM applications in general, highlights a frustrating situation for security practitioners. The challenge is that more tools designed to help organizations manage endpoints are becoming mechanisms to compromise them. Similar to the illegitimate use of RMMs, this further complicates what we can safely consider trusted software, because reputation alone is just not sufficient to determine intent. Neither Hexnode nor Rippling are at fault here—users are simply being socially engineered into installing their software.

So where does this leave us? MDM enrollment should be treated as security-sensitive activity as opposed to a routine administrative task. An unexpected enrollment can establish persistence, provide a privileged deployment path, and allow an attacker to introduce additional tooling without relying on conspicuous payloads like known malware.

These incidents also demonstrate how detection cannot treat RMM installation as an isolated event. While the RMM client, and its subsequent activity, may have been the most visible part of the intrusion, removing it does not remove the unauthorized management architecture that delivered it.

The sequence of events observed makes for a stronger signal—social engineering -> a new MDM enrollment -> RMM installation -> outbound communication with an unfamiliar relay. Because the chain can vary, correlation across identity, MDM, endpoint, and network telemetry is our best hope in providing the resiliency needed to defend against these attacks.

Mitigation Guidance

Organizations can reduce the risk faced by these techniques by controlling both the enrollment path and the applications that MDM platforms are allowed to deploy.

Maintain an inventory of authorized MDM products, tenants, agents, and RMM instances. Treat any unexpected enrollment, management agent, or RMM instance as a security event.

Train users to verify unexpected meeting, document-signing, and proposal-review requests. Email and web controls should also scrutinize business-themed lures.

If a compromise is suspected, isolate the endpoint, remove the endpoint from the unauthorized MDM tenant, disable attacker-created accounts, revoke active sessions or tokens, reset affected credentials, and reimage the endpoint if its integrity cannot be confirmed.

Title: Serial ransomware crook gets 70 months behind bars for Nefilim, Hive roles
Context: One of Nefilim's most high-profile attacks was on Australian logistics giant Toll Group in 2020, encrypting its files roughly three months after it suffered a separate Mailto...
Full Text: Ukrainian ransomware crook Artem Stryzhak has been sentenced to 70 months in the slammer by a New York federal court for his role as an affiliate of the Nefilim and Hive ransomware gangs. Prosecutors believe the cybercriminal began working with Nefilim in or around June 2021, while living in Barcelona, Spain. The Nefilim ransomware-as-a-service (RaaS) operation was known for targeting wealthy companies, with its operators encouraging affiliates to pursue businesses capable of paying substantial ransom demands. One of Nefilim's most high-profile attacks was on Australian logistics giant Toll Group in 2020, encrypting its files roughly three months after it suffered a separate Mailto ransomware attack. Court documents [PDF] state that Stryzhak agreed with alleged Nefilim boss Volodymyr Tymoshchuk, who remains at large, to pay the ransomware crew a 20 percent cut of the ransom proceeds he collected. Tymoshchuk told Stryzhak that his preference was for attacks to target companies based in the US, Canada, and Australia that turn over more than $100 million annually. This guidance was soon tweaked to encourage targeting companies in the same regions with more than $200 million in annual revenue. Prosecutors claim that around the time Stryzhak joined forces with Nefilim, he also signed up to the Hive ransomware operation as "one of its earliest affiliates," and used its platform to attack approximately seven victims. Hive's operators claimed they targeted circa 1,500 victims worldwide between June 2021 and January 2023. According to separate court documents [PDF], Hive's victims included a law firm and an Ohio hospital, which paid approximately $1.7 million in Bitcoin after the gang initially demanded $2 million during the COVID-19 pandemic. Before its infrastructure was seized in an international law enforcement operation in January 2023, Hive was known for attacking healthcare facilities during the COVID-19 pandemic, as well as being one of the ransomware groups that battered Costa Rica in 2022. Brett Leatherman, assistant director at the FBI’s cyber branch, described Stryzhak as a “prolific cybercriminal” who played a role in groups that were responsible for more than $100 million in victim damages. “Today’s sentence reflects the seriousness of Stryzhak’s crimes and demonstrates the FBI’s global reach and extensive network of international partners,” he said. “Multiple field offices contributed to this investigation, and our work does not end here. We will continue to leverage every tool at our disposal to track down Stryzhak’s co-conspirators and hold them accountable, including Volodymyr Viktorovych Tymoshchuk.” Stryzhak was arrested by Spanish police in June 2024 before being extradited to the US in April 2025. In announcing Stryzhak's sentencing, the Justice Department took the opportunity to remind the public that rewards totaling up to $11 million are available for qualifying information about alleged Nefilim operator Volodymyr Tymoshchuk and other key ransomware suspects. ®

Title: Attackers Hide Malware Behind Signed ChatGPT and Claude Binaries
Context: Attackers have used fake ChatGPT and Claude desktop applications hosted on GitHub to distribute a malware chain that abuses legitimate signed binaries to evade security protections
Full Text:
Attackers have used fake ChatGPT and Claude desktop applications hosted on GitHub to distribute a malware chain that abuses legitimate signed binaries to evade security protections.

In research published October 27, Check Point said it had tracked the campaign, which it calls Yoba, for two months, though an earlier variant posing as the Cursor coding agent appeared in early June. The fake projects impersonated artificial intelligence (AI) applications including GPT-5.6 Sol, GPT-6 Astra and Claude Opus.

Their releases sat in GitHub repositories with GitHub Pages landing pages, and some of the repositories appeared among Google’s top results, most likely through search engine optimization (SEO) poisoning.

Yoba Uses Signed Binaries to Hide Malicious Components

The fake applications bundled legitimate signed OpenAI and Anthropic executables with a malicious dynamic link library (DLL). Check Point found that the signed Setup.exe files loaded the malicious component through DLL sideloading, a technique often used to bypass security protections.

The malicious DLL, dubbed YobaDropper, ran several checks before deploying a second-stage loader, including the name of its host process and whether it had administrator privileges.

It also checked keyboard layouts to avoid machines in Commonwealth of Independent States (CIS) countries other than Ukraine and used lengthy sleeps to frustrate automated analysis. Check Point said the actor showed indicators suggesting Russian origins.

The dropper then created a directory under ProgramData, copied a legitimate Windows executable into it and used Scheduled Tasks to establish persistence, with a task running under the Local System account and disguised as a Microsoft task.

Read more on fake AI tools spreading malware: Attackers Combine ChatGPT Feature Abuse With ClickFix to Deliver Trojan Malware

YobaLoader Uses Telegram and DNS to Fetch Payloads

The second-stage YobaLoader used Telegram and encrypted Domain Name System (DNS) lookups, known as DNS-over-HTTPS (DoH), to obtain instructions without dedicated command-and-control (C2) infrastructure, according to Check Point.

It took an image from a Telegram channel and used data from it to generate domains through a domain generation algorithm.

It then queried Google’s DoH service for encrypted data stored in DNS records, which was cryptographically validated before the loader retrieved and decrypted the next-stage payload.

Check Point advised organizations to be cautious when installing AI applications from unverified repositories and to restrict the execution of software from unknown sources.

The observed payload was an XMRig cryptominer, but the researchers said YobaLoader is a generic loader, so future waves could deliver other executable or PowerShell payloads.

Title: Attacker Relentlessly Scans for Credentials by Impersonating AI Bots
Context: Cyber Risk Cyberattacks & Data Breaches Threat Intelligence Vulnerabilities & Threats News Attacker Relentlessly Scans for Credentials by Impersonating AI Bots The threat actor...
Full Text:
A threat actor lurked behind more than 30 different AI bots to find and steal exposed credentials, continuously scanning for sensitive data without success. The findings highlight a growing problem for organizations: distinguishing between which AI agents belong in their networks and which may be malicious.

A scanner impersonating 32 bots — including crawlers and assistants from OpenAI, Anthropic, Perplexity, Meta, and others — hunted for exposed credentials to various organizations, according to a report published today by CQ Prime Research, part of Cequence Security. The scanner requested files from affected organizations — which spanned retail, financial services, telecommunications, energy, and software — that hold passwords, API keys, and cloud credentials.

The scanner has been running since late September and was still active as of late October, according to the researchers. They identified the activity on Oct. 21, discovering that on a single day this month, 48% of Cequence-protected organizations received the malicious AI bot traffic.

Related:Rethinking Cybersecurity Awareness in the AI Era

The findings highlight a growing challenge for security teams at a pivotal time, as businesses must figure out which AI agents to trust and permit access to their services.

"Attackers can test every one of those allow and deny decisions, and Cequence is seeing them probe which agents a business trusts, then impersonate the agents they expect to get through," Will Glazier, director of CQ Prime threat research and data science, wrote in the report.

Malicious Scanner Gives Itself Away

The scanner operates by firing off a burst of 50 to 190 requests in about 8 seconds and then moving on, working through targets one at a time, around the clock. Fortunately for the organizations affected, nearly all of the requests were blocked or failed, according to the report.

"It sends random nonsense paths first to find websites that answer every request, a common scanning technique," Glazier wrote.

CQ Prime Research identified the traffic as malicious through some telling behaviors that undermined the scanner's attempt to blend in with other traffic. The scanner rotates through about 32 bot identities evenly, which real bots do not do, according to the report; one machine claimed to be an agent from OpenAI, Anthropic, Meta, and Perplexity, all within seconds.

The attacker also used the contact address of Anthropic's crawler for all of its fake Claude identities, even when posing as different Claude agents, which shows the text was copied and not unique to each agent, according to CQ Prime Research.

Related:Threat Modeling With 4 Simple Questions on a White Board

The scanner also makes requests for configuration files, cloud credential files, and private SSH keys, from a list of about 90 paths, while never identifying itself or providing a contact address. Legitimate Internet-scanning services would never need these files and always identify themselves.

"The requests gave it away," observes Collin Hogue-Spears, senior director of solutions management at security firm Black Duck, which means "what Cequence documented is the test, not a breach."

Financial Accounts at Risk

However, what happens when AI agents scanning a network get through? This is what organizations are facing, particularly banks and financial institutions, with growing concern among experts that rogue agents are already logging into customer accounts at these organizations without them knowing. The result of such activity could cause global economic fallout.

For now, CQ Prime Research found that at financial services firms, AI agents acting for customers represented fewer than 1 in 4,000 requests. "The agents banks worry about most log in with a customer's own credentials through an ordinary browser and don't announce themselves," Glazier wrote in the report.

At this point, financial institutions should be starting to take action to identify which AI agents are legit and which aren't. But acting now already could mean they're playing catch-up to the activity of threat actors, observes Shane Barney, chief information security officer at Keeper Security.

Related:3 Frameworks to Protect CISOs & Orgs Against AI Liability

"Banks are currently scrambling to figure out which AI bots belong on their networks, but cybercriminals have already moved on to the next phase," he says. "They are no longer trying to break into these systems. Instead, they are simply logging in disguised as trusted AI agents."

Defending Against AI Agent Impersonation

To mitigate the growing threat from AI bots and agents, security leaders must treat AI agents, API keys, and service accounts with the same operational rigor as human administrators, Barney suggests. "That requires eliminating implicit trust across every access path," he says.

Indeed, organizations should not trust a bot's claimed identity on its own, according to CQ Prime Research, and they should verify agents through signed requests, published address ranges, or direct integrations.

They also should monitor for behavior that does not match the claimed identity, "such as an AI assistant requesting configuration or credential files," Glazier wrote.

Organizations also should stop leaving static credentials in vulnerable files where scraping bots can easily find them to eliminate obvious security gaps. Instead, Barney says, "Security teams must move away from long-lived local credentials in favor of centralized, zero-knowledge secrets vaults."

Full Text:
One of the world’s largest natural gas suppliers has notified an undisclosed number of customers that their personal data may have been compromised in a recent breach.

French multinational Engie employs over 90,000 people across 30 countries, supplying gas, nuclear power, and renewables. Its revenue in 2025 was almost €72bn ($80bn).

According to screenshots of the customer notification posted to X, the compromised data could include: full name, postal and email address, telephone number, unique IDs for energy supply (PCE/PDL), customer ID, and contract number.

The firm confirmed that no banking data was involved in the breach.

Read more on cyber-attacks impacting French firms: French Supermarket Cyber-Attack Impacts More Refrigeration Controllers

Engie urged customers to be on the lookout for potential fraud and phishing stemming from the incident.

“A malicious person could use the information mentioned above to impersonate you or use your personal details to contact another organization in your name, obtain additional information, or attempt to make a payment,” it warned. “Fraudulent emails may appear to come from trusted sources, such as organisations you know, in order to deceive you.”

According to a statement from the firm sent to Infosecurity, its own IT systems weren’t compromised. Engie blamed a third-party marketing platform used by its partners which was then compromised by threat actors.

“Engie recently identified unusual data access activity within a tool used by partners as part of their customer prospecting activities and the marketing of energy offers in France,” it explained.

“As soon as this activity was detected, the relevant access was disabled. At the same time, Engie launched an in-depth technical investigation to understand the circumstances of the incident, accurately assess its scope by identifying customers potentially affected, and ensure that the situation was fully secured. Enhanced monitoring measures were also put in place.”

No Group Has Claimed Responsibility

At the time of writing, no extortion group had admitted responsibility for the breach, which Engie said is now contained.

However, in October last year, extortion group Scattered LAPSUS$ Hunters listed the firm on its leak site, after compromising over 100 Salesforce instances and claiming to have extracted more than one billion records.

In that incident, Engie’s US retail energy business Engie Resources was the victim, with the group claiming to have obtained 3GB of data.

According to claims data from insurer Resilience shared with Infosecurity, no UK or European energy and utilities clients have reported ransomware since July 2025.

European claims with a recorded cost involved only fraud or exposed customer data. That contrasts with the US where ransomware comprises around 70% of incurred losses across claims on record in the sector, Resilience said.

Title: Banks are blocking AI agents from customer accounts
Context: Where supported, choose read-only access if all you need is analysis or budgeting help
Full Text:
This week, Axios reported that major US banks were detecting third-party AI agents operating inside customer accounts. In many cases, customers have given the agents their usernames and passwords so they could act on their behalf. This kind of access can violate a bank’s rules.

Bianco Research president Jim Bianco raised the question during Unchained’s Bits + Bips livestream on October 26:

“Are you protecting me, or are you protecting your own profits?”

Bianco described traditional finance’s business model as “based on laziness.” Customers may leave idle cash in low- or no-interest bank accounts rather than move it into a money market fund. An AI agent could make that move for them. “Now that you’re able to do it, the banks are afraid they’re gonna lose that revenue stream,” he said.

The banks offer a different explanation. JPMorgan Chase CEO Jamie Dimon said the bank wouldn’t allow just any outside agent into its systems because doing so was “too risky for clients and for JPMorgan.”

Both explanations can be true: banks can want to retain deposits while also facing real security problems when software acts through customers’ accounts.

Handing over your banking login introduces another service into the security chain. A vulnerability in that service could expose your credentials or allow your account to be misused. And as Bank of America reportedly pointed out:

“If you do share your credentials, keep in mind that you’re responsible for activity resulting from that access.”

That’s the bank’s stated position, not a universal ruling on consumers’ legal rights. Still, it’s a warning worth taking seriously.

Pros and cons

An AI agent with permission to make purchases might find and buy an item at a lower price. But giving an agent access to your bank account also means sharing sensitive banking information with a third party. We’ve seen shared AI chats become searchable online too.

Axios reported that many banks allow, or are moving toward allowing, read-only access. This can let a tool analyze transactions without giving it permission to move money.

That’s an important boundary, but it doesn’t make the information harmless. An agent that can read bank statements may still disclose them if it’s compromised or manipulated. Preventing transactions and protecting confidentiality are separate security goals.

How to keep control of your money

For consumers, the practical question is not whether banks have perfectly selfless motives. It’s what access you’re giving away, and what could happen if the agent makes a mistake.

Don’t paste banking passwords or security codes into a general-purpose AI assistant. Major banks have explicitly warned customers against sharing their credentials.

Use your bank’s approved connection methods rather than giving an agent your login. Where supported, choose read-only access if all you need is analysis or budgeting help.

Give agents access to as little sensitive information as possible. An assistant comparing publicly advertised savings rates doesn’t need your bank statements. OpenAI recommends limiting agents to the data and credentials they need for the task.

Review consequential actions yourself. If an agent asks for confirmation, check exactly what it intends to do and what information it will share. Don’t treat a confirmation prompt as a formality.

AI can make it easier to compare financial products and spot opportunities you might otherwise miss. But an assistant that finds a better rate and an agent that can act inside your account are different propositions.

Let it help with the homework, but be cautious about handing it the keys.

Let’s face it, an incognito window can only do so much. Breaches, dark web trading, credit fraud. Malwarebytes Identity Theft Protection monitors for all of it, alerts you fast, and comes with identity theft insurance.

Title: LABScon26 Replay | Keynote: A Sober Analysis of AI Impact
Context: He concludes that at present the only good AI research is safety research, which he defines broadly to include economic and emotional security alongside computer security
Full Text:
In his LABScon 26 keynote, delivered in his inimitable comedic style, Harvard University professor James Mickens questions whether the scale of current AI investment is justified. Starting from US tech capex of roughly 1.4% of GDP in the second quarter of 2025, he argues that computers are already good enough, and notes that the world has so many CPUs and GPUs that they are put to work solving cryptocurrency puzzles to make imaginary money. More seriously, the AI models that investment is building, he says, grow increasingly opaque as their parameter counts rise.

Mickens then cites research and incident reports on model behaviour, including models acting to prevent another model being shut down and recent sandbox escapes at OpenAI and other labs. On economics, he rejects the assumptions that AI will create more jobs than it destroys and that universal basic income will follow widespread automation.

He concludes that at present the only good AI research is safety research, which he defines broadly to include economic and emotional security alongside computer security. Mickens own contribution is Guillotine, a hypervisor design that runs a model’s CPU code on isolated cores unable to read or write the hardware state of the cores running the hypervisor. Arguing that hardware-based mechanisms for isolating misaligned frontier models will be an important direction for research over the next five years, he invites those interested in this approach to collaborate.

This keynote speaks to security practitioners and researchers interested in AI risk, the economics behind current AI investment, or hardware-level containment of frontier models

About the Author

James Mickens is a Gordon McKay Professor of Computer Science at Harvard University. His research focuses on the performance, security, and privacy of large-scale online services; a current focus is the interpretability and sandboxing of potentially misaligned frontier models. Prior to becoming a professor at Harvard, Dr. Mickens spent seven years at Microsoft Research, working in the Distributed Systems group.

About LABScon

This presentation was featured live at LABScon 2026, an immersive 3-day conference bringing together the world’s top cybersecurity minds, hosted by SentinelOne’s research arm, SentinelLABS.

Title: Cisco open sources tool for detecting AI agents on hacking sprees
Context: Cisco has open sourced a behavior detection engine that watches AI agents, to help security teams prevent rogue agents from going off the rails like they did with the Hugging...
Full Text: Cisco has open sourced a behavior detection engine that watches AI agents, to help security teams prevent rogue agents from going off the rails like they did with the Hugging Face hack – or worse. It’s called Project Quarry, and it aims to provide a “shared language” for evaluating agent behavior, along the lines of what Snort, which Cisco also maintains, did for detecting malicious network traffic and what YARA did for rule-based malware identification. Most detection tools rely on specific interactions with an AI model or agent. Did it attempt prompt injection? Or did the agent call an attack tool? “But what is missing is the entire context under which something may occur,” Amy Chang, head of AI threat and security research at Cisco, said in an exclusive interview with The Register. She likened this to credit card fraud detection. Without context, individual transactions such as a small test charge or a single purchase in a location far away from a card-holder's usual location may not raise any flags. “And then you try again,” making another fraudulent purchase, “and that went through, too. So now I’m gonna buy the PS5,” Chang said. “Those are the things that Quarry addresses by taking into consideration the entire agent session,” she explained. “One tool call may seem in-scope until you realize that that next step is taking that information and sending it to an attacker-controlled inbox or server.” Even data theft is a sequence and not a single agentic action. Agentic AI security firm Invariant Labs demonstrated this with a proof-of-concept attack against GitHub's MCP server that hijacked a user's agent via a malicious GitHub Issue, and coerced it into leaking data from private repositories. Simply reading a configuration file, or sending a request to an external endpoint may be legitimate agentic actions. However, combining the two can lead to data exfiltration – and shows “why action relationships matter,” wrote Chang and fellow Cisco researchers Adam Swanda, Ravikumar Balakrishnan, and Konstantin Berlin in a blog post about Quarry shared with The Register ahead of publication “A policy can produce a finding when the trace shows a sensitive file read followed within a defined window by an external send,” they wrote. “The risk comes from the relationship between the two actions, so the finding should preserve evidence from both." Quarry covers single- and multi-turn large language model conversations, agents, tool use, Model Context Protocol (MCP) interactions, and multimodal inputs. In addition to the open source code itself, the project’s GitHub repository includes installation instructions, supported Python versions, plugins for Claude Code, Codex and other MCP-compatible agents, configuration examples, rule-writing guidance, and a rule starter pack. For instance, with the rule pack, “If a base-64 encoded malware is somewhere in the tool call, that would result in a block,” Chang said. The rule format looks similar to a YARA or Snort rule, with a header that details the traffic to examine, content to match, and metadata for tracking the rule. Here’s a Quarry rule that flags an agent that reads a credentials file: While the Cisco Ai researchers have not run Quarry against data describing the OpenAI-Hugging Face incident, they suggest that if the intrusion had been read as a complete, step-by-step record of a single session, there were several points where the AI agents’ steps would have given a Quarry rule something to act on and flag for humans. For example, Quarry would probably have flagged internet access from a sandbox. “The rule can flag specific tool calls that reach an external server asset that wasn’t in the task’s allow list,” Chang said. “Another one would be credentials found and used somewhere else.” According to OpenAI’s technical report about the Hugging Face intrusion, this is exactly what happened on July 10, when an agent validated 14 exposed Hugging Face tokens with write access and shared them. “The rule would flag that there was a credential in the tool result that then called an outside service, which is likely not within the parameters of what you would want to do in this case,” Chang said. “We don't want you to go and search for credentials that may have been leaked or inadvertently exposed and then utilize them to conduct a task.” The Cisco team is quick to say that rules along are not a substitute for chain-of-thought monitors, or other forms of human oversight – but they do help record a pattern that other teams can then “review, test, and apply to their own agents,” they wrote. Herein also lies the benefit of open source, and a collective approach to defending against adversarial use of AI, Chang said. “Do we have all the answers? No,” Chang said. “We all see slices of the problem, and it’s important for us to share what we see.”®

Full Text: UK domain registrar 123 Reg (no relation – Ed) says it was the victim of an “AI-driven cyberattack” that exposed customer data. Customers began receiving their notification emails this week, informing them that their contact information, "related customer relationship data," company VAT numbers, and "product information from an application programming interface (API)" were compromised. A company spokesperson elaborated, saying this means that names, phone numbers, countries, language and currency preferences, account creation dates, the products on the account, and marketing preferences were affected. 123 Reg described the September 18 intrusion as "the first known AI-driven cyberattack against our company," and told The Register that early signs point toward a China-nexus attacker. "Our investigation identified IP addresses that we assessed to be the core attacker infrastructure, which were hosted in China and Singapore, indicating a strong Chinese nexus," the spokesperson said. "Our investigation further identified AI cyberattack 'skills' hosted on Chinese infrastructure, including copies of skills open sourced by Anthropic and several other AI exploitation frameworks and scripts." They went on to say that many of the artefacts left behind led 123 Reg to suspect that a Chinese state-sponsored group, known for abusing Claude Code in attacks against at least 30 organizations, could be behind the break-in. There is also a suspicion that the same group that hit a number of South Korea’s financial institutions using open-source Chinese AI tool ARTEX, was behind the attack on 123 Reg too. "The TA's mirror of 'anthropic_skills,' and the account naming conventions found on the Chinese servers are consistent with preparation of this class of AI-augmented operation," the spokesperson told us. "In addition, on October 7, 2026, CrowdStrike published CSA-261162, describing an unknown, likely Chinese-speaking actor that targeted several South Korean financial organizations starting in late September 2026, which is the same period during which we were attacked. "That actor used ARTEX, an open-source Chinese-developed agentic penetration-testing tool released in July 2026, which was also observed to be used in the attack that targeted us." The GoDaddy-owned registrar reported the attack to law enforcement agencies, brought in outside cybersecurity support, and notified the FTC, as well as the data protection authorities in the UK and EU. The company spokesperson added that it worked with Singapore-based ISPs to shut down the attacker's servers in the region, which helped disrupt the attack, in addition to "other actions by us and industry partners." 123 Reg's email to customers stated the attacker's activity "was limited to reading" customer data, although the spokesperson told us "it's possible they created copies of the information," and that this is what prompted the notification. The registrar urged customers to stay alert to the potential misuse of their data, and to treat communications appearing to come from the company with caution. "If you receive a message or call and aren't sure it's from 123 Reg, go directly to our website and log in," the email said. "We will never contact you to request your password, payment details, or verification codes by email, text, or phone. "We also strongly recommend turning on two-step verification (2SV), which helps keep your account protected even if someone tricks you into sharing your password. You can find instructions for setting up 2SV in your 123 Reg account. "We apologize for any inconvenience this may have caused." ®

Modules: Vulnerability Management
Title: Lessons from Cybersecurity Black Week
Context: In the highest-risk setups, a demonstrated exploit can trigger the vulnerability before application code runs, meaning application-level authentication offers no protection
Full Text:
The week leading up to October 25, 2026, was every cyber defender’s nightmare: a barrage of critical vulnerabilities in PHP and the Linux kernel, a compromised LiteLLM release, a maximum-severity flaw in GitLab, a Node.js Brotli flaw, and a certificate authority incident affecting TLS trust.

A few years ago, a backlog like this would have filled a defender’s to-do list for a whole month. In the age of AI, all of this was reported within a single “Cybersecurity Black Week,” an exceptionally eventful seven-day period amid an already turbulent Black October. AI-assisted research helped uncover at least two of these flaws: PHP2Shell and the Brotli bug. On top of the breakneck patching pace, security teams faced mounting pressure to deliver status reports to other departments, management, customers, and the media.

Beyond their severity, the issues stood out for the variety of responses they demanded. Some required emergency runtime patches and upgrades; others called for containment, credential rotation, or the replacement of outdated certificate trust bundles. In several cases, installing the latest version was only the beginning of a long remediation process.

With so many problems landing at once, the main challenge was separating real risk from hype and prioritizing accordingly. Here is our assessment.

PHP2Shell: The loudest headline, with real-world limits

PHP2Shell generated the biggest media frenzy of the lot and, with it, a major headache for security teams, prompting many organizations to take their websites offline and look for emergency fixes. The name refers to two memory-safety vulnerabilities in PHP core, CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, affecting PHP versions 5.4 through 8.5.11. Both vulnerabilities received a CVSS v4.0 score of 9.2 and can allow unauthenticated remote code execution (RCE) on vulnerable PHP servers. In the highest-risk setups, a demonstrated exploit can trigger the vulnerability before application code runs, meaning application-level authentication offers no protection.

With PHP powering an estimated 69% of websites whose server-side programming language is known, government agencies in the United States, Europe, and elsewhere urged organizations to patch immediately, with some advising that affected internet-facing systems be isolated or taken offline if they could not be patched promptly. Government websites in the Netherlands, Germany, France, and other countries were temporarily taken offline as a precaution. The PHP project released fixes on October 21 in versions 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36, and 8.2.35, along with source-only backports for the end-of-life 7.4, 8.0, and 8.1 branches. The rollout was complicated by a premature public leak, which forced the coordinated disclosure timeline forward.

While the flaws clearly belonged near the top of the patching list, early evidence suggested they were considerably harder to weaponize than initially feared. Successful exploitation requires specific conditions and knowledge of the target, and public proof-of-concept exploits did not work against a default PHP installation, according to Sansec.

On October 22, ESET was among nine security companies that told NBC News they had not seen any successful attacks, even though more than 200 proof-of-concept exploits were circulating. The remediation challenge extends beyond obvious web servers: PHP can also be embedded in appliances, network devices, management interfaces, and third-party products, while end-of-life PHP branches do not receive normal upstream binary releases.

Linux kernel: Reports went public before fixes were ready

As if the PHP issues weren’t severe enough, on October 21, Trend Micro’s Zero Day Initiative (ZDI) sent several reports on unpatched Linux kernel vulnerabilities to the kernel’s private security address while also copying public mailing lists. As a result, technical details of vulnerabilities for which fixes were not yet generally available became public, prompting stable kernel maintainer Greg Kroah-Hartman to question why the reports had been sent to public lists without patches.

The two most severe issues, both rated CVSS 9.0 by ZDI, affect KSMBD, the Linux kernel’s built-in SMB server. ZDI-CAN-33549 is an integer underflow in the SMB Direct path that could lead to RCE, while ZDI-CAN-33774 is a race condition that could also lead to RCE. Exploiting ZDI-CAN-33549 requires an RDMA-capable interface, a writable KSMBD share, and SMB Direct negotiation, significantly narrowing the number of systems exposed to that particular attack. Other reports concerned local privilege escalation vulnerabilities in the networking stack and the VMware graphics driver, as well as an information disclosure issue in the NVMe target code (NVMET).

To remediate, security teams had to track each report independently, consult distribution advisories, and restrict exposed services where practical while awaiting verified fixes. Kernel updates also required rebooting into the patched kernel and checking the running version, not merely confirming that a new package had been installed.

LiteLLM: Compromised, not merely vulnerable

On October 21, attackers published a malicious version of LiteLLM, 1.107.0, to PyPI and pushed compromised images to the project’s official container registries. According to the project’s incident report, its release pipeline was breached using GitHub CLI credentials associated with three developers. One of the stolen tokens belonged to an owner of the project’s GitHub organization, allowing attackers to disable branch protections and modify the release workflow to point to a lookalike repository. LiteLLM, a Python proxy for LLM providers, has about 23 million weekly downloads, and the malicious version remained available on PyPI for roughly two hours before it was quarantined. It was the project’s second supply-chain compromise of 2026, after malicious versions 1.82.7 and 1.82.8 appeared in March.

The payload combined a credential stealer with a second-stage remote access trojan (RAT). By abusing Python’s startup mechanisms, including a .pth file, it ran every time Python started, even if an application never imported LiteLLM. Execution therefore did not depend on exploiting an application flaw: simply running Python in an affected environment could be enough.

Affected environments had to be treated as potentially compromised, not merely vulnerable. According to LiteLLM, these included environments that ran litellm==1.107.0 and containers that executed affected images distributed under the v1.107.0, latest, main-latest, or main-stable tags during the compromised intervals. Removing or replacing the package was insufficient: teams needed to determine whether the malicious code had run, contain affected systems, rebuild from clean sources, and rotate exposed secrets from a clean environment. Cloud, source-control, and CI/CD logs also had to be reviewed for unauthorized activity.

Node2Shell: From Node.js to HTTP2Shell

Node2Shell (CVE-2026-111497) is an out-of-bounds write in Google’s Brotli decoder, which Node.js bundles. Malformed compressed input can cause crashes, memory disclosure, or potentially RCE when an application decompresses attacker-controlled Brotli data. This can happen through explicit decompression, compressed request bodies, or automatically decompressed responses. Node.js rates the flaw as high severity, while the broader Brotli vulnerability carries a CVSS v4.0 score of 9.2. According to Aikido, researchers demonstrated code execution against the official, unmodified Node.js 24.22.0 image on Linux ARM64. Although the exploit did not work on every attempt, the demonstration showed that exploitation was practical, if not universally reliable.

Node.js shipped fixes on October 21 in versions 22.23.4, 24.22.1, and 26.12.1, and Bun followed with version 1.4.4 or later. Node.js 25.x, 23.x, 20.x, and earlier releases are end-of-life and will not receive the fix. Within days, the story outgrew Node.js. The same decoder is compiled into the Python Brotli and brotlicffi packages as well as into other HTTP software, which led researchers to rename the issue HTTP2Shell. The operational challenge was therefore not simply upgrading a single runtime but identifying every container, serverless deployment, and library that bundles the vulnerable decoder. The issue was fixed upstream in Brotli 1.2.1. Notably, OpenAI’s Codex Security had reported the underlying bug, and the fix had been present in the Brotli source since February without being recognized as a security issue.

GitLab: Credential leaks and authorization failures

On October 21, GitLab shipped a critical out-of-band patch release (versions 19.5.1, 19.4.3, 19.3.6, 19.2.9, 19.1.9, 19.0.10, and 18.11.13) addressing 12 security vulnerabilities. The headline flaw, CVE-2026-110264, rated 10.0 under CVSS v3.1, is an integer overflow triggered when GitLab compiles a specially crafted regular expression. Under certain conditions, it could allow an unauthenticated attacker to execute arbitrary code on the server. The affected versions date back to GitLab 7.0.

The other fixes addressed credential exposure, cache poisoning, authorization bypasses, and failures to enforce membership or merge-request approval policies. Reported unauthenticated attack paths included exposure of sensitive credentials through internal response headers and manipulation of a shared OAuth/OIDC discovery cache, while other issues required authenticated access. GitLab did not publish individual severity scores or exploitability details for these issues.

GitLab.com and GitLab Dedicated were already patched, so the work fell on administrators of self-managed instances. GitLab strongly recommended upgrading immediately, but with a catch: the older backport releases (19.2.9, 19.1.9, 19.0.10, and 18.11.13) included only the critical fix, while the remaining 11 issues were fixed only in 19.3.6 and later. Administrators also had to verify that all deployment components had been updated and assess the potential exposure of credentials and private project data due to the fact that patching would not invalidate stolen credentials or reverse unauthorized changes.

eMudhra/emSign: Compromised certificate trust

The high-priority eMudhra/emSign incident involved no software vulnerability at all. Several eMudhra intermediate certificate authorities (CAs) had insecure private keys, meaning attackers could potentially create certificates that would be trusted through the affected emSign certificate chain. While browsers had updated their trust stores and revocation lists, some Python tooling continued to trust the compromised intermediate CAs through its own certificate bundles. This created a risk of man-in-the-middle (MITM) attacks against TLS connections, including those to python.org and pypi.org.

The Python Software Foundation urged users to upgrade immediately to at least certifi 2026.10.19, pip 26.2.2, and uv 0.13.4, and the Python core team shipped expedited releases 3.15.2, 3.14.10, 3.13.18, 3.12.16, and 3.11.18 to update the bundled pip. The updates had to reach every host, application, and existing virtual environment. Container images had to be rebuilt with layer caching disabled to fetch the latest system certificates. The decisive check was whether deployed clients rejected the compromised trust paths; simply upgrading Python was not enough.

Cutting through the noise

Cybersecurity Black Week showed that a severity score rarely tells the whole story. A 9.2-rated PHP flaw that attackers struggled to exploit, a 10.0-rated GitLab bug, exposed kernel reports with no patches, and a poisoned package that ran at Python startup each called for a different response. What they all had in common was a window of exposure: the time between disclosure and when the last affected system is patched. For the leaked kernel flaws, that window opened before any fix existed, and for end-of-life PHP versions, it may never fully close. This is where ESET’s multilayered protection comes in, using behavioural detection and other security mechanisms to help block exploitation attempts and keep systems protected until patches are applied.

At the same time, the signals defenders rely on were buried in noise, from scanning that was largely benign to a single behavioural rule firing hundreds of thousands of times in a week. What mattered most was quickly understanding which incidents actually affected an organization's environment and what each incident required. That is the problem ESET’s correlation engine, ESET LiveCortex, and its specialized cybersecurity model, ESET NeoCortex, are designed to solve: turning an overwhelming volume of raw data into understandable incidents so that defenders can act before attackers achieve their goals. To learn how they work, read Beyond the alert: How ESET is teaching AI to understand security incidents.
