Title: Know How Cyble Brand Intelligence Can Help Stop ClickFix Campaigns in its Tracks
Context: Five Storm-1865 attack steps, each paired with a Cyble Brand Intelligence capability Step 1: Pick a trusted brand and a target list What the attacker did
Full Text:
Booking.com's systems were never breached. Its name was. Storm-1865 spent months borrowing Booking.com's identity to get into hotel computers, and every step of that borrowing left traces on the open internet.

The open internet is exactly where Cyble Brand Intelligence & Protection works. Walk through the campaign one step at a time, and at each step there is a point where it could have spotted the attacker, cut the attack short or limited the damage.

What happened

From December 2024, a group Microsoft tracks as Storm-1865 posed as Booking.com to target hotel and hospitality staff across North America, Europe, Oceania and South and Southeast Asia. Microsoft Threat Intelligence published its findings on March 13, 2025, and said the campaign was still running as of February 2025.

The attack had four moving parts:

The lure. Emails styled as Booking.com messages about negative guest reviews, guest enquiries, promotion offers or account verification.

The landing page. A link, sometimes inside a PDF, opened a fake CAPTCHA laid over a faint copy of a real Booking.com page.

The trick. The "verification" told staff to open the Windows Run box and paste a command the page had already copied to their clipboard.

The payload. That command used mshta.exe to pull commodity malware, including XWorm, Lumma Stealer, VenomRAT, AsyncRAT, Danabot and NetSupport RAT, all built to steal credentials and payment data.

This was not a one-off. Microsoft says Storm-1865 targeted Booking.com guests in 2023 and e-commerce buyers in 2024 before adding ClickFix. Booking.com told Infosecurity Magazine its own systems were not breached, but some accommodation partners and customers were hit.

Why the impersonated brand holds the first move

Booking.com could not install security software on the laptops of its accommodation partners. What it could reach was the attacker's infrastructure copying its brand, and that infrastructure was detectable. Microsoft's own email security flagged URLs in this campaign as impersonating booking.com.

The stakes are high. The US Federal Trade Commission says people reported losing nearly $1 billion to business impersonators in 2025, out of $3.5 billion lost to imposter scams overall. Every copy of a brand caught early is one fewer victim.

Five steps, five chances to step in

Storm-1865 needed Booking.com's credibility at every stage of the attack. Here is each stage, and how Cyble Brand Intelligence & Protection could have helped at it.

Fig. Five Storm-1865 attack steps, each paired with a Cyble Brand Intelligence capability

Step 1: Pick a trusted brand and a target list

What the attacker did. Storm-1865 was a repeat player. Microsoft says it went after Booking.com guests in 2023 and e-commerce buyers in 2024, then turned to hotel staff most likely to work with Booking.com.

How Cyble could have helped. Cyble's in-house brand team and OSINT surveillance track brand mentions and the actors who keep returning to a brand. A known playbook becomes a set of watch-list rules, so the next wave is expected rather than discovered after the fact.

Step 2: Register the infrastructure

What the attacker did. The campaign needed domains and URLs to host its fake pages. Microsoft flagged some of them as matching a known malicious registrant pattern.

How Cyble could have helped. Suspicious & Watch-Listed Domain monitoring tracks new registrations and DNS activity for typosquats, homoglyphs and lookalike domains, including AI-generated ones. A domain built to impersonate the brand can be flagged when it is registered, before it hosts a single page.

Step 3: Build the fake Booking.com page

What the attacker did. Victims landed on a fake CAPTCHA laid over a faint copy of a real Booking.com page. The familiar look was the point: it made a strange request feel routine.

How Cyble could have helped. Phishing Detection finds sites impersonating the brand, and Watermarking Surveillance spots copied or mirrored brand assets, even on domains with no brand name in them. Automated Takedown then works to get confirmed pages removed. Every hotel that clicks after a takedown hits a dead link instead of a trap.

Step 4: Send lures across regions

What the attacker did. Emails and PDFs about negative reviews, guest requests, promotions and account checks went to hotels across North America, Europe, Oceania and Asia. Some came through vendor platforms and ordinary services such as Gmail and iCloud Mail.

How Cyble could have helped. Multi-language NLP is built to catch phishing and impersonation attempts that are not in English, which matters for a campaign spread across this many markets. Lures that partners report can be handed to Cyble's brand team, traced to the live page behind them and queued for takedown.

Step 5: Cash in on stolen credentials and payment data

What the attacker did. Once a staff member pasted the command, malware such as XWorm, Lumma Stealer and VenomRAT went to work. Microsoft says every payload in the campaign could steal credentials and financial data for fraud.

How Cyble could have helped. Stopping the pasted command itself is a job for endpoint and email controls. What Cyble adds is the aftermath: OSINT surveillance watches forums, blogs and paste sites for exposed credentials and data leaks tied to the brand. Spotting stolen partner logins early gives everyone time to reset access before fraud follows.

This walkthrough maps public research to Cyble's capabilities. It is not a claim that Cyble took part in the response to this campaign.

Strongest alongside your other defenses

Brand intelligence works outside your network, so it pairs naturally with what runs inside it. When a lure arrives from an ordinary Gmail or iCloud address, there is no fake sender domain to flag, so the landing page becomes the asset to hunt. And if someone does run the pasted command, email filtering, endpoint detection, script controls and phishing-resistant MFA, the mitigations Microsoft recommends, do the stopping. Brand intelligence makes sure far fewer people ever reach that moment.

Is your brand the next Target? Six questions to ask

Any brand that sits between businesses and their customers can be borrowed the same way: travel platforms, marketplaces, payment providers, logistics firms and SaaS vendors. Ask your team:

Do we know which of our emails, notices and portal pages are most copied by attackers?

Are we alerted when a domain containing our name, or a homoglyph of it, is registered?

Can we spot a cloned page even when it sits on an unrelated domain or free hosting?

How long does it take us to get a confirmed phishing page taken down?

Do our partners know how to report a suspicious message that uses our name?

Do we watch criminal forums and channels for kits or templates built around our brand?

If more than two answers are "no" or "not sure," the attacker's preparation phase is happening without anyone watching.

The takeaway

Look back at the five steps and a pattern stands out. Storm-1865 needed Booking.com's credibility at every one of them, and every one left a trace outside the victims' networks.

With Cyble Brand Intelligence & Protection watching, each trace becomes a chance to step in: a repeat actor on the watch list, a lookalike domain flagged at registration, a cloned page taken down, a lure traced to its source, a leaked login caught early. If your partners and customers trust your name, Cyble helps make sure nobody else gets to use it.

Title: Deploying AI agents securely: how Kaspersky products mitigate AI threats
Context: To this end, we added profiles to the Kaspersky Threat Intelligence Portal that describe various AI agents and how attackers exploit them
Full Text:
Introduction

AI agents and associated tooling are becoming increasingly common in corporate infrastructure. Agents can perform a range of actions with the user’s privileges, such as accessing data, running commands, and interacting with external services. This creates new security risks, especially when these tools are used without the security team’s oversight or well-designed policies.

Detecting, tracking, and controlling AI agents is becoming one of the most pressing tasks for security teams today. We closely follow technological developments and continuously update our solutions to respond to new threats in a timely manner amid a rapidly changing technology landscape. This post describes new expertise built into Kaspersky products that helps counter the threats posed by the proliferation of AI agents. We approach this problem from several angles.

First, you need to thoroughly understand the threat you are dealing with. To this end, we added profiles to the Kaspersky Threat Intelligence Portal that describe various AI agents and how attackers exploit them. At their core, AI agents are programs (processes) that run in the operating system on endpoints and can also launch other processes. This means that Endpoint Detection and Response solutions are among the key endpoint controls for this threat. These solutions detect the presence and launch of AI agents, track their activity, and identify potentially dangerous behavior. When needed, they also take action, such as stopping a suspicious process, blocking the activity, or isolating the host, to reduce the likelihood of an incident escalating. For this purpose, we developed specially adapted detection rules.

You can use Kaspersky Endpoint Security, now also available as Kaspersky Next, to control and restrict the launch of AI agents. This solution uses two components to detect AI agents and control how they are used. Application Control categorizes the application processes launched on endpoints, and Web Control manages access to specific categories of web resources for users on endpoints.

Finally, even harmless AI agents can contain malicious instructions (skills), such as those downloaded from unsafe external sources. Kaspersky Scan Engine analyzes installed applications to detect these threats and also checks LLM files for malicious code. Let’s take a closer look at these solutions and technologies.

Popular AI applications and services in organizations

Tools from Anthropic and OpenAI take the top spots in the September 2026 ranking of AI agents by popularity among Kaspersky users. This list is based on telemetry from Kaspersky solutions. It shows the number of users who had the relevant AI vendors’ products installed at the time of the study.

Application Control and Web Control

To enforce the organization’s security policy for AI agents and other AI applications on the corporate network, Kaspersky products offer application control based on KL categories. These categories classify installed software and give you granular control over which approved applications can run in the organization.

Application Control analyzes the processes launched on endpoints, tracking which AI agents are running in corporate systems at any given moment, on which hosts, and under which accounts. Application Control also shows how long a given program has been in use.

This makes it easier for the Kaspersky Security Center (KSC) administrator to control applications. Administrators can use KL categories to allow or block AI agents inside the company for specific groups of employees.

Here is what this functionality looks like to KSC administrators:

In Kaspersky Endpoint Security (KES), Application Control can operate in two modes:

Denylist. In this mode, Application Control lets users run any applications except those blocked by Application Control rules. This is the default mode.

Allowlist. In this mode, Application Control blocks users from running any applications except those explicitly allowed by Application Control rules.

Below are the steps to configure Application Control to block AI tools.

Configuring Application Control for the AI Tools category in KES

With this setup, when a user tries to launch an AI agent, they get a notification and the agent doesn’t start.

For more on how to configure Application Control in KES, follow this link. Our public portal also lets you explore information on KL categories and the applications that fall under them, in particular details on how AI agents are categorized and how popular they are.

The View applications drop-down list shows products for a specific vendor.

Similarly, Web Control lets you manage user access to web resources. If a user tries to open a denylisted website, KES blocks access and shows a warning.

KES notification about an attempt to access a prohibited web resource

When configuring access, the administrator can block websites that provide AI as a service.

For more on configuring Web Control, follow this link. The help portal also provides information on website categories that can be assigned to resources to configure access control.

Kaspersky Endpoint Detection and Response

To an EDR solution, an AI agent is a regular process. It has its own executable, a tree of child processes, and network communications, all of which need to be monitored for suspicious activity. An attacker can use an AI agent as an automation tool. An AI agent installed as a legitimate user tool can also be leveraged in a ClickFix attack, where it executes a malicious instruction received from an untrusted source, such as a document, web page, or email. That said, unsafe actions by an agent do not always indicate an attack. There may be no malicious intent in the chain at all. An incident can result from what looks like an ordinary instruction from a user who doesn’t fully understand the consequences of having it executed. The mere fact that an agent was launched does not reveal whether it is being used in an attack. That is why Kaspersky EDR (KEDR) uses both conventional behavioral rules and rules written and adapted to detect AI tools. The latter identify risky agent actions and settings, and help determine which AI tool was involved in suspicious activity.

Conventional KEDR rules detect the vast majority of familiar malicious techniques, including when performed by an AI agent. A suspicious PowerShell launch, persistence via Task Scheduler, or an attempt to steal credentials leaves clear, identifiable traces. These traces look the same no matter what initiated the actions. The rules analyze launch parameters, process relationships, affected files, network activity, and other telemetry events.

For example, in a recent Armored Likho campaign, we found signs that AI had been used to create loader and dropper samples, which were later compiled with NSIS (Nullsoft Scriptable Install System). The key telltale artifacts were icons in the scripts and excessive comments on every function, which is uncharacteristic of human-written code. In addition, the group continues to generate new modules for its BusySnake Stealer and BusySnake RAT samples. For example, the attackers used AI to develop a module that runs multiple checks for virtual environment artifacts and calculates a score. Depending on the score, the sample either runs or exits with code 0. Even though the initial access samples, payloads, and their modules were AI-generated, the commands they execute via rundll32 and PowerShell are detected by the shell_creation_by_rundll32 and suspicious_powershell_cmd_or_script_spawning rules.

So, for detecting an attack like this, it is not important who wrote the loader, the payload, or its modules: they are given away by the commands they execute, process relationships, and other traces of activity in the system. AI can be involved both in preparing the code and in carrying out the attack directly on the device.

In the latter case, the attacker uses the agent to carry out their tasks and lets it choose and run the required commands within the privileges it has. For effective protection, it is critical to link suspicious actions back to the AI tool and the conditions under which it operates. In KEDR, several specialized rules handle this task.

We have created separate rules for popular AI agents, ai_agent_*_access_to_sensitive_file_**, where * is the tool name and ** is the operating system. They generate alerts when an agent accesses files that contain credentials, tokens, or keys.

The ai_agent_dangerous_execution_mode rule detects agents launched with auto-approval of all actions (so-called YOLO mode) or with the sandbox disabled. These settings do not indicate an attack on their own, but they let the agent perform dangerous actions without user confirmation.

ai_agent_dangerous_execution_mode Tap to previewTap to hide

The suspicious_mcp_server_artifact rule triggers when MCP server scripts are created or modified in hidden, temporary, or cache directories. Attackers can place an MCP server in these locations to quietly connect it to the agent: through the MCP server, they can pass instructions to the agent, call third-party tools, and access the user’s data.

The llm_api_access_by_unusual_apps rule generates an alert when an application on Windows, Linux, or macOS connects to the API of a known external LLM service, unless this activity falls under predefined exclusions. This helps spot model access by applications that do not normally behave this way.

llm_api_access_by_unusual_apps Tap to previewTap to hide

Some Kaspersky EDR rules tag events for investigation but do not generate alerts. For example, the ai_agent_**_execution rules flag launches of known agents on Windows, Linux, and macOS. The local_ai_model_artifact rule records the creation or modification of AI model files in typical application, runtime, and cache directories. These events reveal AI tools on the device, including tools that run on local models and never call an external API.

AI agent profiles

The Kaspersky Threat Intelligence Portal offers a large number of software profiles, including profiles of AI agents. You can sort them by the ai_ prefix:

The profile of an AI agent such as Claude Desktop includes a detailed description of the software, the privilege level required to run it, supported platforms, and threat actor groups known to use it. It also lists tactics and techniques mapped to the MITRE ATT&CK framework, with descriptions of the procedures the tool can be used for.

The description also lists ways to detect the software through standard system auditing mechanisms:

Linux: syscall audit events and Sysmon events

The detection section lists the main artifacts the software leaves in the system: command lines, possible launch parameters, names of the services and scheduled tasks it creates, and the key network artifacts.

Detection section in the Claude profile

Hunt Hub

In December 2025, the Kaspersky Threat Intelligence Portal added Hunt Hub (HH), a repository of detection rules. This is a unique Kaspersky project, and we developed it in response to growing market demand.

This functionality is available in the Threat Landscape section of the portal. It gives analysts access to detection rules: their descriptions and their mapping to MITRE ATT&CK tactics and techniques, as well as to the associated cybercriminal groups.

In the Hunt Hub section, customers can explore the detection logic of EDR, NDR, and NGFW products, including the logic for detecting AI agents.

Groups that use the technique covered by the rule

Detection rule card in Hunt Hub

Kaspersky Scan Engine

Skills are a key component of the AI agent ecosystem. They’re prewritten sets of natural-language instructions that extend agent functionality. We previously covered the risks that malicious skills pose to agent users. A skill can require the usage of additional programs and services, come with helper scripts (for example, written in Python), or contain a malicious command embedded right in the instruction text. This means that adding skills to an originally harmless AI agent opens up several new ways for malicious code to enter the system. To prevent this, any skills obtained from external sources must be scanned. Kaspersky Scan Engine is well suited for this task. This is a cyberthreat detection and response solution that seamlessly integrates with various applications. It can detect malicious code in agent skills, associated scripts, and in files generated by running agents.

Detection of a malicious agent skill in Kaspersky Scan Engine

Trained LLMs come in many formats. Some of them (PTH, PT, PKL, KERS, and others) also store parameters and weights (training datasets). These files can also contain malicious code, so it’s critical to scan them before running and using them. Kaspersky Scan Engine scans potentially dangerous LLM formats for infected data. It can deserialize and analyze models to detect malicious code regardless of model size.

Detection of an LLM with malicious code in Kaspersky Scan Engine

Conclusion

AI agents are rapidly making their way into corporate environments: they help employees work faster and take on a wide range of tasks, but they also open up new opportunities for attackers. To take advantage of this technology without compromising security, organizations need to build multi-layered protection and minimize risks. A range of Kaspersky solutions can help with this:

Kaspersky TIP keeps you up to date on current scenarios in which attackers use AI agents, and its Hunt Hub section provides rules for detecting suspicious AI agent activity.

Kaspersky EDR detects AI agents in the infrastructure and monitors their activity on endpoints. If it detects potentially dangerous actions, the product can log the event, notify the SOC, and take response actions, such as stopping the process or isolating the host.

Application Control in Kaspersky products can fully restrict the use of AI agents within the company by using application categorization. The Web Control component can restrict access to AIaaS web resources.

Kaspersky Scan Engine can be integrated into various company processes to detect malicious code in any files, including AI agent skills and LLMs.

When companies combine the tools described above in a comprehensive approach, they can adopt AI agents in an informed way: with an understanding of the associated risks and effective means of minimizing them.

Title: Code security for new coders
Context: There are also many security tools available, but it can be confusing to know what type of tool to use and when
Full Text:
Coding agents enable anyone to turn their ideas into reality. However, building with security in mind is imperative to keep your application secure. There’s a lot of reference information about application security out there, but it often is jargon-heavy and targets developers or security professionals, not vibe coders. There are also many security tools available, but it can be confusing to know what type of tool to use and when. This post breaks down essential security terms and tools so that you can build safely from the start.

If you aren’t sold on the importance of application security or think it only matters to large companies, consider the PHP2Shell vulnerabilities disclosed in October 2026. These two vulnerabilities affect PHP, a programming language used by more than 70% of websites. They could allow an attacker to take control of a website’s server. The vulnerabilities are so serious that some organizations temporarily took services offline while installing security updates.

What is code security?

In simple terms, code security is the practice of writing secure code. Because application security starts with code security, taking a proactive approach early prevents major vulnerabilities later.

There are two main things we need to be concerned with when thinking about code security: the code you (or your agent) is writing (i.e., first-party code), and the code that is written by someone else but being used by your application (i.e., third-party code). With first party code, you are directly responsible for fixing the problem. Third-party code is treated differently because you are not the one who can fix the code, but you are responsible for using a version that does not have vulnerabilities. We often refer to third-party code as being part of the software supply chain, but more on that later.

What is first-party code?

First-party code is the code that you are producing and are thus responsible for. While being responsible for maintaining secure code might seem intimidating, you can most likely fix security issues by prompting the agent to fix them. There are automated security scans you can run to discover vulnerabilities, or you can simply ask the agent to do a security check. Checking for OWASP top ten vulnerabilities is always a good place to start.

What are secrets?

One of the simplest, yet most impactful ways to improve security is to avoid hardcoding secrets. This means that you should never write in the code any password, token, key, or any secret or credential that can be used to gain access to your resources. Instead, you can use environment variables that act as a placeholder that point to a specific hidden configuration file or a secret manager.

What is the software supply chain?

The software supply chain refers to everything that is used to develop and run an application, including dependencies, tools, and infrastructure. There are also open source code components used in the software supply chain, such as GitHub actions and Docker images, which can help you deploy and run your code. Of all these elements, third-party dependencies are usually the main focus in discussions about code security.

Now you might be thinking, why do I need to use third-party code? Technically you don’t, but it makes writing code much easier, whether it’s done by you or an agent. By relying on these open-source dependencies, you are using code that was already written by someone else and that is shared with the community to solve a problem. What’s important to understand in the context of AI-generated code is that coding agents use dependencies by default, often relying heavily on outdated versions.

Dependencies rely on other dependencies, so the risk starts to grow as you start to use them. There are two things in particular you need to be concerned about with third-party dependencies: vulnerabilities and malicious packages. Vulnerabilities in third-party dependencies are accidental code issues that usually require upgrading to the latest version once the issue is fixed. Malicious packages represent a more intentional threat and are becoming more common. With these packages, someone has purposefully added a malicious script in the version and released it for personal gain.

Overall, the concern with using third-party code is that dependencies can quickly accumulate vulnerabilities if the maintainer doesn’t have the time to address these security flaws.

Security questions to ask your coding agent

The cool thing about vibe coding is that you can ask the agent any questions you may have. The difficulty can be knowing exactly what to ask. Below is a list of good places to start, but it is not exhaustive.

Setup questions

These are the types of questions that should be asked before any code is written. The goal is to have some security requirements planned out so an agent has a path to follow.

What sensitive data will this app handle (passwords, payment info, personal data, API keys), and how should each type be protected?

What authentication and authorization approach fits this app, and what are the tradeoffs?

Follow-up questions

After the code is written, you should make sure the agent made the best decisions for security. Ask questions that make the agent explain why certain security decisions were made. This will force the agent to go back through the code, which might lead it to suggest a change.

Can you do a security review on the application? Are there any concerns?

Do any OWASP top 10 vulnerabilities exist in this code?

What security tradeoffs did you make to keep this simple, and what would you fix before real users touch this?

If you were a penetration tester, what's the first thing you'd try to break in this app?

What third-party packages did you use? Are any of them outdated? Do any have known vulnerabilities?

Does any of this code contain hardcoded API keys, passwords, or tokens? If so, where, and how do I move them to environment variables or to a secrets manager?

Are default credentials or debug modes left enabled anywhere?

Is there a .env or config file here, and is it excluded from version control (.gitignore)?

Are there any insecure coding patterns or logic flaws present?

Is there anything concerning about the current authentication and access controls configuration?

Are cloud storage buckets, databases, or admin panels publicly accessible when they shouldn't be?

If this is deployed, what's exposed to the internet that doesn't need to be?

What are the different types of code security tools?

Security tools come in all shapes and sizes. While many tools are paid, there are also open source tools that function similarly. The list below includes the most common types of tools.

Software Composition Analysis (SCA)

Tools of this type scan all the open-source dependencies that are being used in the application and alert you if there are any vulnerabilities. Most providers will also tell you what version you can upgrade to in order to eliminate that vulnerability.

Static Application Security Testing (SAST)

This type of tool is focused on looking at your first-party code for vulnerabilities. Most commonly, these tools scan the written code without running that code. They are good for early detection while you are actively coding but can provide more false positives than other tools do.

Interactive Application Security Testing (IAST)

Tools in this category look at how data is flowing into a running application to find code vulnerabilities. Since they require a running application, they are generally used later in the software delivery life cycle compared to SAST tools. However, they also tend to be more accurate.

Dynamic Application Security Testing (DAST)

Tools that perform this type of security scan run pre-configured automated tests against a running application. They are not interchangeable with SAST or IAST tools.

Infrastructure as Code (IaC) Scanning

Tools that use this type of scanning are focused on looking at any IaC files for risky settings and misconfigurations.

Secret Scanning

Secret scanners search your codebase for hardcoded credentials, API keys, and passwords.

How Datadog can help

Security scans are a great way to understand what is happening in your code. Datadog Code Security has many types of tools you can use to gain visibility into your application, including SCA, SAST, IAST, IaC, and Secret scanning tools.

Datadog also has two open source tools that can be used for supply chain security: GuardDog to flag malicious packages and Supply Chain Firewall to block malicious packages from being installed.

Conclusion

The good news is that you do not need to become a security expert before bringing an idea to life. Start with a few basics: keep secrets out of your code, scan both first-party and third-party code, update your dependencies, and ask your coding agent to check for common vulnerabilities.

The goal is not to build a perfectly secure application on your first try. It is to understand what your application uses, recognize the risks, and make security part of how you build from the start. Addressing issues along the way is much easier than responding after your application or its users have been put at risk.

Title: Kernel eviction notice: What wesp.sys reveals about the Windows Endpoint Security Platform
Context: Any features or functionality not currently available may not be delivered on time or at all
Full Text:
Microsoft is building a way for EDR products to run outside the Windows kernel. It is called the Windows Endpoint Security Platform, and two of its binaries already ship in Windows Insider build. One is the kernel driver wesp.sys, the other the user-mode API espclient.dll. Microsoft wants one kernel driver it maintains itself, in place of the one every security vendor currently ships, after the July 2024 CrowdStrike update crashed 8.5 million machines. WESP is undocumented, but the binaries carry public symbols, so a kernel debugging session gets you a fair way in. wesp.sys is a file system mini-filter at altitude 329500, talking to user mode over a filter communication port.

Kernel mode vs user mode: How EDR works today

Are you tired of the Windows Blue Screen of Death? Well, Microsoft decided to take significant action to remove security products from running within the Windows kernel, as kernel components are the ones that can cause Windows to Blue Screen, which can have a significant impact, as was demonstrated a couple of years ago with a bug in a third-party kernel component.

Typical Endpoint Detection and Response (EDR) software consists of two main components: a kernel-mode driver and a user-mode service, communicating in some way, as the following image shows:

The process boxes represent normal user applications running on a system, like Word, Explorer, or Paint. The Service and Kernel Driver are installed by the EDR product.

The kernel driver’s main purpose is to register for various kernel notifications, such as process creation and file writes. Any notification of interest is typically forwarded to the user-mode service where more processing can be done:

Forward the notification data to a server for further analysis and aggregation.

Consult a set of rules that may lead to blocking the operation entirely.

Alert the human user of the operation, perhaps requiring an interactive decision.

This is all well and good, if everything works as planned. Unfortunately, kernel drivers cannot perform illegal operations, such as dereferencing a bad pointer. In that case, the system crashes with the infamous “Blue Screen of Death” (BSOD), and restarting the machine is the only way back in, assuming the offending driver doesn't crash when it loads early at boot.

Why the CrowdStrike outage changed Microsoft’s mind

That is exactly what happened on July 19, 2024, when a bad configuration file update caused CrowdStrike’s EDR kernel driver to crash on millions of machines worldwide. The risk of kernel drivers crashing systems has existed in Windows since its inception, but this incident was particularly nasty because it rendered so many machines unusable, taking airports, banks, and other critical facilities offline for hours.

Microsoft took this to heart; after all, it's Windows. They launched a new initiative to move EDR products out of the kernel so similar incidents can’t happen. This is non-trivial, however, for a few reasons:

The Windows kernel will now have to deliver notifications that EDR kernel drivers expect to the EDR’s user-mode service. This has to be efficient to be usable.

Existing products will take time to migrate, even if Microsoft provides a full solution, so we must support the existing behavior.

Any such framework must be flexible enough, and complete enough, to be adopted successfully. If features EDR products require are missing, adoption and migration will be partial at best.

What is the Windows Endpoint Security Platform (WESP)?

The Windows Endpoint Security Platform is Microsoft’s framework for moving EDR products to user space. The project is in its early stages, as shown in Windows Insider builds that include the new platform’s binaries. The main component is a kernel driver, wesp.sys, built by Microsoft, and a user-mode API implemented in espclient.dll that EDR’s user-mode service would use to connect and receive notifications of interest.

It may seem ironic that the implementation centers on a kernel driver (wesp.sys), but there is no way around it; at the end of the day, the kernel must provide the notifications the EDR service expects. So, wesp.sys will play the role of an EDR kernel driver, but since Microsoft implements it, there will be only one driver to test and debug properly, rather than the current state where every EDR platform has its own in-house kernel driver.

What EDR vendors need from WESP

At the time of writing, the WESP platform is not publicly documented. There are some expectations, however, that the platform must provide if EDR systems are to adopt it:

It should be comprehensive. EDRs today register for notifications in several different ways, each with its own mechanism:

Event type

Current registration mechanism

Process, thread, image, handle

Registration functions with a callback

Registry

Registration functions with a callback

File system

File system mini-filter

Network

WFP callout driver

All these variations add to the complexity of EDR drivers. WESP should provide all of these; otherwise, EDR drivers will continue to exist, albeit with less code for what WESP covers. It’s reasonable to assume that not everything will be provided on day one, but I expect everything to be provided eventually.

Some notifications a kernel driver can register for are very “noisy”. For example, Registry and file read operations are happening all the time in large quantities. You can get a sense of that by running Process Monitor (ProcMon) from Sysinternals and watching the hundreds of events (or more) displayed every second related to the Registry and the file system (especially read operations). Passing all such events to user mode is not feasible; it would be too slow, or at least inefficient. This means WESP will have to provide some filtering capability, so that events that are not interesting can be dropped “at the source” (the WESP driver), rather than being sent to user mode and dropped there. Flexibility in these rules is paramount, as it can significantly lower the load on the user-mode service.

A power that only certain kernel notifications have is blocking an operation, something that cannot be done in user mode. The classic example is creating a process – a kernel driver can register for such events with PsSetCreateProcessNotifyRoutineEx – a documented function all EDRs use. The callback is invoked while process creation is in progress, allowing it to set a failure status for the process creation if it so desires (for example, by inspecting the new process command line and deciding it’s malicious). Such power does not exist in user mode – you can get notified when a process is created, but you cannot veto creation. WESP clients (user mode) must be given this power so they can block process creation under certain conditions. These conditions should be flexible enough to be configured in most cases. Ideally, it should let the user-mode service run custom code before replying to the driver with whether to allow or block process creation.

Client processes that work with ESP must run elevated to access the platform. They will likely need to run as Protected Processes Light (PPL), signed by Microsoft, which is how EDR services run today, at least with most vendors, since it’s not currently required.

Inside wesp.sys: What the binaries reveal

Though not documented yet, we can get some WESP details by examining the binaries provided. As a nice bonus, the symbols for these binaries are provided by the Microsoft public symbol server.

Running a local kernel debugging session on a VM with WESP installed can give us some insights into how WESP works. First, the WESP driver file is wesp.sys located in the System32\Drivers directory, where most drivers live. We can examine the Registry where drivers are installed to find the key name, which is also the driver kernel object name:

Clearly, the driver’s name is simply wesp. With that detail in hand, we can look in WinDbg for the major functions supported by the driver (some formatting done for better readability):

lkd> !drvobj wesp f Driver object (ffffc0e9fe2e6310) is for: \FileSystem\wesp Driver Extension List: (id , addr) Device Object list: Flags: 0x00000012 0x00000002 DRVO_LEGACY_DRIVER 0x00000010 DRVO_INITIALIZED DriverEntry: fffff80564281000 wesp!DriverEntry DriverStartIo: 00000000 DriverUnload: 00000000 AddDevice: 00000000 Dispatch routines: [00] IRP_MJ_CREATE fffff805d07a14d0 nt!IopInvalidDeviceRequest [01] IRP_MJ_CREATE_NAMED_PIPE fffff805d07a14d0 nt!IopInvalidDeviceRequest [02] IRP_MJ_CLOSE fffff805d07a14d0 nt!IopInvalidDeviceRequest [03] IRP_MJ_READ fffff805d07a14d0 nt!IopInvalidDeviceRequest [04] IRP_MJ_WRITE fffff805d07a14d0 nt!IopInvalidDeviceRequest [05] IRP_MJ_QUERY_INFORMATION fffff805d07a14d0 nt!IopInvalidDeviceRequest [06] IRP_MJ_SET_INFORMATION fffff805d07a14d0 nt!IopInvalidDeviceRequest [07] IRP_MJ_QUERY_EA fffff805d07a14d0 nt!IopInvalidDeviceRequest [08] IRP_MJ_SET_EA fffff805d07a14d0 nt!IopInvalidDeviceRequest … [0e] IRP_MJ_DEVICE_CONTROL fffff805d07a14d0 nt!IopInvalidDeviceRequest [0f] IRP_MJ_INTERNAL_DEVICE_CONTROL fffff805d07a14d0 nt!IopInvalidDeviceRequest [10] IRP_MJ_SHUTDOWN fffff805d07a14d0 nt!IopInvalidDeviceRequest [11] IRP_MJ_LOCK_CONTROL fffff805d07a14d0 nt!IopInvalidDeviceRequest [12] IRP_MJ_CLEANUP fffff805d07a14d0 nt!IopInvalidDeviceRequest [13] IRP_MJ_CREATE_MAILSLOT fffff805d07a14d0 nt!IopInvalidDeviceRequest [14] IRP_MJ_QUERY_SECURITY fffff805d07a14d0 nt!IopInvalidDeviceRequest [15] IRP_MJ_SET_SECURITY fffff805d07a14d0 nt!IopInvalidDeviceRequest … [1b] IRP_MJ_PNP fffff805d07a14d0 nt!IopInvalidDeviceRequest Device Object stacks: Processed 0 device objects.

From the output, we can see there are no driver-provided major function code handlers (I omitted a few for brevity, but they all point to the kernel-provided handler, IopInvalidDeviceRequest); in fact, no device objects exist at all. This means talking to this driver cannot be done with a classic DeviceIoControl, where a device is opened by name with CreateFile (really a symbolic link) or NtOpenFile (actual device name); there is no device to open. We see the driver object is stored in the \FileSystem object manager directory, where file-system mini-filters are typically stored. Another clue leading to the same conclusion is the Registry showing the “Type” value as 2, which represents a file system-related driver.

We expect the WESP driver to register for the various notifications a “standard” EDR driver would. We can see that when opening wesp.sys in some PE viewer (screenshot is from one of my tools, Total PE):

It also depends on FltMgr.Sys, which is the Filter Manager driver, managing file system mini-filters, proving that wesp.sys is a file system mini-filter. Another tool you can run to reinforce this conclusion is the built-in fltmc command-line tool in an elevated command window:

Filter Name Num Instances Altitude Frame ------------------------------ ------------- ------------ ----- bindflt 1 409800 0 UCPD 5 385250.5 0 wesp 7 329500 0 WdFilter 5 328010 0 storqosflt 0 244000 0 wcifs 0 189900 0 PrjFlt 0 189800 0 CldFlt 1 180451 0 FileCrypt 0 141100 0 luafv 1 135000 0 UnionFS 0 130850 0 bfs 7 100010 0 npsvctrig 1 46000 0 Wof 3 40700 0 FileInfo 5 40500 0 WinSetupMon 1 40300 0

WESP is in the list, showing its altitude (higher altitude drivers get notifications before lower altitude drivers).

How wesp.sys talks to user mode

How is the driver communicating with user mode if it has no device objects, taking DeviceIoControl off the table? File system mini-filters have a mechanism available to them, which is using FilterCommunicationPort kernel objects. These provide bidirectional communication with user mode clients, which is more flexible than DeviceIoControl-style communication, which is unidirectional in nature (user to kernel). We can also see this in the imports called from FltMgr.sys, like FltCreateCommunicationPort, the fundamental API for creating such an object. You can also see a port named ESPFilterPort under the root object manager directory (shown in WinObj from Sysinternals):

Can a user-mode client block process creation?

What about the user mode client? We can open espclient.dll (located in the System32 directory) in Total PE to get some hints:

As you can see, the DLL exports lots of functions, all starting with Esp. We can identify rules and filters, confirming the assumption that these are necessary, so events can be filtered at the source, i.e., not sent to user mode if there is no interest. The API is C-based (not COM) – at least as it’s exposed to consumers. The client DLL’s imports include FltLib.Dll, which is the client DLL for using filter communication port objects. The three functions being used by EspClient.Dll are FilterConnectCommunicationPort (open a handle to a FilterCommunicationPort object), FilterGetMessage, and FilterSendMessage. A missing function (in my mind) is FilterReplyMessage, which allows a direct reply to a message from the driver. This missing function implies that user mode has no “response” capability, and that communication is one-way. This means that running custom code in user mode and then “replying” to the driver with a “decision” (such as blocking a process from being created) is probably not implemented, at least not yet.

Conclusion: What WESP means for EDR vendors

WESP is Microsoft’s attempt to reduce third-party kernel code that Microsoft can't fully control. It aims to increase Windows reliability by reducing the chances of BSODs or other nastiness that could result from kernel driver code. The hope is that, by leveraging WESP, we can reduce the need for third-party kernel code and potentially remove it entirely. WESP isn't broadly available or well documented yet, but EDR providers are preparing to use it. Elastic is among them: Elastic Defend, Elastic’s XDR solution, is preparing to support WESP.

Context: Trust Is Not What It Seems — and Fraudsters Are Counting on It Threat actors don't need to rely on malware to breach organizations anymore
Full Text:
Cyber Risk

Trust Is Not What It Seems — and Fraudsters Are Counting on It

Threat actors don't need to rely on malware to breach organizations anymore. They're simply calling help desks and politely asking for access, with a little help from artificial intelligence.

Arielle Waldman,Features Writer,Dark Reading

October 23, 2026

6 Min Read

Source: Nico El Nino via Getty Images

After a disruptive cyberattack hits, customer trust can take a while to rebuild. But now threat actors are impersonating trusted brand names and existing customer accounts to abuse customer relations.

"Trust has become easier to exploit and harder to establish," a new TransUnion report warns. Threat actors use social engineering, deepfake technology, text spoofing, compromised credentials, and artificial intelligence (AI) to become whoever they need to be, whether that's a new or existing customer or the organization itself.

In light of more attacks, many organizations have improved security during sign-up and onboarding processes. Organizations must continue to adapt since "most fraud now occurs after the customer relationship has already been established," the report states. It found 58% of organizations were very or extremely concerned that fraud is evolving faster than their abilities to detect or prevent it.

Related:Rethinking Cybersecurity Awareness in the AI Era

The use of synthetic identities plays a big role. Threat actors can spin them up with ease, given widespread data breaches that exposed millions of individuals' sensitive information, says Brian Killeen, vice president of global identity solutions at TransUnion. Scammers will replicate leaked documents or use deepfakes to bypass identity proofing checks at onboarding.

The credit reporting agency found that account login accounted for 53% of all suspected digital fraud during the first half of 2026. Conducting scams has become easier for threat actors as tooling advances, Killeen adds. Threat actors aren't just automating account creation with scripts; they're actually building logic into automated pipelines to reverse-engineer security controls, he says. That allows them to pinpoint exactly where and how defenses are blocking their attacks.

"Trust is under pressure," Killeen tells Dark Reading.

You Can't Spell 'Impersonation' Without AI

Last year the FBI warned of an uptick in cybercriminals targeting employee self-service portals — websites used for payroll, benefits, and other human resources services — at both private companies and government agencies. Threat actors created fake search engine advertisements to lure users into visiting malicious sites that mimicked legitimate companies' logos and layouts. Once the victim logged in, attackers stole login credentials and financial information.

And the situation continues to evolve. Over the past year, AI has helped criminals personalize attacks and spread them across channels — from email to Teams. Deepfakes add another layer of credibility, says Javvad Malik, lead chief information security officer (CISO) adviser at KnowBe4.

Related:As AI Risks Grow, Insurers Split on Covering the Damage

Amid booming AI adoption that security has trouble matching, the security awareness company is also seeing more attempts to exploit AI systems or take advantage of poorly configured AI tools and agents, he adds.

"The social engineering techniques remain similar, but attackers are also using AI to find weaknesses and are beginning to target AI agents directly," Malik tells Dark Reading.

The AI attack surface is ripe for the taking. New research from Check Point on brand impersonation trends from Q3 flagged a phishing campaign where threat actors impersonated Anthropic's Claude assistant. Fraudulent emails, playing up urgency with a due payment notice, requested 500 euros with an "update payment" link intended to trick users into clicking, putting their credentials and financial information at risk. Since April, KnowBe4 tracked a 228% increase in AI brand impersonation, says James Dyer, head of threat intelligence. Attackers are abusing the global focus on using AI within businesses as a perfect covert operation for their phishing attacks, he adds, warning that the problem compounds when attackers center their attacks around breaking news headlines.

Related:Security Threats Don't Stop at the Office: Why Executives' Families Need Training, Too

Moving Target

When it comes to attacks against customer relations, attackers' methods have evolved from deploying malware to exploiting identity because there's no need to write a script when they can just get a password reset, says Dave Lewis, global advisory CISO at 1Password.

The industry spent a decade training people not to click links, and attackers responded by simply asking nicely, he adds. The most common attacks he has observed don't involve "anyone in a hoodie typing furiously" but instead phoning the help desk to manipulate users into giving away multifactor authentication (MFA) codes.

"[It's] the most effective zero-day of 2026," Lewis says.

Walking in through the customer relationship management (CRM) system's front door is another tactic he has seen, pointing to the data-theft campaign against Salesforce customers that started in 2025 and continued into 2026.

"Nobody 'hacks' the CRM," Lewis tells Dark Reading. "They just log in with a key you handed to a vendor or a guest account nobody remembers creating."

The target moved from the data center to the software-as-a-service layer, where one compromised integration gives attackers many targets per compromise. Detection lags because SaaS platforms log differently from traditional infrastructure, Lewis adds.

Threat actors also use AI to build voice deepfakes from executives' public recordings, deploy them in high-pressure desk calls, and then use AI again to move through hybrid environments within minutes of gaining access. But that doesn't exactly signal an increase in sophistication, Lewis says.

"Technical sophistication is down," he says. "Operational sophistication — research, patience, scripting, follow-through — is up. It's less of the 'evil genius' and more 'well-run call center with bad intentions.'"

Recommendations: Rinse and Repeat

"What once looked legitimate and trusted can change" as threat actors slip further under the radar, cloaked behind more convincing and personalized impersonation tactics. Killeen stresses. Organizations across industries are seeing more scams, authorized fraud, and good customers being manipulated, he says.

Organizations must learn and adapt quickly because attackers aren't wasting any time. Killeen recommends that organizations take a look at their existing controls to uncover vulnerable points and understand where the biggest losses are. Even if organizations stand up strong security at the front door, they could still fall victim to downstream risks.

"It's taking a risk-based approach, looking at things holistically, and how you prioritize those things accordingly, based on your vulnerabilities," Killeen advises.

Killeen and Lewis agree that attacks against customer relations warrants checking every door leading into the CRM. That includes every OAuth application, integration, guest or portal user, and API key.

"Revoke anything without a named owner," Lewis says. "Scope the rest. Repeat quarterly because they grow back."

He also recommends that organizations fix the help desk process attackers continually abuse, rather than people who work it. Scripted identity verification for resets, callback to a number of record, and manager approval for any privileged or MFA reset are ways to reduce risk in that area.

"Drop speed metrics, like average handle time, for identity-sensitive support interactions," Lewis adds. “They drive agents to prioritize speed over verification.”

Holding less customer data is another area organizations can prioritize to limit risks. Implement retention limits on customer records, purge dormant accounts, and don't include production customer data in sandboxes, Lewis recommends.

"Data you don't hold can't be stolen," he says.

Title: Exposed to PHP2Shell? Cyber Experts Weigh in With Advice
Context: Related:Claude Model Builds Exploits Across Major Browsers & OSes Using discoverable deployments on Shodan as a sample, Ox Security researchers found that more than 99% of...
Full Text:
New data shows that organizations aren't moving to patch PHP2Shell as fast as attackers are moving to exploit it. It's understandable, cybersecurity experts say, because updating in this case is especially complicated.

The data began trickling in on Oct. 21, painting a picture of the world's initial response to the new PHP vulnerabilities. The picture wasn't pretty.

Some well-positioned experts picked up on a remarkable volume of threat activity. Cloudflare CEO Matthew Prince stated that in the 10 hours before the vulnerabilities were publicly disclosed on Oct. 21, his company observed thousands of exploitation attempts. "That jumped to tens of thousands in the 45 minutes post announcement, hundreds of thousands within 2 hours, and millions now," he wrote on X, late on Oct. 21.

The next day, Check Point Research claimed that attempts at exploitation had already reached 10% of organizations worldwide. On the flip side, only a small percentage of vulnerable organizations have been visibly updating to new PHP releases.

Related:Claude Model Builds Exploits Across Major Browsers & OSes

Using discoverable deployments on Shodan as a sample, Ox Security researchers found that more than 99% of instances were not yet advertising a newly patched version 24 hours after fixed versions were made available. Researchers at Flare piled on, noting that 73% of those instances advertised PHP branches that no longer receive updates from the PHP Foundation. (It also qualified these figures, noting that basic Internet scanning misses some crucial nuances.)

Meanwhile, Cisco Talos estimated, based on open source intelligence (OSINT), that around half of all PHP systems won't receive patches.

On the morning of Oct. 23, Eastern time, Ox informed Dark Reading that its 99% figure had dropped to 97.5%. And Flare told Dark Reading that of the 27% of public records reflecting upstream-supported branches, about 5% have been updated.

Addressing PHP2Shell is often not as simple as clicking "Update," practitioners acknowledge. Still, there are steps that most organizations can take to protect themselves immediately, like diligently looking for PHP deployments across an organization's entire fleet of systems, hunting for signs of compromise, and restricting access to or otherwise taking offline any systems that can't be patched immediately.

Step 1: Find PHP, Everywhere

In principle, protecting against PHP2Shell should be simple. There are new versions one can update to, which cover the vulnerabilities in question, CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619. In practice, addressing PHP2Shell will look very different from one organization to the next, and require more or less effort, depending on how, where, and in what ways they use PHP.

Related:GhostAction Hacking Wave Fizzles, but Attackers Lurk on in GitHub

The unanimous first step all cybersecurity experts point to is that organizations should discover and inventory all of the assets they have running PHP. It's easier said than done. As the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) noted in an Oct. 21 security alert, PHP isn't just something that runs websites; it's "often a component of other software and prevalence may not be directly observable."

Flare researchers saw that firsthand when examining the attack surface. "What stood out to me during the research was how much PHP we found outside conventional web hosting," says Adrian Cheek, senior cybercrime researcher at Flare. "We identified it in storage devices, physical access-control systems, cameras and remote-access interfaces. If you're only looking at your main websites or limiting an external assessment to ports 80 and 443, you're going to miss some of that."

For organizations with this sort of exposure, he continues, "You generally can't log into a storage appliance or physical access-control unit and independently upgrade its PHP installation. You need the manufacturer to provide updated firmware. If the manufacturer has stopped supporting that product, the organization may have no patch available."

Related:In-the-Wild Attack Abuses AI Agents' Trust in Markdown

Not So Simple as Clicking "Update"

Putting edge cases aside, let's assume that an organization has managed to find and list out all of its PHP deployments. From there, remarkably, things only get more complicated.

Publicly available data seems to suggest that most PHP out in the world is running on old branches. "If you’re running an application built around PHP 5 or PHP 7, moving to a current PHP release could mean rewriting parts of the application, replacing dependencies, and testing everything that might break. There’s a good reason why organizations avoid doing that casually, particularly when the application supports something operationally important," Cheek explains.

In these cases, remediation will be a slow process, if organizations choose to pursue it at all. Luckily, and confusingly, old PHP versions aren't always unsavable.

The most common version in public records, 7.4.3, is what shipped with Ubuntu 20.04. As Cheek points out, "Linux distributions frequently retain an older PHP version number while backporting security fixes. So an old version number doesn't automatically mean the software hasn't been patched." Besides operating systems, applications can also backport fixes for the PHP they come packaged with.

Thus, organizations running outdated PHP actually fall into very distinct buckets: Some organizations will need to do the heavy lifting necessary to migrate or replace their applications or products. In the meantime, experts say, they should consider taking their vulnerable systems offline entirely. Cheek also offers one pro tip to mitigate CVE-2026-109619, for those that can reach the PHP configuration.

"The reported attacks run through PHP session upload progress, a feature that is on by default and needs no session_start call in the application. Disabling session.upload_progress.enabled and restarting the PHP workers blocks the confirmed session-upload-progress attack paths without requiring a PHP version upgrade," he explains, with the qualification that it doesn't address the other PHP2Shell flaw, CVE-2026-109618, so it's a temporary measure at best.

Some organizations will be privileged enough to install backported fixes through their vendors. On Oct. 21, Ubuntu developer Canonical published fixes for PHP2Shell for all versions since 14.04. Even these relieved parties will have more accounting work to do, since an OS or application update doesn't necessarily carry a full PHP version upgrade. If one takes advantage of Ubuntu's updates, future scans could continue to show it ostensibly running PHP 7.4.3.

And don't forget, Cheek says: "The restart matters. Installing a corrected PHP package doesn't necessarily replace the interpreter already loaded into running worker processes."

Each PHP2Shell Case Will Be Different

Besides all of the technical details, size will determine a lot about how organizations can respond to PHP2Shell.

As with any urgent cybersecurity vulnerability, small businesses may start off with disadvantages in awareness as well as the resources needed to get themselves cleaned up. Yet after 48 hours of working nonstop to help more than 1,000 organizations with PHP2Shell, OX Security CEO Neatsun Ziv is quicker to point out the advantages in being small. "

At small organizations, you can do whatever you want. You just go in and patch. You wait five hours. Nobody complains about breaking anything," he says.

But larger organizations are different, he says. "They've got a golden image — one server baseline they update," Ziv says. "It's always a downstream model: you deploy a new golden image, this golden image is then being built with new software, this new software goes to production, and nobody can change production. This is the norm in deployments today. Nobody goes to servers and actually patches them. It just becomes unmaintainable in the long term."

And that's to say nothing of just how many people from different teams need to be involved in major updates within a large organization; or of how major organizations run disproportionately significant systems that can't afford to break; or of how prevalent and varied PHP can be even within organizations. As Ziv notes, "Most of the organizations that we work with found hundreds of servers that are running PHP."

Check Point chief security and trust officer Alex Spokoiny adds that even beyond one's own house, organizations also face risk from how all of their suppliers handle PHP2Shell.

"The first step is to engage the relevant suppliers and understand how they are responding. Are they affected? What protections have they put in place? When do they expect remediation to be completed? If you cannot get clear or reasonable answers to those questions, that is itself something you need to factor into your risk assessment and potentially consider alternative options," he advises.

Organizations can also team up, to everyone's benefit. "For example, where technically possible, they may be able to extend their own Web application firewall (WAF) protection to applications operated by third parties, helping reduce exposure while the provider works toward a permanent fix," Spokoiny says.

Title: Inside the LiteLLM 1.107.0 supply chain compromise: Credential theft through Python startup hooks
Context: Attack overview LiteLLM is commonly deployed as a gateway between applications and model providers

References

Learn More

On October 21, 2026, a compromised LiteLLM 1.107.0 release was published to the Python Package Index (PyPI) and distributed through official container images. The malicious package added files that Python could execute during normal interpreter initialization. An application did not need to import LiteLLM for the payload to run: starting Python in an affected environment could be enough.

Microsoft analyzed two execution paths in the affected wheels: a credential collector launched through a path extension, and a Unix-oriented loader persisted through site-specific configuration. The collector targeted authentication material across developer tools, AI applications, cloud environments, browsers, and infrastructure. A separate database module attempted to read selected credential and model-configuration records from the LiteLLM proxy.

Endpoint observations on Windows and macOS matched the recovered collector’s discovery, encryption, and outbound-connection behavior. In one Windows example, a routine Python invocation to install an unrelated dependency activated the collector. This distinction matters for response: investigators should not start Python or pip inside a suspect environment to determine whether the malicious package is present.

This blog explains the startup mechanisms, the credentials the payload could reach, and the evidence defenders can use to investigate exposure. It also provides Microsoft Defender detection information, advanced hunting queries, and recovery guidance. Removing the package or a release tag is not sufficient recovery. Organizations must address the affected Python environment, any surviving processes, and credentials accessible to the compromised identity.

Attack overview

LiteLLM is commonly deployed as a gateway between applications and model providers. In that position it may have access to model-provider API keys, database connection strings, workload identities, routing configuration, and tenant policy data. The same package is also used on developer workstations, build agents, test systems, and containers, which widened the set of environments that could be exposed by the compromised release.

According to LiteLLM maintainers, stolen developer GitHub credentials were used to alter the release workflow and redirect it to the lookalike repository Berri-AI/litellm rather than the legitimate BerriAI/litellm repository. A credential associated with another developer account was then used to satisfy a production approval step. Microsoft has not independently determined how the attacker first accessed the upstream environment or obtained those credentials.

The compromised package used Python startup mechanisms to execute malicious code automatically, meaning exposure was not limited to systems actively using a LiteLLM gateway. Developer workstations, continuous integration and continuous delivery/deployment (CI/CD) agents, test environments, containers, and other systems that started Python with the affected package installed could also execute the payload. The malicious code supported credential collection and, on Unix-based systems, retrieval and execution of additional Python code.

Figure 1: Compromised LiteLLM 1.107.0 execution flow.

1. Compromised package distribution

The compromised LiteLLM 1.107.0 release delivered malicious Python startup files to environments where the package was installed.

2. Automatic payload execution

Python startup processing launched the credential collector without requiring the application to actively use LiteLLM gateway functionality.

3. Credential and sensitive-data collection

The collector targeted developer credentials, cloud credentials, browser data, SSH material, environment variables, and LiteLLM database data accessible to the affected process.

4. Encryption and exfiltration

Collected data was encrypted and transmitted to an attacker-controlled endpoint.

5. Conditional retrieval and execution of additional code

On Unix-based systems, the payload supported retrieving and executing additional Python code, although this activity was not confirmed.

Technical details

Compromised package distribution and automatic payload execution

The compromised wheel packaged cook.pth, cook.py, and sitecustomize.py under litellm-1.107.0.data/purelib/. During installation, these files were relocated into the Python environment’s library directory, outside the normal litellm application directory. This placement enabled execution through Python’s normal site initialization, which processes executable import statements in .pth files and later attempts to import the sitecustomize module.

The first execution path began with the single executable line in cook.pth: “import cook”. This loaded cook.py, whose wrapper Base64-decoded and zlib-decompressed an embedded Python program before executing the recovered source. The program identified itself as PRIVCOLLECT and performed credential collection in a daemon thread.

Figure 2. The executable .pth line imports cook, and the recovered collector starts a daemon thread after checking its inherited environment flag.

Before starting the thread, the collector checked the inherited PRIVCOLLECT_ACTIVE environment variable. A nonempty value caused it to return; otherwise, it set the flag, limiting duplicate collection in descendant processes. After an upload returned HTTP 200, it attempted to write /tmp/.pc_once_72129118c59f5636c0bb. These duplicate-suppression gates were not containment controls: startup alone did not prove collection or upload completed, because a short-lived process could exit before the thread finished, while write failures or temporary-storage changes could leave the marker absent.

Figure 3. Encode Cook.py file and decoded PRIVCOLLECT credential Stealer configuration.

A second startup mechanism used sitecustomize.py, providing a separate Unix-oriented execution path with an embedded collector and functionality to retrieve and execute additional Python code from a remote host. Remote retrieval and execution through this path were not confirmed.

Together, these mechanisms extended potential exposure beyond active LiteLLM deployments: simply starting Python in an affected environment could activate the malicious code, even when LiteLLM itself was never imported. Because the startup files resided outside the litellm application directory, removing only the application files could leave the malicious startup components behind.

Credential and sensitive-data collection

The recovered collector was designed to gather sensitive authentication material across developer tools, AI applications, cloud environments, browsers, and infrastructure. It runs multiple collection modules sequentially with independent error handling, allowing collection to continue even when individual targets are unavailable or inaccessible.

Target

Recovered collection behavior

Developer and AI tools

Reads selected authentication and configuration files for AI assistants, integrated development environments (IDEs) , GitHub Copilot, VS Code, and MCP integrations. Collects fixed paths and top-level JSON files in selected tool directories under a collection budget.

Source control and package ecosystems

Searches Git credentials, package-manager configuration, selected dotenv files, and private-key extensions. Shallow directory walks and file-size limits constrain these searches.

Cloud and workload credentials

Reads AWS, Azure CLI, and Google Cloud configuration or credential caches; Kubernetes service-account files; Docker configuration; and mounted secrets. It also attempts AWS and GCP metadata credential retrieval.

Browsers and user histories

Accesses Chromium-family and Firefox credential-related data and browsing history, plus shell, database-client, and interactive-tool histories. Password decryption is platform- and format-dependent.

Process environments

Collects its own environment and, on Linux, other process environments readable through procfs. This can expose secrets beyond variables explicitly configured for the LiteLLM process.

Private keys and infrastructure

Targets readable Secure Shell (SSH) material and selected GNU Privacy Guard (GPG), Transport Layor Security (TLS), CI/CD, Vault, and infrastructure-tool configuration. A target appearing in the code does not establish successful access.

LiteLLM proxy data

When its prerequisites are satisfied, starts a Python child using Prisma to read selected fields from two proxy database tables, with a 500-row limit for each query

Encryption and exfiltration

After collection, the payload serializes module results and host metadata as JSON. Each run generates a 32-byte AES key and a 16-byte initialization vector. AES-256-CBC encrypts the collection document; an embedded 4,096-bit RSA public key wraps the AES key using OAEP. The OpenSSL path tries SHA-256 and then SHA-1 for OAEP, and the resulting metadata records the selected digest.

Figure 4. The collector generates a fresh AES key and IV, wraps the key with RSA, and packages the encrypted collection in a gzip tar archive before attempting upload. Selected code excerpts are wrapped for readability.

The collector places three members in a gzip-compressed tar archive: data.bin, containing the initialization vector (IV) and encrypted collection; key.bin, containing the wrapped AES key; and hdr.json, containing plaintext envelope metadata. It then attempts an HTTP POST to hxxp://www[.]litellm[.]dev/healthcheck, using application/octet-stream, a fixed browser-like User-Agent, and a body checksum in an X-SHA256 header. The upload routine retries and treats only HTTP 200 as success.

The OpenSSL backend creates temporary directories beginning with .pc_e_, stages input and output files and removes them after use.

Conditional retrieval and execution of additional code

In addition to the credential collector, the compromised package contained a separate Unix-oriented loader in sitecustomize.py, designed to retrieve and execute additional Python code. When Python starts, the loader takes an exclusive lock on /tmp/remote_code_loader.lock so that only one instance runs per host and detaches into the background. Each cycle reads a GitHub-hosted domain.txt file, which acts as a mutable pointer to an attacker-controlled server.

Figure 5. The remote-loader path checks the pointer and DNS before retrieving code, then compiles and executes the response without a content-signature check.

If a valid server address is returned and successfully resolved, the loader is designed to request /codepy from that server, compile the returned content, and execute it as Python code within the affected environment. This gives the attacker a mechanism to change the second-stage payload without publishing another compromised LiteLLM package. This loader is separate from the credential collector delivered directly in the compromised package.

At the time the cited researchers examined domain.txt, it was empty and no second-stage retrieval or execution was confirmed. Because the file could be changed, the loader remained a re-armable remote-code execution mechanism.

Mitigation and protection guidance

Microsoft recommends the following actions for organizations that installed, mirrored, or built images with LiteLLM 1.107.0:

Find and contain every affected copy. Identify LiteLLM 1.107.0 across installed environments, uv and pip caches, internal package mirrors, lock files, build outputs, and container images. Scope mutable container tags and the relevant exposure windows once validated and compare artifacts with the customer-ready hashes in the indicators of compromise section. For background, see secure software supply chain practices and Docker image digests. Digests are preferable to mutable tags because they identify immutable image content.

Prevent Python execution and investigate from outside the environment. Isolate affected developer workstations, build agents, test systems, containers, and AI gateway hosts. Where operationally safe, stop running Python processes and prevent automation from restarting them. Do not run python, pip, or other commands that invoke the affected interpreter during evidence collection; inspect the environment with trusted tools from a known-clean system. Python normally processes site configuration, including executable import lines in .pth files, during initialization.

Rebuild from verified artifacts. Confirm that cook.pth, cook.py, and sitecustomize.py were removed from the environment library path. Rebuilding is more reliable than assuming that deleting the litellm directory cleaned the top-level startup files.

Rotate reachable credentials from a known-clean machine. Include model-provider keys, cloud and workload credentials, CI/CD secrets, source-control and registry tokens, SSH and GPG keys, AI coding-tool tokens, and browser sessions available to the affected identity. On proxy hosts, include stored provider credentials and DATABASE_URL. Revoke affected identity sessions rather than assuming password or key rotation immediately invalidates every active token or application session. See revoke user access in Microsoft Entra ID.

Correlate before declaring compromise. Combine file hashes, Python process ancestry, .pc_e_ cryptographic staging, network destination, workload identity, and subsequent cloud or identity use. Do not use package presence or a generic filename as the sole verdict.

Strengthen dependency controls. Use hash-pinned lock files, verify package and image provenance, use container digests instead of floating tags, and admit packages to internal mirrors only after review. See best practices for a secure software supply chain and dependency scanning in Azure DevOps.

Restrict outbound access. Developer workstations, build agents, test systems, containers, and AI gateway hosts should not have unrestricted outbound HTTP access unless required. Route outbound traffic through managed egress controls, deny unnecessary destinations, and allowlist required services. See control outbound internet access from Azure.

Enable Microsoft Defender for Endpoint protections. Onboard supported developer workstations, build agents, and AI gateway servers to Microsoft Defender for Endpoint, and enable Microsoft Defender Antivirus real-time and cloud-delivered protection where supported. See configure always-on protection and configure cloud protection.
